# TO THE MOST SERENE AND ILLUSTRIOUS
## Prince, Lord Otto Henry, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of both Bavarias, and most invincible Elector of the Holy Roman Empire; Lorenzo Ventura, citizen of Venice and Doctor of Arts, wishes happiness.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'M' depicting a winged dragon or serpentine creature intertwined with elaborate foliate scrolls.</image-desc>

MANY things, O most excellent Prince, compel men toward the study of the liberal arts <term>liberal arts (bonarum artium): the traditional academic subjects of the Renaissance, which for Ventura includes the "higher" art of alchemy</term>, but four—to omit the rest—are the most powerful. These present themselves to me of their own accord, enticing upright men to seek them out; in this glorious contest of the wrestling-ground <note>original: "palaestrae"; a Greek-derived term used here metaphorically for intellectual or spiritual struggle and training</note>, they almost entirely remove the heavy burden of labors and firmly promise the reward of victory. The first of these, I say, is that natural [desire] for knowing—

### EPISTOLA

*...[all] things <note>Continuing from the previous page: "the natural desire for knowing all things"</note> given to all by God, best and greatest; second, the sought-after summit of praise and honor; third, the expulsion of idleness—which is like a grave for the living and a fuel for vices; and finally, the acquisition of a good and blessed life. Truly all these things, for many years now, have bound me with a most fervent love to the more secret decrees of nature and to the knowledge of the medical art. And finally, for that higher discipline—whether of the hidden stone <term>hidden stone (lapis occultus): a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone</term> or of the "lesser world" <note>original: "minoris mundi"; the concept of the microcosm, the idea that the human body and soul represent a miniature version of the entire universe</note> (to use Aristotle's phrase)—they have destined me, like a second Sisyphus <note>Sisyphus: a figure from Greek mythology condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever; Ventura uses this to describe the grueling, repetitive labor of alchemical experimentation</note>, to so vast a task. This is so even though I have very often been hidden and tossed about in the midst of the waves without a Delian swimmer <note>original: "natatore Delio"; an allusion to the "Delian diver," a term used in antiquity for someone capable of understanding the "deep" and obscure writings of the philosopher Heraclitus</note>. In this state, although I was weary of both a difficult life and death at the same time, it was not permitted to proceed further; yet the bitterness of the hostile storm, and the fear and losses that followed, did not permit me to return. And so, dashed against the rocks, I was dreadfully oppressed. But behold, under a faint light,*

...[followed] <note>Continuing from the previous page: "...the bitterness of the hostile storm, and the fear and losses that followed"</note> among so many monsters of beasts, you, most Serene Prince <note>original: "princeps Serenissime"; a formal title for high-ranking nobility, specifically Elector Otto Henry</note>, encountered me. You fortified me with the strength of the steady hope found in your letters. 

What was I to do with such a Leader going before me? My strength restored, and prepared to endure even heavier trials, I manfully girded myself for the burden placed upon me. I traveled abroad to Italy and France, and now the fourth year is passing; from those places, I have collected two hundred and fifty of the most fortunate handwritten volumes of this art <note>The "art" refers to the alchemical and medical studies mentioned previously</note>—God is my witness to the great expense, loss, and sweat it took to acquire them. # THE PRINTER TO THE
## Gentle Reader, Greetings. <note>original: "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting wishing the reader health or prosperity.</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'Q' depicting a figure (possibly a philosopher or naturalist) kneeling in a garden or natural landscape, observing or tending to something on the ground. The scene is enclosed within the circular body of the letter 'Q', which is further set within a square decorative border with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

Those who are wounded by scorpions, most kind Reader, seek a remedy from them: for Nature was indeed so provident that she created the foundations of help in the very things from which the danger of poison threatened. Nor indeed will you find this to be true in only one matter, but in many: if not in exactly the same way, then at least by a certain proportion. For it is the common opinion of all <term>natural philosophers (physicorum): those who study the physical laws of the natural world</term> who have committed anything memorable about the nature of things to written records, that in this "theater of the universe," the generation of all things, as well as their corruption <note>The Aristotelian concept that for something to be born or created, something else must be destroyed or changed.</note>, has its origin in opposites. Thus, it is manifest from this that the first and principal causes by which any natural thing is produced <note>original: "geratur," literally "carried out" or "conducted"</note> are the same ones which cause it finally to be dissolved and perish. And indeed, regarding that matter, which concerns the nature of all [natu-] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "naturalium" (natural) on the next page.</note>

<summary>In this preface, the printer introduces the reader to the paradoxical laws of nature, where remedies are found within the source of the harm and where the forces of creation and destruction are one and the same.</summary>
<keywords>natural philosophy, generation and corruption, nature, opposites, scorpions, alchemy, printer's preface</keywords>

praised by their praises, is in actual fact and by its very nature most useful to the human race: it is established by certain universal precepts, illustrated by particular examples, and through it, many noble and most health-giving <term>medicines (medicamenta)</term> can thereafter be prepared: namely, by those who observe the true method in their actions, which they have previously acquired for themselves from the study of **philosophy**. On the contrary, however, if it should fall into the hands of those who, being ignorant of all good discipline, nevertheless claim knowledge for themselves: while the art, for the sake of avenging itself, turns the practitioners themselves into <term>charcoal-burners (carbonarios)</term> <note>A derogatory term for "puffers"—unskilled pseudo-alchemists who focused only on the heat of the furnace and bellows without understanding the science, often ending up covered in soot and bankrupt.</note> instead of philosophers, the art itself is thereafter also despised as if it were some vile mechanical craft. Since these things are so, I believe that remedies must be sought from the same sources that gave birth to the cause of the disease. This will indeed happen if, setting aside the trifles about which the <term>Agyrtae</term> <note>original: "Agyrtæ"; an ancient term for wandering charlatans or quacks who cheated the public with superstitions and fake cures.</note> boast, the art itself is restored to its true uses. For we have determined to gather all the best authors who have written concerning the **chemical**...

# THAT THE ART OF ALCHEMY IS TRUE.

## CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial 'M' depicting figures in a classical or mythological landscape with trees and foliage.</image-desc>

Many hold the opinion that the art of Alchemy is not a true art: they are moved toward this conclusion by two fundamental arguments. First, because Aristotle says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*: "Let the practitioners <note>original: "artifices"; referring to the craftsmen or alchemists themselves.</note> of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot be transmuted." Second, because they see all those laboring in this art making nothing but deceptive <note>original: "sophisticas"; refers to "sophistical" or false imitations that look like gold but do not possess its inner properties.</note> transmutations, and no one making true ones: for which reason they think and believe that, since they see it done by no one, it truly and realistically can be done by no one at all.
<margin>J d</margin>
But neither of these arguments compels us to believe that this most precious and excellent art is not true. For the first argument of our adversaries is not valid: because it is indeed true, as the philosopher Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemist frequently cited in medieval European texts.</note> and the *Rosarius Major* <note>The "Greater Rosary," an influential alchemical manuscript often attributed to Arnald of Villanova.</note> say; namely, that the *species* of things are not transmuted, but certainly the *individuals* of certain species can be transmuted into one another. 
<margin>A 1011</margin>
And this is evident to the eye, especially in those things that share a common correspondence <note>original: "symbolum"; in this context, it refers to shared qualities or "sympathies" between different substances.</note> with one another in one or two qualities, as is established in the elements; and thus stone is made from earth, and from li-

<summary>This page opens the treatise by defending alchemy against critics who cite Aristotle's claim that metals cannot change their nature. The author argues that while the abstract "species" of a metal remains fixed, individual pieces of matter can indeed be transformed if they share common elemental qualities.</summary>

<keywords>alchemy, transmutation of metals, Aristotle, Alphidius, Rosarius Major, elemental theory, scholastic philosophy</keywords>

-># CONCERNING THE STONE<-

...wood comes ash, and from ash and stones, glass, etc.
So also it happens in metals: because all metals share in one matter, which is quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; often regarded by alchemists as the "mother" or passive principle of all metals.</term> with its sulfur <term>sulfur: regarded as the "father" or active, combustible principle of metals.</term>. And metals differ only through a greater or lesser digestion <note>In alchemy, digestion refers to the process of maturing a substance through gentle, consistent heat, much like food in a stomach.</note>, which occurs through the maturation of their sulfur, by means of decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or change its state.</note>.

For sulfur is the form of metals, and especially of gold: not indeed the common sulfur of the masses, but altered sulfur, as Master Bonus the philosopher <note>Referring to Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century physician and influential alchemical writer.</note> says. From these words it is gathered, that if by art a medicine <note>The "medicine" is another term for the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, which "cures" base metals of their impurities to make them gold.</note> can be made, which has within itself the power and property of the aforesaid altered mineral sulfur, such a medicine made by art will be able to transform imperfect metals and quicksilver into the nature of perfect ones.

On account of which John Scotus <note>Likely referring to the famous medieval theologian John Duns Scotus, to whom several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed in the later Middle Ages.</note> and many other philosophers say, and grant it to be true, that metals cannot be transmuted in any way or by any ingenuity, unless they are first reduced to their primary matter <term>primary matter: *materia prima*; the original, formless substance from which all material things are created.</term>. However, the primary matter of all metals is quicksilver and sulfur—not indeed in their [raw] nature, but altered, that is, converted into a vapor.

<margin>Note</margin>
And thus the primary matter of metals is a moist, oily vapor, containing within itself the nature of both: namely, of sulfur and of quicksilver. From these things it therefore necessarily follows, that if by art such an oily vapor can be extracted...

<summary>This page argues that all metals share a common "primary matter" consisting of specialized sulfur and mercury, and that alchemy works by reducing metals to this vaporous state to "mature" them into gold.</summary>

...[extracted] from those things in which it is found, and is discovered to be very similar to that which generates metals within the mines of the earth, a medicine <note>The "medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, which was thought to "cure" base metals of their impurities to turn them into gold.</note> can be prepared. This medicine, when cast upon <note>original: "proiecta"; "projection" was the final step of the alchemical Great Work, where the Elixir was thrown into a crucible of molten base metal.</note> simple, imperfect bodies and upon quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; often called 'argentum vivum' in Latin.</term>, transforms them into a true and perfect metallic body, even more perfect than any produced by nature. But it must be understood *that this medicine* is extracted more easily and abundantly from some substances, while from others it is extracted with more difficulty and less perfectly, whether these be the metals themselves or any other things whatsoever. However, this cannot happen unless such things are first broken down through putrefaction <note>Putrefaction was considered the essential first stage of the alchemical process, where the matter "died" or decayed to allow for a new, nobler form to emerge.</note>, and through proper boiling and long digestion <note>In alchemy, digestion refers to the process of maturing a substance through consistent, gentle heat.</note>, they acquire a new and nobler form.

The second foundation also, by which they argue against our art, is not compelling. Our reasoning is as <term>Geber</term> <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan. However, the *Summa Perfectionis* cited here is a 13th-century text likely written by a European monk now called "Pseudo-Geber."</note> says in his <term>Summa of Great Perfection</term> <note>original: "Summa magnæ perfectionis"; this was the most influential alchemical textbook of the late Middle Ages.</note> in Chapter 11, in which he handles the refutation of those arguments that simply deny the art. His point is this: the opponent's method of arguing carries no logical necessity. One who looks only at a few details is pressured into believing this art is not true; because by using analogies, or by arguing from a greater premise to a lesser one, he merely reinforces his own fantasy and error. In these arguments, there is no absolute necessity, but only a likelihood of how things happen in most cases. Furthermore, it is certain in our own times that very few philosophers are found who truly know the secrets of nature; indeed, they neglect to even seek or understand them.

It also begins a defense of alchemy against skeptics, citing Geber's view that critics rely on faulty logic and a lack of deep natural knowledge.</summary>

<margin>
...of them
Delta Omega <note>These Greek letters—the triangle for Delta and the final letter Omega—often carried symbolic weight in hermetic texts, representing the beginning and end, or the elements.</note>
</margin>

...therefore, through proper operations, they do not know how to improve and perfect imperfect things: and they are often ignorant [of how] to discern the suitable from the unsuitable, and things that are near <note>original: "propinquas"; refers to substances chemically or spiritually "close" to the desired gold.</note> from those that are remote. And because of this, many wander and act foolishly. However, the ancient philosophers were of a higher intellect and more diligent in their working. For, as Lodovico Lazzarelli <note>Lodovico Lazzarelli (1440–1500) was an Italian poet and hermetic philosopher who believed in the spiritual transformation of man alongside alchemy.</note> says: "Philosophers, for the sake of knowing the deep secrets of nature, sometimes dared to enter caves and dwell in forests and mountains, so that with skillful intellect they might examine the stars, what powers they have, and which places of the earth are suitable for metals, what the materials are, and what difference exists between them." And therefore, for their own benefit and that of their sons <note>In alchemical literature, "sons" or "sons of art" refers to initiated students and future practitioners, rather than biological offspring.</note>, this divine mastery <term>magisterium: the 'Mastery' or 'Great Work,' the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term> was discovered through their long investigation, because only philosophers and their sons understand the power of nature and are not ignorant of its disposition. 

Since, therefore, many great philosophers assert that this transmutatory art <note>The art of alchemy, specifically the changing of base metals into gold or silver.</note> can be performed, and have left many books in writing behind them, it is unjust and foolish to deny that the art itself is true, even if [at first] no reason or <gloss>experiment</gloss> <note>original: "experientia"; in this period, experience and experiment were often used interchangeably to mean knowledge gained through practice.</note> attests to and confirms it. Therefore Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> said well: that there is a great distance between the wise and the foolish, and between the blind and the seeing; and the same judgment applies between the one who works poorly and the one who is ignorant. It is concluded, therefore, from these things, that this art is true.

a 3

### That not all who believe the art to be true know how to use it, and how to work according to it.

### CHAPTER II.

There are indeed those who firmly believe this most noble art <note>The "noble art" refers to alchemy, the pursuit of transmuting base metals into gold and seeking spiritual perfection.</note> is true, but they have not attempted to discover whether it is true through experience, nor do they know how to prove it. Some among them believe in whatever weak way they can, and likely consent and adhere to the truth either because of the sheer number of sayings or the greatness of the authors, yet they yield when they are confronted by the struggle of the work.

There is, however, one thing that easily draws all men to belief: namely, the desire for possession and the greed for pleasures. For pleasure alone makes men most intensely desirous. For as the same philosopher Lodovico Lazzarelli says: "Men devoted to earthly delights desire earthly delights above all things, and to obtain them, they overlook no work or labor," following that saying of Virgil, the distinguished poet <note>original: "vatis eximij"; the term "vates" implies both a poet and a prophet, reflecting the high esteem in which Virgil was held.</note>:

> To what do you not drive mortal hearts,
> O cursed hunger for gold! <note>original: "Quid non mortalia pectora cogis / Auri sacra fames." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 3.</note>

Therefore, because all men seek delights, and so that they might be able to live as well and as happily as possible, and since almost all the delights of this world can be obtained primarily through riches—according to that common adage: All things obey money <note>original: "Pecuniæ obediunt [omnia]." A common Latin proverb derived from Ecclesiastes, often used in alchemical texts to explain why people are drawn to the art for the wrong reasons.</note>—

<summary>This page argues that many people believe in alchemy for the wrong reasons—specifically greed and the desire for worldly pleasure—and lack the practical skill or perseverance to actually perform the Great Work.</summary>

-> DE LAPIDE <-
<note>original: "DE LAPIDE"; translated as "On the Stone," referring to the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

...all things: and the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"; in medieval texts, this almost always refers to Aristotle.</note> says in the fifth book of his *Ethics*: money was invented for this purpose, that it might be as it were a guarantor of having, in exchange for it, whatever a person might desire. Moreover, the greatest riches are promised through the mastery of this art, namely true gold and true silver, and both in great quantity without much labor, from which coins might be shaped, through which all things may be possessed: therefore, men—both the learned and the unlearned—easily believe, and through testing they desire it, and through testing they seek to acquire it.

There are, however, few who reach the truth of the art through their labor, the primary cause of which was explained previously—namely, ignorance of secrets and negligence in study. There is also a specific twofold reason for this difficulty: the first is **metaphorical speech**.

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to both medicine and alchemy in Europe.</note> says: "I have considered the books of those who affirm the art, and I found them empty of the reasons or logical arguments that are found in every [other] art; and I found that most of what is contained in them is similar to 'alienation'—that is, metaphors or allegories. But when I brought myself back to natural principles, I then recognized that the art was true."

The second reason is the **mixing of false things with true**; hence Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Testament*: "The Philosophers have placed a twofold manner in their books. One true and the other false; the true, however, is expressed through obscure words, so that they cannot be understood except by the <term>sons of doctrine</term> <note>original: "filijs doctrinæ"; a term for initiated students or those worthy of spiritual and scientific secrets.</note>, lest the way of acting [be revealed] to the wicked..."

<summary>This page explains that while alchemy promises the wealth necessary to fulfill all human desires, its truths are hidden from most people through the use of complex metaphors and the intentional mixing of truth with falsehood to protect secrets from the "wicked."</summary>

These were considered the two fundamental "parents" of all metals in medieval alchemy.</note>—do not remain under that form in which they existed in their first mixture; instead, they act and suffer upon one another continually <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept of change, where an active principle (sulfur/heat) works upon a passive principle (mercury/moisture).</note> until the form of the metal is generated from them. 

And first, indeed, the form of an **imperfect metal** is generated, in which the sulfur (which is the active agent) is not yet fully separated from its matter (which is the quicksilver). This is demonstrated by the dross and combustibility <note>Imperfect metals like lead or tin were thought to be "burnt" or corrupted by excess, impure sulfur.</note> of those same metals. But if the **digestion** <note>Original: *digestio*, the process of slow, natural maturation within the earth or the alchemist's vessel.</note> continues until the very end—that is, until the agent is totally separated from the matter—then a new form is generated, which is the form of **gold**. This is the ultimate and most perfect form, and the one principally intended by nature. 

And these minerals are composed of their elements. Indeed, they are composed of elements in determined quantities and measures, known to nature but entirely unknown to us, mixed together from the beginning in one mineral place, in which the **celestial virtue** <note>Original: *virtus cælestis*, the invisible influence of the stars and planets believed to direct the growth of minerals underground.</note> is preserved. Hence, nature mixes the two aforementioned principles from the start in certain measures...

In alchemy, "digestion" refers to a slow, gentle heating process, likened to the way a stomach matures food, which "ripens" the metal.</note>, the pure and digested portion is separated from its pollutions and dross; it is then perfected into a **metal**. The more complete the digestion, the less impurity the metal contains. 

When the digestion is finished, the **active form** <note>Original: *forma agens*. In the philosophy of the time, the "form" is the active, organizing principle that gives a substance its specific identity, while "matter" is the passive stuff it works upon.</note>—which is **sulfur**—is totally separated from the matter of the **quicksilver** <note>Original: *argentum vivum* (mercury).</note>. This is because, from the start, sulfur is external to the quicksilver and contrary to its nature. Therefore, it does not enter into its substance as part of its matter, but only acts upon the quicksilver itself as upon a thing suited to be acted upon. Thus, having been changed itself, it changes the quicksilver through digestion, separating the pure from the impure. 

In this way, after a long digestion, it prepares the matter by its own power for the most noble state of simplicity. Finally, it draws out from the potential of the matter a new form, which establishes it as a different species than it was before. For this reason, the form of the metal itself—especially that of **gold** <note>Original: *auri*.</note>—can no longer be called "sulfur." Although it is a substance in the sense that it is the principal part of the substantial whole, it should not be called its "matter" <margin>other</margin>. It does not possess the same way of being <margin>ways</margin> within the finished compound as it did when it was outside of it. This is proven by its power; for although it becomes similar in part <margin>partly not</margin>, it is nevertheless of a far different nature, possessing a more excellent and distinct power, or...

Because sulfur is found in the manifest <note>In alchemical philosophy, the "manifest" is the outward, physical appearance of a substance, while the "occult" or "hidden" is its internal, potential essence.</note> appearance, but quicksilver is in the hidden interior—specifically when it is sublimated to the whiteness of snow—seekers ought to exhaust themselves with anxiety and labor in investigating, reasoning, and frequently experimenting to gain knowledge of this hidden matter which exists within arsenic.

We call "hidden" that which exists in the thing potentially and is understood by the intellect first; but we call "manifest" that which is first understood by the senses and exists actually in the thing itself. 

Therefore the Philosophers—namely **Hermes**, **Geber**, **Avicenna**, and **Rhazes** <note>These represent the foundational authorities of alchemy: Hermes Trismegistus (the mythical founder), Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), Avicenna (Ibn Sina), and Rhazes (al-Razi).</note>—said it possesses the nature of sulfur rather than that of quicksilver, although quicksilver greatly predominates in its composition. They did this to hide, as much as they could, the greatest secret that lies within it. And for this reason, they said nothing clearly about the nature of the quicksilver existing within it, except from a distance and as if disparaging it. 

Thus **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "Orpiment turns copper <note>original: *æs*; this can refer to copper, bronze, or brass.</note> white, although it corrupts the copper somewhat; to heal this corruption is the work of a wise man." PHILOSOPHY.
<sig>b 4</sig>

### That the philosophers have hidden this stone and its governance.

### CHAPTER V

The philosophers have hidden this precious stone in two ways. First, by speaking of it through **allegory** <note>original: *sub allegoria*; a common device in alchemical literature where chemical processes are described as myths or stories to hide them from the uninitiated.</note>; hence **Morienus** says in the *Castrensi* <note>original: *Morienus in Castrensi*; likely referring to the *Liber de compositione alchemiae*, a foundational text attributed to the hermit Morienus.</note>: There are books concerning this science composed in figures, the greater part of which is very obscure and so bound up in complex sentences that they cannot be understood except by their own authors. For this reason, they have called the stone by many names which do not correspond to the terms used among common people; yet they kept its own proper name—the one by which it is known to the common folk—a secret. Even if they sometimes call it by its proper name, they always add something to it so that it might distract even the intelligent, lest it be recognized, as the *Lilium* <note>original: *Lilium*; likely the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae* or "The Lily of Intelligence."</note> says.

Second, they devise various operations and weights <note>original: *pondera*; the specific proportions or measurements used in a recipe.</note>. Hence it is said in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>: Philosophers propose many things, none of which they actually do. They do this for two reasons. First, so that they might make the practitioner <term>artificem; the "artist" or alchemist performing the work</term> intelligent, diligent, and cautious in his operation. For it is necessary that the practitioner who reads their books should not only pay attention to the literal text <note>original: *literae*</note>, but consider the very natures of things. Indeed, everyone knows that if imperfect metals are to be perfected, it is necessary that they be perfected by **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: *sulphure et argento vivo*; the two primary principles in alchemical theory thought to be the "parents" of all metals.</note>; but not everyone knows that...

Just as, therefore, the two spirits of nature—namely, **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: argentum viuum; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>—are bodies in potentiality, because they are the starting points of metallic bodies, and vice versa both materially and formally, as is clear by the evidence of one's own eyes in the mines.

### ON THE STONE ###

...such **spirits** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances—most commonly sulfur, mercury, arsenic, and ammonia—that can be "fixed" or made solid through chemical processes.</note> through suitable **digestion** <note>original: digestionem; here referring to the slow, steady application of heat over time, similar to how food is broken down or how a chick develops in an egg.</note> receive the property, nature, and essence of a **body**, and are fixed by themselves alone. Therefore, the **Art** also creates a fixed **elixir** <note>term: elixir; from the Arabic *al-iksir*, referring to the medicinal powder or potion capable of transforming base metals into gold.</note> from spirits alone upon its own fire. And just as mineral spirits are not of the common sort, but are altered <note>meaning they have been refined or processed by the earth’s natural heat.</note>, so also are the spirits of the Art.

And just as nature makes bodies in actuality from spirits alone—namely, from those spirits which are bodies in potentiality—so also should the Art do. And just as nature mixes nothing else with its own principles, because it would hinder generation, so also does the Art.

And just as nature has two principles—one which holds the nature of the **agent** <note>the active, masculine principle, usually associated with sulfur.</note>, and another which holds the nature of the **matter**, or the **patient** <note>the passive, feminine principle, usually associated with mercury.</note>—so also does the Art. And just as nature composes these principles together in certain measures and determined weights, so also should the Art compose them; but the Art cannot know the required weights by itself: therefore it is necessary that, like a **handmaid** <note>original: ancilla; a common alchemical trope where "Art" or the alchemist is the servant who follows the footprints of Nature.</note>, it receives such things already composed by nature. There will be, therefore, one matter weighted by nature in which the Art must work, and that is sufficient.

From which it is concluded that it is necessarily required that all the qualities <note>original: differentiæ; the specific "differences" or characteristics that define a substance.</note> which are in mineral **gold** in actuality must also be in the **Stone** and in the **Elixir** in potentiality. These qualities are manifested in the gold that is made by the Elixir in actuality: namely, that it becomes heaviest, most yellow, most brilliant, unaffected by burning things <note>meaning it resists oxidation and does not "burn away" in the furnace.</note>, most tempered, and most medicinal.

From all these things, it is further concluded:

These principles are three: namely, **quicksilver** <note>original: argentum vivum</note> and **sulfur** that have been altered and combined by nature in the due measure; the digesting mineral heat; and the power of the place (which is the principle of generation) impressed by the celestial bodies.

Each of these induces diversity by itself in the bodies being generated, but all of them together do so even more. From the first follows the diversity of elements—or rather of **elementated things** <term>elementatorum; substances already formed from the four primary elements which then act as building blocks for more complex matter</term>—from which metals are generated. From the second comes the diversity of perfections: because through different **digestion** <term>digestio; the natural maturation or "cooking" of minerals in the earth's heat over long periods</term>, purer or more impure elements of metals are generated and mixed; once mixed, they take on their specific properties. From the third principle, indeed, the different species of minerals are procreated. But if the digestion is continued to the very end—until the agent is totally separated from the matter—then a new form is generated: that of the perfect metal, which is the **form of gold**.

From this, it is evident that all minerals are composed of their elements in specific quantities and mixed measures. In this mixture, one part is neither prior to nor later than the other; rather, the generation of the simple elements and the compound happens all at once. This is just as it occurs in the generation of **milk**, which is composed of three substances: **curds** <note>original: caseo; literally "cheese"</note>, **butter**, and **whey**. The generation of these three parts occurs simultaneously with the milk itself.

From these points, it is concluded that since metals are composed only of two things—namely quicksilver and sulfur—
<margin>^ because + whence</margin>
and likewise their ores are so composed, and because **Art** <note>human skill or alchemy</note> must imitate nature, it is entirely necessary that Art proceeds from these same principles (or similar ones) used by nature for the generation of the **elixir** <term>elyxir; the substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term>, and that Art observes the same weights. From this, it is clear that those who work with sulfur alone labor in vain. First, indeed, because...

### CHAPTER 10. <insert>/</insert> I

## CONCERNING THE STONE

...then the quicksilver is coagulated into **Arsenic** by "dry water" <term>Dry water: Latin *aqua sicca*, an alchemical paradox referring to a substance that behaves like a fluid in reactions but does not wet the hands, often identified with purified mercury</term>. Thus, therefore, Master **Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century alchemist known for his work *Margarita Pretiosa Novella*</note> calls the stone **Arsenic**, so that it may be understood—namely, that both natures are united in it within a third nature, which is neither the **common sulfur** nor the **common quicksilver** <term>Common sulfur/quicksilver: The "vulgar" or everyday versions of these elements, as opposed to the "philosophical" versions required for alchemy</term>. Rather, it is a single thing possessing the powers and properties of both. 

It is also called this so that it may be understood that in the **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again, used here to purify the Stone</term> of our stone, one proceeds first to the **whiteness** <term>Whiteness: Latin *albedo*, the second major stage of the alchemical process, signaling purity</term>; in whose "belly" the true and perfect **redness** <term>Redness: Latin *rubedo*, the final stage of the Great Work, representing the attainment of the Stone</term> lies hidden. 

Whence **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a semi-legendary 7th-century hermit and teacher of the prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: "Know that sulfur and *Arzenech* <note>original: *Arzenech*, a variant spelling of Arsenic</note>—that is, the **pigment of gold** <term>Pigment of gold: Latin *auri pigmentum*, known today as orpiment, a yellow arsenic mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>—are burned, and are quickly consumed by that burning. How then do you expect, or wish to expect [the Stone], from that which is quickly consumed by the burning of fire and reduced to charcoal?" etc. 

Explaining this statement, Master Bonus says: That considering **Arsenic** as it is produced by nature, it is entirely burned, because the combustible sulfur is never separated from its other parts, but all vanish together. Similarly, even in the **lesser work** <term>Lesser work: Latin *minor opus*, the process of creating the White Elixir which transmutes base metals into silver</term>, if it is fixed in such a way, it never "enters" <note>In alchemy, "entering" or "ingression" refers to the Stone's ability to penetrate and transform a base metal</note> the metal. But considering its **hidden nature**, which is of the nature of gold, it is not thus burned; for its hidden parts are separated from the sulfurous ones by the most profound ingenuity. And therefore it seems that Morienus spoke in allegory, just as he and other philosophers have always been accustomed to do.

### CONCERNING THE STONE ###

The observation is beautiful: because every thing that can be generated and corrupted possesses its own contrary <margin>within itself</margin> within itself in potential, which can be brought into actuality without the presence or mixture of an external contrary. In this way, that which was **fixed** <note>original: *fixum*. In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand fire without evaporating</note> in potential, having been reduced to a **non-fixed** <note>original: *non fixum*. Referring to a "volatile" state that evaporates or changes easily</note> state in actuality, retains that non-fixed state. Wherefore **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father of chemistry."</note> says: If the total of the **volatile** <note>The gaseous or spiritual aspect of the matter</note> overcomes the total of the fixed, it will fly away with it; but if the total of the fixed overcomes the total of the volatile, it will be **fixed** <note>Stabilized into a solid</note> together with it. It is clear, however, that the fixed overcoming the volatile completes the work; but the volatile overcoming the fixed ruins and annihilates the work.

Wherefore in the **Turba** <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> it is said: Stir up a war between **copper** <note>original: *æs*. Often used to represent the base "body" of the metal</note> and **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum* (mercury)</note>, for they strive together, etc. To "stir up war" is to destroy it; that is, at the time when they wish to be at peace after the war, and this is the union of the **Sun** and **Moon**, of **Sulfur** and **Mercury**. In this process, it is necessary to make the fixed volatile and vice-versa so many times until they are fixed together, and flow into a true **moon-maker** <note>original: *lunificum*. A substance capable of producing silver</note> and **sun-maker** <note>original: *solificum*. A substance capable of producing gold</note>, through transformation.

And this quicksilver is "wedded" to gold, and vice versa, according to the philosophers. And because one substance is the subject of both the fixed and the volatile, it is possible that the fixed might ascend with the volatile, and conversely, the volatile might be fixed with the fixed. And all this happens in a single vessel, without the "rubbing of hands" <note>This suggests the process is a natural chemical reaction that occurs without manual intervention or mechanical grinding once the components are sealed</note>. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the **Stone** is most appropriately called **Mercury**, although it is also named the **gold of the philosophers** extracted from quicksilver, and by many other infinite names.

...therefore approve, etc. And a certain poet says:

### *Chapter XV: That it pertains to the regimen to have a suitable vessel.*

There is also something else that is necessary for the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: *regimen*; the systematic management of the alchemical process, including heat and timing</note> itself: namely, a vessel suitable for the preparation of the Stone. Therefore, once the good "root" is known—which is the first priority—it is necessary to know the vessel—which is the second—in which the Stone is born as if in its own proper place. For every single thing is generated in a place that is suitable for it. Therefore, for this Stone, such an admirable vessel is very necessary. Whence says Morienus <note>original: *Morienus*; a legendary hermit-alchemist of the 7th century, famously the teacher of Khalid ibn Yazid</note>: If the wise had not found their explanations concerning the quality of the vessel in which the creation of the Stone is accomplished, they never could have reached the perfection of the complete <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterij*; a common term for the "Great Work" of alchemy or the art itself</note>. For I have shown above that this Mastery does not differ much from the creation of a human being; and the creation of a human is only completed in the mother’s womb. For animals are nourished and perfected in the wombs of mothers by a tempered warm moisture, through the mixture of seeds.

Glass is also solid and has no pores; therefore, spirits cannot evaporate from it, as is said in the same book; whereas from any other material <margin>Behold, for a long time</margin> whatsoever, it would not be effective.

Fourthly, it should be good and thick. Whence *The Lily*: For few of those stone-like vessels which glassmakers use endure; indeed, they are either corroded in the work or they split. Therefore Morienus says: And place the mixed things in a thick <margin>note</margin> vessel.

Sixthly, only one single vessel is sufficient. And Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous of the early alchemists</note>: And all this is done in one furnace and in one vessel. This is therefore the wondrous vessel, which is called by various names.

It is called, first, the "vessel of the philosophers," frequently found by the philosophers alone as being most suitable for the <term>working of the stone</term> <note>the *opus*, or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. It is also called the "egg of the philosophers" <note>original: *ovum philosophorum*</note>: because it is arranged in the shape of an egg; and it is called a "sublimatory" <note>an apparatus used for sublimation, where a solid is heated to vapor and then condensed back to solid</note>, because the stone is sublimated within it. It is also called a "sieve" <note>original: *cribrum*</note>: because in it the stone descends drop by drop, just as water passes through a sieve. Whence Mireris says: It must be sifted in its own sieve. It is further called a "sphere," because it is made in the likeness of one. And because in it the stone [rises] above...

### *That the manner of placing the stone into its vessel is varied, and to know which is appropriate and which is inappropriate, is necessary.* CHAPTER XVI.

There are many who know the stone, but who nevertheless place it inappropriately into the vessel, and therefore they do not achieve what they seek. And concerning this, there is a twofold error. The first indeed is of those who separate the male from the female, and couple males with males apart, and females with females apart. And these are deceived by the words of the philosophers, about which Alphytris Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a central figure in the *Turba Philosophorum*; his "dream" or journey is a famous alchemical allegory</note> dreamed when he went through the bottom of the sea and found the king and his people, who were not reproducing: because they inappropriately joined males to males, and females to females; and he joined the son of the king to his sister <note>an "alchemical marriage" of related substances</note>, and immediately the son of the king died.

### *That Sealing is Necessary for the Management.*

## CHAPTER XVII.

It is not only necessary for the vessel to be very strong, but also for the sealing to be most secure; for as it has been said, unless the most subtle spirits <note>refers to the volatile gases or essences released during heating which must not be allowed to escape</note> are retained, the entire Mastery <term>magisterium</term><note>the "Mastery" or "Great Work" refers to the entire process of transmuting base matter into the Philosopher's Stone</note> is betrayed. However, as soon as the stone is placed in the vessel, it begins to sweat because of the narrowness of its prison, and the most subtle parts begin to exhale; the longer it is cooked, the more the spirits are multiplied, refined, and strengthened. And so, right from the beginning, it is necessary to close the vessel and block it with a strong seal <note>original: *sigillum*; in alchemy, the "Seal of Hermes" refers to an airtight, often glass-fused, closure</note>, lest the "flowers" <note>the refined vapors or "spirits" that rise and condense during the process</note> escape, and the whole Mastery be lost. Wherefore the pleasant, supreme elements—having already been purified—must be kindled over a gentle fire until they are joined and behold <note>original: "contemplantur"; a poetic way to describe the substances reacting with or "facing" one another in the vessel.</note> one another, and are gradually burned until they are dried out in that gentle fire. Likewise in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turb."; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between Greek sages.</note>: "Our science is the conversion of the four elements and their qualities into one another." Convert the elements, therefore, and you shall find what you seek. 

Note also that the separation of the four elements is not as the ignorant and unskilled understand it. Instead, there is a certain hidden secret in the nature of the elements—namely, that the work and power of two elements, which are earth and water, can be felt; the other two elements, fire and air, are neither touched nor seen except within the former elements (earth and water). For fire, during the process of <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctione"; the boiling or prolonged heating of a substance to refine it or extract its essence.</note>, transforms their colors. 

<margin>the mother produced</margin>
Earth is the greatest of all elements, and <insert>from</insert> it the others proceed, and to it they return; and unless these four elements are joined, we achieve nothing. The stone is therefore one, possessing four colors according to the four elements.

...it must be seen <note>original: "dendum est," likely "videndum est."</note> that at first, the fire ought to be slow. Whence the *Lily* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous alchemical text often attributed to Arnald of Villanova.</note> says: "Know that without heat, nothing is ever generated, and that intense heat causes the work to perish, and that a cold bath drives away the composite." But through tempered fire, the body becomes gentle and suitable. For by a light fire, the corrupting humidity is extracted. Indeed, the Philosophers all testify that they have found no other fire for extracting corrupting humidities than a light one, commending a long duration while simultaneously—and rightly—condemning haste. For if the composite is ruled more intensely than it ought to be, it is extinguished. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: "The whole operation lies in the governance of the fire: because he who knows how to rule the fire will come to perfection." He who rules his matter with a slow fire is able to reach the <term>arcanum</term> <note>A secret or mystery; in alchemy, it refers to the hidden transformative power of the Stone.</note>, and thus the matter is not <term>vitrified</term> <note>original: "vitrificatur"; turned into glass. Alchemists feared this because glass is stable and "fixed," making it impossible to further refine or transform the material.</note>, and always remains soluble; whereas with a violent fire it is vitrified, and is hardened to such an extent that it cannot be dissolved except with the greatest labor, which is of no use. For it is necessary to separate the subtle parts from the gross parts, and the non-fixed from the fixed; however, this does not happen except with a slow fire. For if these were handled with a violent fire, either the matter would be burnt, or the gross parts would ascend together with the subtle parts and infect them. And therefore all philosophers desire the fire to be gentle. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy. This quote is from the famous *Emerald Tablet*.</note> says: "You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently—

### PHILOSOPHY

...with great skill. And Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously the teacher of the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "That which best fits these bodies together is oily in nature; for it vivifies and joins them, and from all of them one body is made." Learn, therefore, the governance of the Sun: because therein lies the whole perfection.

You can learn this governance from two sources: by turning to nature and to scripture. First, let nature be your imagination. For nature performs its <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "concoctionem"; the process of "cooking" or maturing a substance through heat.</note> plainly and continuously through the heat of the sun in the bowels of the earth, until metals are generated from the mineral spirits of vapor: so you too, govern your work, and you will find perfect knowledge. Yet we cannot imitate nature in this regarding every detail: nor is it necessary, as <term>Master Bonus</term> <note>Likely Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century Italian physician and alchemist known for the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*.</note> said, but it suffices to apply continuous and slow heat, according to the operation due to our work, just as nature does to its own: although not at the same degree of heat.

...diverse and contrary effects, and it receives various names, and diverse works are done in one thing; which nevertheless, because they tend toward one goal, are also called one work. Therefore, one work is <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimatio"; in alchemy, this is the process of purifying a substance by vaporizing it and re-solidifying it, often seen as "raising" the spirit from the material body.</note>: yet many works are <term>solution</term> <note>original: "solutio"; dissolving a solid into liquid.</note>, <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactio"; the breaking down or "rotting" of matter to allow for new growth.</note>, <term>calcination</term> <note>original: "calcinatio"; reducing a substance to a fine powder through high heat.</note>, <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>, and similar things.

Thus, then, this art considers three principal colors from which it can be conjectured whether the work is proceeding well and if there is hope of achieving the effect. 

These three are **black**, **white**, and **red**: black in the beginning, white in the middle, and red at the end of the work. **Blackness** indicates the <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "corruptionem"; in alchemy, "corruption" is a positive stage where the raw matter breaks down or "dies" so it can be reborn in a purified state.</note> of the matter, and a good blending or mixing of the moist with the earthy, and it is the beginning of generation. For nothing is generated unless from something else that has been corrupted. 

**Whiteness**, truly, is the sign of the removal of superfluous moisture. Wherefore heat acting upon the moist generates blackness, and [heat] acting upon the dry, by drying out the moisture, generates whiteness. 

**Redness**, truly, is caused if heat is continued upon the dry white matter. Wherefore all philosophers have commanded that these three colors be diligently considered in the <term>governance</term> <note>original: "regimine"; the specific method of managing heat and time during the alchemical process.</note> of the stone, and in the order in which they have been stated.

First, one must consider the end <note>The purpose or goal.</note> for which it is done. It is done for two reasons: first, indeed, so that bodies may be reduced to the highest simplicity—that is, so they are rendered as simple as they can possibly be, as John Scotus <note>Likely referring to a medieval authority attributed with alchemical knowledge, though often confused with the theologian Duns Scotus.</note> says. For this reason they are first dissolved, so that later, by **sublimating** <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again to purify it.</note> them little by little, we may be able to reduce them to the greatest subtlety <note>In alchemy, "subtlety" refers to the fineness, volatility, and purity of a substance.</note>. Moreover, the work of dissolution (as the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text.</note> says) was invented for no other reason than for the sake of thinning and refining.

---

First, therefore, the bodies are dissolved with the spirits, so that they may become like spirits: and so that after this they may be thinned more and more, until they are totally reduced to the nature of spirits. Therefore, the more times it is dissolved, the medicine is thinned and <margin>and by so much more, as much as it seems more powerful</margin> **coagulated**, the more subtle and powerful it is made. Hence all things that are sublimated are sublimated in two ways: some by themselves, and some with others. Mercury, therefore, since it is a spirit, is sublimated by itself: but our earth, since it is the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue or "ash" left after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly roasted or oxidized.</note> of a body, is not sublimated unless it is excellently incorporated with Mercury. Therefore, grind the calx and soak it <note>original: "imbibe"</note> with our Mercury, and cook it until it becomes one body: and let it not weary you to repeat this same thing many times: because the body will not ascend upward unless it is incorporated with

It details the technique of repeatedly combining a metallic "calx" with Mercury to ensure the solid body can eventually rise or sublimate along with the spirit.</summary>

This dissolution, therefore, is called the **first sublimation** of the stone: and we perform this sublimation so that we may lead the bodies back to a refined nature, so that they become like spirits, and so that we may return them to their **first matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless, original state of all things in alchemical theory.</note>, and so they may take on a single color. Unless this dissolution comes first, other sublimations are unsuitable and do not follow appropriately. This dissolution is also called a **grinding** <note>original: "contritio"</note> which is not done with hands but with fire, as was said above.

This dissolution into "water" is also not understood to happen in the way common dissolution happens in rainwater, but it is a dissolution that happens in an **unctuous** <note>oily or fatty</note> or thick water, as **Scotus** <note>Likely referring to Michael Scot or a pseudo-epigraphical alchemical author attributed to the name.</note> and others say, until the whole is resolved into water and finally becomes one thing. However, this dissolution is not, strictly speaking, a dissolution—though it is called so—but rather a **liquefaction** in the manner of wax. 

<margin>A</margin>
From this first dissolution, therefore, it begins; and thus through many stages the **philosopher's stone** is ground down until, at the very last, it remains most perfectly refined, possessing an entirely spiritual power to penetrate all solid and hard things, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founding figure of alchemy.</note> says. And in this way, it is led out from **potentiality** into **perfect act** <note>Aristotelian terms: moving from a state of "could be" to a state of "fully realized being."</note>. For it was said above that from the beginning the stone is imperfect and also composed of body and spirit, having in itself in part a **volatile** nature, that is—

Therefore, the first method of dissolution is to **putrefy** <term>Putrefaction: In alchemy, this is the process of decay or fermentation where the substance breaks down, often turning black, to allow for its eventual purification and rebirth</term> the matter. For putrefaction begins from the start at the same time as dissolution, but putrefaction is not yet completed when all the matter is dissolved into water; rather, it is completed afterward. Odor is also a sign of complete **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the "rotting" or breakdown of the material, also called the Nigredo or "Blackness" stage, necessary for the transformation of the stone</term>—not just any odor, but one that is heavy and altogether unbearable. In the work itself, one must take the greatest care that its odor is not smelled, because putrefaction is not completed if the odor can still be detected <note>This suggests that if the alchemist can smell the material, the "hermetic seal" of the vessel has been broken, and the vital vapors are escaping</note>.

### ON THE STONE

Odor is also a sign of absolute **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the alchemical stage of decomposition where the "body" of the metal is broken down so its "spirit" can be released</term>, and not just any kind, but a heavy and entirely unbearable one. Satur." referring to an alchemical text attributed to the planet/deity Saturn, associated with lead and darkness</note>, specifically before its perfection, as it kills human bodies; but afterward, it kills metallic bodies. However, this odor of its is perceived more by the intellect than by the senses, because we have learned through experience what it is like in the work before the work begins. During the work, one must take the greatest care that its odor is not smelled, for the putrefaction is not complete if the odor can still be detected. This double property of the **stone** is expressed through the likeness of a corpse. For in the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilio," the *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> it is said that the stone requires a light fire from the beginning and appears like a corpse for many days, like a man in his tomb. So that the order and the causes with their effects in this operation may be clearly revealed by the author, it must be written about more extensively here.

First, therefore, you should know that it is necessary to wash the **dead body** <term>corpus mortuum: the "corpse" or residue of the matter after it has been broken down by putrefaction</term> with fire and water. And concerning this water Morienus <note>Morienus: a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit, said to be the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> testifies: This earth rots with its water, and is cleansed with its water. All know that their water washes away filth. Concerning fire, however, Avicenna <note>Avicenna: the Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical theories were central to medieval science</note> says: Heat acting upon a dry thing causes **whiteness** <term>albedo: the second major stage of the Great Work, signifying purification and the creation of the Silver Stone</term>: because in this way it consumes the corrupting moisture. Therefore, as it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: Fire whitens the calxes of stones. And concerning both, Morienus says: **Azoch** <term>Azoch: a term for the "universal solvent" or philosophical mercury</term> and fire wash and cleanse the **Laton** <term>Laton: an impure, dark metallic alloy used as a metaphor for the matter of the Stone before it is purified</term>, and they utterly strip away its darkness from it. 

And for this reason, hot water washes more strongly than cold. Wherefore wax is whitened by dew and heat, while linen is made white by moisture and the sun. And this is the reason why, after the **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the decomposition of the substance, often called the "death" of the matter</term> of the stone, it is necessary to continue the fire until it becomes white. For by the continuation of the fire, the earth is continually **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a fine powder</term> and ground down further, and gradually dried out, and thus finally whitened. In this whitening, the water works together with the earth; it is continually absorbed and exhaled by the heat; or rather, it is incorporated with the earth and dried within it. Therefore the Unknown Author <note>original: *Ignotus*, a common way of citing anonymous but authoritative alchemical texts</note> said: Grind it often with its water, and calcine it again, until through the washing of water and fire, the darkness utterly recedes. Afterward, however, with the body itself arranged and reduced to the nature of the fifth essence <term>fifth essence: also known as the "quintessence," it is the purest form of matter that transcends the four elements of earth, air, fire, and water</term>, which is simple, it pours the soul back in. The body, embracing it, rejoices. The spirit also, entering the body with the soul, perfects it and makes the dead living: and when it rises again, it lives forever. And this soul is the mediator <term>mediator: a middle-man or bridge that allows two incompatible things to connect</term> between the body and the spirit, and she joins and binds them in an inseparable union. For the spirit cannot be united with the body except through the soul, which is the tincture <term>tincture: in alchemy, a powerful liquid or "stain" capable of transforming the properties and color of a base metal into gold or silver</term> of the Sun and of the philosophers. Therefore, the soul, seeing her body dead and dry, descends in compassion and brings it to life. And because she has been made sublime from her heavenly dwelling, and most pure and powerful, she also gifts her body with eternal and immortal life, etc. And Mireris the philosopher <note>Mireris is an authority frequently cited in alchemical florilegia like the *Rosarium Philosophorum*; he is often associated with the "blackening" and "whitening" stages of the work.</note> says: The spirit that is extracted is the soul. The black dregs <term>black dregs: original Latin "fex nigra," the dark, solid residue left at the bottom of a vessel after distillation</term> remaining and left behind is the body, in which there is no life. The soul is thin, which is air; the body, however, is thick, which is earth. It is necessary, however, for each of them <margin>proper<br/>^ and</margin> to have its own rule and order, until the thick is made thin, and the thin is made bodily. For what you seek is in the dregs, not the ashes...

...nor should you despise those things existing in the lower part of the vessel: but cook them with a fire of coals for many days, until they become charcoal. Then, once the spirit has been separated from it, grind it and return the moisture to it with which you previously liquefied it, etc. Moreover, after this, it must be made liquid so that it may be altered from its own nature, until after the dissolution it becomes spiritual and subtle. Therefore, when its soul—which was its essence and life—is restored to it, it becomes subtle; for when the soul is restored to the body, it brings the dead back to life.

Thirdly, you should know that the craftsman must not only whiten the stone, but must also give it a perfect whiteness. It is therefore necessary to understand this whiteness beforehand, so that he may know how to reach it through certain stages; for not every whiteness is sufficient to stain <note>original: "tingit"</note> the metal into Moon <term>Moon: in alchemy, "Luna" refers to silver, the second most perfect metal after gold</term>, nor is the stone immediately "fixed" <term>fixed: a substance that is stable in fire and does not evaporate or change further</term> as soon as it appears white.

Therefore, it is necessary to sublime <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify and whiten the matter</term> the stone, and by subliming it, whiten it until it is most white and remains fixed against the battle of the fire. Thus, we wait a long time for the transition from blackness to true whiteness, passing through many colors before the proper color intended by the art is generated in the final digestion <term>digestion: a process of gentle, continuous heating to mature the alchemical substance</term>. And as Master Bon. <note>likely referring to Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century alchemist and author of the "Precious Pearl"</note> says in chapter six: All colors preceding the final one, however many they may be, result from an incomplete digestion. And therefore the craftsman does not stop there, but strives toward the final goal as it was pre-determined in his mind. Let us see, then, how great it ought to be...

<header># OF THE STONE</header>

Moreover, this art is called divine by reason of that part of the governance <note>original: "regiminis"; in alchemy, the "regimen" refers to the specific sequence of operations or the controlled application of heat at different stages</note> that exists above nature and understanding, as all philosophers agree. This divine governance occurs during the time of whitening <note>original: "dealbationis"; the *albedo* stage of the Great Work, following the "blackening" or purification</note>, specifically when the conjunction of whitened souls, spirits, and bodies takes place, for this union depends upon divine protection.

For it happens suddenly—that is, the medicine congeals the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, not the common kind, but the mercury of the Stone, unless it is suddenly congealed at its birth with that medicine of which Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of early chemistry and alchemy</note> speaks. Otherwise, it flies away and escapes along with the entire medicine. For he does not speak there of common quicksilver—though his words may seem to suggest it—but rather of the quicksilver that has been congealed and fixed within the **Elixir**. 

Hence, it is necessary that from the very beginning there be only one single matter, which contains the power of the body, spirit, and soul. It is like a mineral medicine that requires no external assistance, but possesses within itself everything it needs for its operation under the administration of the "governance"—be it for **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify materials</term>, **fixation** <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates</term>, liquefaction, congealing, or any such process. 

For Lull <note>Raymond Lull (Ramon Llull), a 13th-century philosopher and polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> says: "It is one single thing, containing within itself the body, soul, and spirit that provide the tint <note>original: "tingentia"; the power of the stone to change the color and nature of other metals</note> all at once; in its operation, no other helping hand is required," and so forth. Each of the aforementioned bodies and spirits is also, if it has been prepared through perfect preparation, the white or red **Elixir** in and of itself. For there is one ferment for the white and for the red—

...um. Hence, Rhazes <note>original: "Raf."; refers to Abu Bakr al-Razi, a foundational Persian alchemist and physician</note>, speaking of the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"</note> of the philosophers, says: "I do not want you to wonder that I have counted quicksilver <margin>the work... <unclear>t-y</unclear></margin> among the **bodies** in this argument, and among the **spirits** in the previous one, for the transformability <note>original: "convertibilitas"; the ability of a substance to change its state or nature</note> of its own nature requires this. Therefore, it is associated now with bodies and now with spirits. For it is reasonably associated with spirits because of its flight from the fire <note>referring to volatility; spirits evaporate when heated</note>, which it possesses before it is corrected. And because it exalts <note>original: "exaltat"; in alchemy, to 'exalt' is to raise a substance to a more noble or potent state</note> bodies when it has been corrected, it is also rightfully associated with bodies: because all bodies can be converted into it, and it can be drawn out of all bodies." Likewise, that beautiful debate which Rhazes presents between **mercury** and **gold** shows that the philosophers wish the Stone to be entirely mercurial, and to have gold, or sulfur, within its hidden part. From these things, it is gathered that the **Philosopher's Stone** is mercury alone: because it is entirely a fleeing spirit. And therefore, although quicksilver behaves as the female in the composition of the **Elixir**, yet its entire first operation is as the male. And this is why it is volatile for so long, as long as it is not contained by a body, which is the **sulfur** coagulating <note>original: "coagulans"; the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</note> it. However, this body is not added to it from elsewhere, but it possesses it potentially <note>original: "in potentia"</note> within its own nature; it is, however, brought into action <note>original: "in actum"</note> when, through proper digestion <note>prolonged, gentle heating</note>, it takes on the property and nature of a body. And then it is called a body from its own self alone. Hence also, in almost all operations involving metals and minerals, the composition is made from spirits alone, or from their own vapors, or...

...to comprehend: because at the end of the **digestion** <note>original: "digestionis"; a process of slow, continuous heating in a sealed vessel</note>, and nearly all the elements, likewise bodies, spirits, and souls, and **sulfurs** and **tinctures** are all mixed together in one subject, and at the end of the first **purification** <note>original: "mundificationis"; the cleansing of the matter from dregs or impurities</note> from all impurities: because then the **soul** <note>the vital, transforming essence of the material</note> alone arises and not before. ### *That just as fixation is the completion of the stone, so it is necessary to know the root and order of fixation.*

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

Nevertheless, the craftsman must always perform each step not by chance, but most prudently and by reason, especially concerning the <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixionem"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat</note> of his medicine: because it is fixation that perfects all things and makes them remain permanent forever. As is clear from what was said above in the third chapter, the goal is to make the medicine permanent in the fire, so that it is neither burned nor destroyed, nor diminished—neither in substance, nor in power, nor in color or <term>tincture</term> <note>the staining or transformative power of the stone</note>—but rather is increased. Hence a certain most skilled philosopher says: "Our stone must be held under the governance of the fire for so long, until it can no longer be changed from one nature into another." For it is necessary to make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed, so many times until the whole is fixed and flows, and transforms into the true <term>sun-maker</term> <note>original: "solificum"; a substance capable of producing gold</note> and <term>moon-maker</term> <note>original: "lunificum"; a substance capable of producing silver</note>.

# PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>of the red</margin> <note>original: "rubri"</note>
The seeds are most perfectly united and mixed together, which occurs especially during <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactione"; the alchemical stage of decomposition where the matter turns black and the elements are released to recombine</note>. Therefore, they pass into a single nature, power, and color. For this reason, a single <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: "Elyxir"; the refined substance used to transform metals</note> for both the white and the red stages can be generated through the art; however, not at the same time, but one after the other through different modes of <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "digestionum"; the process of maturing the substance through steady, controlled heat</note>. 

Since, however, the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "sol"; representing Gold and the masculine principle</note> is worthier than the <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "luna"; representing Silver and the feminine principle</note> and its nature is more fixed—and it is capable of being fixed by a more fixed metal—the mastery of the <term>ferment</term> <note>original: "fermenti"; a substance that acts like yeast, "leavening" the base metal into a higher state</note> is attributed to it. Thus, the Sun is said to be the ferment of both the white and the red Elixirs, and the work is neither improved nor completed by anything other than it.

Therefore, <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> said: "A true red <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; the power of the Stone to impart its color and quality to other metals</note> is never made without the red stone." For the white alone, without the red stone, would not dye the matter into a perfect red. In the red stone, there is a greater power of "non-burning" <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphuris"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle</note>. This is because the masculine is hotter, purer, more substantial, and more thoroughly digested than in the white stage, where the feminine is colder, more impure, and more <term>fugitive</term> <note>original: "fugitiva"; volatile or prone to escaping the vessel as vapor</note>.

But because the Moon first holds dominion and converts its Sun to itself—giving it its own nature, color, and property—it is not without reason called the ferment of the white Elixir, even though it partakes more of the nature of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury, the fluid and receptive principle</note> than of sulfur, owing to its volatility. 

Nevertheless, each ferment is derived from both bodies, though it comes more principally from the Sun. For both bodies, because of the closeness of their natures—having been born from one father and one mother—are transmuted by alteration into one primary nature of quicksilver; so that thereafter from that, that is, from its hidden...

# ON THE STONE

...converts it into the truest "sun" <note>original: "solem"; in alchemy, the sun represents gold</note> better than any natural gold, as the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> and Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> say in the new translation. The second property is that it preserves men in comfort and youth, repelling all <margin>In health</margin> ailments from them; it is so powerful that it dispels leprosy, soothes the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, and even removes many other nearly incurable infirmities. And it performs all these things more effectively than all the medicines of physicians, or any potions or preparations whatsoever. # ON THE STONE

...receives the impression of the medicine <note>original: "medicinæ"; the alchemical elixir or Philosopher's Stone used to transform metals</note>: because it is purer and more stable <note>original: "fixius"; referring to "fixity," a substance's ability to remain unchanged by fire</note> by its own nature.
