And if again one part of that is cast upon ten other parts of an imperfect body, the whole is again made into medicine, so that one part of it, cast again upon ten other parts of a body, will <term>transmute (transmutabit)|to change one substance into another, specifically a base metal into a precious one</term> it into a perfect body: namely, into true Sun <note>original: "solem"; gold</note> or Moon <note>original: "lunam"; silver</note>, according to the quality of the medicine. 

And this is said reasonably: because casting one part over a thousand once, and casting one part over ten parts three times, amounts to the same result. But casting one part over a thousand once converts an imperfect body into a perfect body. Therefore, casting it three times will also convert it. 

From this, another conclusion necessarily follows: that casting the medicine upon a perfect body <note>gold or silver</note> makes the resulting second medicine more perfect than if it were cast upon an imperfect body.

### ON THE STONE

...through one part of the <term>medicine of the first degree</term> <note>the most potent, initial form of the Philosopher’s Stone</note>, one thousand parts of an imperfect body are perfected into a perfect body. This is because, just as the medicine is led through many alterations from <term>corporality</term> <note>physical denseness or "grossness"</note> and imperfection toward spirituality and a most subtle nature, so also, conversely, it is led back through many <term>projections</term> <note>the act of casting the medicine onto base metals to transform them</note> from spirituality to the nature of a coarse body, due to the coarse parts into which it is inseparably incorporated.

It must be noted, however, that <term>projection</term> is more easily accomplished than the <term>procreation</term> <note>the initial creation or "birth"</note> of the Stone. For the procreation of the medicine is difficult, because the subtle watery element in the matter of the stone is very strongly united with the dry earthy element, and it can hardly, if ever, be separated except by the greatest and most subtle skill of the craftsman, and only over a long period of time. 

And yet, such a separation is required for the procreation of the medicine. But after the medicine has been created, this kind of separation is easy to achieve within other bodies <note>referring to the base metals being transformed</note>: because the medicine, by its spirituality and subtlety, suddenly penetrates these bodies. By its heat, it alters, digests, and prepares the matter; it perfectly breaks apart and separates the pure from the impure, and the subtle from the coarse. It then assimilates the pure, subtle parts to itself and transforms them into its own substance.

Because the absolute philosophical **medicine** <note>the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone in its finished state</note> is entirely capable of being **multiplied** <note>the process of increasing the quantity or power of the Stone without starting from the beginning</note> unto infinity.

Furthermore, there is a third way, as the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius," likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 14th-century alchemical text</note> holds: that a certain part of the medicine, whether **white** <note>for making silver</note> or **red** <note>for making gold</note>, should be joined to a stone or to "new" **Mercury** <note>not common quicksilver, but the "philosophical" starting material</note> that has never been used in the work. Let it then be placed in **digestion** <note>prolonged, gentle heating</note> as before, and let it be cooked by **putrefying** <note>breaking down into a black mass</note>, **sublimating** <note>purifying by vaporizing and condensing</note>, and **fixing** <note>rendering a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, until the whole becomes a **tincted oil** <note>a concentrated, liquid form of the Stone capable of "staining" or transforming metals</note>. Then you have the perfect Stone once again, and this is achieved in just a few days, and with less expense, labor, and danger. Always carefully keep something back to serve as a **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"; a small amount of the finished Stone used to "leaven" a larger batch of matter, much like yeast in bread</note>, both of the white and of the red. This prudent consideration will spare you from the more arduous labors mentioned above. For **Raymund** <note>Raymundus Lullus, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> seems to intend this same thing in the third distinction, where he speaks of fermentation at the beginning of the book, and in the *Practice* of his *Physical Tree* in the second chapter, and elsewhere also among the wise philosophers.

in the world to come. <note>original: "in futuro seculo"</note> Therefore, study and apply yourself diligently to the best authors, as "day unto day utters speech," <note>A reference to Psalm 19:2, suggesting that knowledge is a continuous, divine revelation.</note> let one book open another, and "night unto night shows knowledge." And finally, be such in virtue as you properly desire the **Stone** to be. You are imperfect; long for the due perfection. You are foul and unclean; purge yourself with tears. **Sublime** <term>Sublimation: in alchemy, purifying a substance by vaporizing it; here used metaphorically for moral elevation</term> yourself with morals and virtues; adorn and color yourself with sacramental graces. Make the soul sublime and subtle through the contemplation of heavenly things and conformable to angelic spirits, so that it may be able to quicken, **whiten** <note>original: "dealbare"; referring to Albedo, the second major stage of the alchemical work</note>, and make incorruptible, immortal, and entirely beyond suffering the putrid body and vile ash, through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus, finally illuminated by the divine vision and drenched in ineffable light, it may be able to illustrate its own body—now raised—with the splendor of eternal glory and a **red glow** <note>original: "rubeo fulgore"; referring to Rubedo, the final "Red" stage of the Great Work</note>. Because this immortal glory will overflow from the hidden depths of the soul into the body. Our most celebrated Stone bears the form and figure of all these things perfectly, and the present allegory suggests the order. And let this be the true seal of the book, stronger than any closure, more awesome than any earthly sign, more useful, and most honorable.

<sig>n 4</sig>

<summary>This concluding page of the treatise links alchemical success to the moral purity of the practitioner, comparing the stages of the 'Great Work' (whitening and reddening) to the spiritual resurrection of the human body and soul.</summary>

# ENIGMA OF THE PHY-
## sical stone by Lorenzo Ventura
### Venetian Doctor

In India (the hottest part of the world),
A stone is sometimes born which encloses within itself
Infinite virtues, which come from heaven:
It is called Pantheora, <note>Likely a reference to the "Pantaura," a legendary stone mentioned in Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, said to attract other stones like a magnet; here it serves as a name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> although in its vile appearance
It is held by many to be vain and foolish.
The Chosen ones, and those who know the high secrets
Of nature, are accustomed to extract its blood
By an artifice second to no other.
And because within it there is Mercury and sulfur,
Gold and Silver—not those of the common people— <note>original: "non già quei del volgo"; a standard alchemical distinction between "vulgar" metals and the "philosophical" principles of the same name.</note>
But a celestial humor, hot and unctuous,
With its subtle earthiness, cold and dry,
Bound together in a marvelous way,
<margin>threefold</margin> Soul, spirit and body, four and one: <note>The "four" refers to the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) and the "one" to the Quintessence or the Stone itself.</note>
Here, with the gift of God, goodness and patience,
Labor, industry, fire and long time,
Such substance rises up from the already captured
Foul body, and makes it clear and shining;
The art darkens it again, and clears
Those parts several times, until well united
Light and heavy, rare and dense, they stand
Exposed to the great martyrdom of Vulcan: <note>Vulcan is the Roman god of fire; "martyrdom of Vulcan" refers to the intense heat of the alchemical furnace.</note>
This is called Elixir, and the medicine
That heals every leper, <term>Leper: an alchemical metaphor for base or "diseased" metals (like lead) that are purified into "healthy" gold.</term> and imperfect thing.

<summary>This page presents a poetic enigma by the Venetian alchemist Lorenzo Ventura, describing the origin and composition of the "Pantheora" or Philosopher's Stone. It emphasizes that the Stone is composed of a "philosophical" mercury and sulfur and must undergo a process of purification through fire (Vulcan) to become a universal medicine.</summary>

Metal, and human body in a marvelous way. <note>This line completes the sentence from the previous page describing the union of the philosophical elements.</note>
This makes man rich, it makes him happy,

First Cause and Mover of nature,
For his divine gifts, and for this friend, <note>The "friend" likely refers to the Stone or the alchemical secret itself.</note>
With true affection and purity of heart,
Render immortal thanks, glory, and honor.

## GIOVANNI AURELIO
### Augurello.

Therefore come, mortals, behold this Light rescued from the darkness, and turn your steps away from blind paths. And only forbid the wickedness, and drive away the hostile poison, by which the common people <note>original: "vulgus"; in alchemical literature, this refers to the uninitiated or "puffers" who lack spiritual understanding.</note> think they can mix their hands with divine powers through an art which is able to see into the secrets of things and causes so deeply hidden. Let no greedy deceiver touch this with impure hands, nor a bankrupt <note>original: "decoctor"; historically a term for a spendthrift, but in alchemy, it refers to those who waste their fortunes on false experiments.</note> likewise, nor whoever is strong only in the craftsman’s art, <note>original: "fabrili arte"; suggesting those who only understand physical labor without the necessary philosophical/spiritual insight.</note> nor even the soft man whose heart is lost to idleness, nor the wandering merchant, nor the citizen devoted to the city, nor he who bends over the earth to cultivate the fields, nor he who especially threatens many and great things in his mind <note>The boastful or overly ambitious.</note>—or anyone like those who are accustomed to seek these things as the common crowd does, only through evil fraud or the sheer love of possessing.

<meta>This page continues the Latin poem "Chrysopoeia" (Gold-making) by Giovanni Aurelio Augurello. *But let the wise man, who worships the heavens above all, and who delights only in knowing causes deeply, betake himself here and follow this art <note>The "art" of alchemy or Chrysopoeia.</note> with all his strength. To him shall cling as a companion the serious exploration of things, everywhere observing the innermost footprints of nature. Then, a period of delay shall follow, holding back his anxious paths; and steadfast patience, destined one day to see the goal. Soon labor and diligence, moving noble steps, will not be absent; he will carry a glass vessel <note>The "vitreum vas" or philosopher's egg, the sealed container where the alchemical transformation occurs.</note>—that is, a single one—*
<margin>one</margin> *a single work, and finally bring the matter to its end. He therefore will travel, surrounded by such a great company <note>The "company" refers to the virtues previously mentioned: exploration, patience, labor, and diligence.</note>, on a long journey; and traversing all things with a slow pace, he will continually feed his eyes and mind with wondrous discoveries, and the things he sees will beguile his tireless labor, until he uncovers treasures hidden in the secret earth: an unknown weight of silver and gold.*

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the alchemist's personal virtues—patience, diligence, and the use of a single glass vessel—to a personified speech by Alchemy herself. While the previous page focused on the "how" of the work, this page defines the "what" and the "who," establishing Alchemy as a divine and exclusive science that rejects the morally corrupt.</meta>

### Alchemy speaking of herself.

I am the heavenly radiance of angelic wisdom, the strength of the soldier, the goal of the world’s machine <note>original: *mundialis machinæ*; this refers to the ultimate purpose or functioning of the cosmic order</note>, the most excellent work of royal glory, set above all sciences of this world; I am a secret of God <note>original: *archanum Dei*</note>, a breath of life, the sister of philosophy, the grace of Kings, the power of lords, the sweat of the Prophets <note>implying that the ancient prophets labored intensely to uncover these truths</note>, the envy of philosophers, an incomparable treasure, a mirror of joy, the flight of sorrow, the mother of virtues, and the footprint of human nature. Therefore, let those who should be rejected be cast away, and let the righteous be further justified for the better: let my voice, a saving joy, be heard only in the dwellings of the righteous. Evil sinners must therefore be cast out—the lustful, the greedy, and the wasteful—lest through these "secrets of secrets," while overflowing with delights, they proceed to commit even worse crimes.

Reigning, I shall reign, and my kingdom shall have no end for all who come to me and perceive me healthfully, skillfully, and with constancy.

->*It is certain that the uninitiated must be kept far from here.*<-

No one can possess this illustrious gift of God unless he purifies his mind toward God the greatest Himself—that is, with a mind and heart both pure and most simple.

<vocab>Alchemy, the secret of God, wisdom, gift of God, philosophy, let them be justified</vocab>

<summary>This page features a personified Alchemy describing herself as a divine, royal, and moral science that acts as the "secret of God." She issues a stern warning that her "kingdom" is open only to the righteous and pure of heart, while the greedy and sinful are strictly excluded.</summary>

# PREFACE.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'E' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or philosopher, holding an open book. The figure is surrounded by intricate foliate patterns and two smaller figures in the background.</image-desc>

I indeed, Hortulanus <note>A pseudonym meaning "The Gardener." This author is traditionally identified as a 14th-century commentator on the Emerald Tablet.</note>, named after the garden, or from the sea fortress <note>original: "arce maritima"; possibly a reference to a specific location or a symbolic "fortress" of knowledge.</note>, wrapped in a Jacobine skin <term>Jacobine skin: Likely referring to the habit of a Dominican friar, who were known as "Jacobins" in France because their first house was on the Rue de Saint-Jacques in Paris.</term>, the newest of philosophers and unworthy to be called a disciple of philosophy: moved by the love of my dearest friend, I shall declare the certain determination of the word of Hermes, the father of philosophers. Which word, although hidden, I shall write down subtly; and in the work, truly, by the labor of my fingers, I will declare the whole arrangement to you, as well as the philosophers' concealment in their words: because concealment is of no use where the teaching of the Holy Spirit is at work.

### *That the art of Alchemy is true and certain.*

### CHAPTER I.

The Philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, whose text is being analyzed.</note> says **TRUE**. For it is true that the art of Alchemy is given without a lie. He says this in detestation of those who say the art is lying, that is, false.

Certain, that is, tested by experience; also, whatever is experienced is most certain and most true. That is, it is most true that the Sun <term>Sun: In the language of alchemy, "the Sun" (Sol) refers to gold, the perfect metal, or the masculine principle of the Great Work.</term> is procreated through the art: and he says *Most True*, in the superlative

### *That the stone should be divided into two parts.*
#### CHAPTER II.

Next, he touches upon the operation of the stone, saying *that which is below*. He says this because the stone is divided into two principal parts through the mastery <term>mastery: Latin "magisterium," referring to the completed alchemical process or the sophisticated substance produced by the alchemist's skill</term>, namely into an upper part, which ascends upward; and into a lower part, which remains fixed and clear. And since these two parts agree together in power, he therefore says: *That which is below is as that which is above, and vice versa* <note>original: "et è conuerso"</note>. And it should be known that this division is necessary to perform the wonders of one thing, namely the stone. Because the lower part, which is called the "nurse," is the earth, which is the ferment <term>ferment: a substance that acts as a catalyst, like yeast in bread, to transform the "base" matter into the "perfect" stone</term>; and the upper part is the soul, which gives life to the whole stone and causes it to rise again. Thus, the stone is celebrated through the separation and joining of the elements. Many wonders are performed in the secret work of nature.

### *That the stone has within itself the four elements.*
#### CHAPTER III.

*As all things come from one, etc.* Here he gives an example of the whole, just as all things were from one,

namely from one confused globe, or a confused mass, by the meditation of the One—that is, the creation of Almighty God. *Thus all things were born from this one thing.* This means that just as all created things are born and emerge from this confused mass <note>original: "massa confusa" — This refers to the primal chaos from which God created the universe, serving as a metaphor for the alchemist's raw starting material.</note> by a single adaptation—that is, by the command of God alone and miraculously—so too our stone is born and emerges from one confused mass. This mass is disorganized within itself, yet it contains all the elements: water, air, earth, and fire, which were created by God and by his miracle alone.

### *That the stone has a father and a mother, namely the Sun and the Moon.*
#### CHAPTER IV.

And just as in the natural world, one or more animals generate others similar to themselves, so in the art of alchemy, the Sun generates the Sun, with multiplication through the power of the aforementioned stone. Therefore it follows: *Its father is the Sun, that is, gold.* But because in every natural generation a suitable receptacle for the sperm <note>original: "spermatis" — in medieval science, this refers to the "seed" or life-giving principle of any substance, not just biological.</note> is required, possessing a certain harmony and likeness to the father; so in this artificial generation, it is necessary that it has a suitable receptacle for its sperm or seed—that is, its tincture <term>tincture: a potent alchemical substance or "spirit" capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold</term>. This receptacle must be harmonious with it and share a similarity to the gold itself, and that receptacle is silver. Therefore it follows: *its mother is the Moon.*

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Hortulanus. Having previously identified the Sun as the "father" of the Stone, he now explains the technical and symbolic necessity of combining Gold and Silver to achieve the Great Work.</meta>

ON ALCHEMY.
A 4

### CHAPTER V.

It must be carefully noted that the joining of these two bodies is necessary in this art for both the white and the red works <note>original: "ad album & ad rubeum" — these refer to the Albedo and Rubedo, the two final stages of the alchemical process to create the Stone.</note>. There are two reasons for this.

The first reason is that although gold is the most noble among metals—being the most compact, perfect, and fixed—nevertheless, if it is dissolved so that it is excessively separated, it becomes "spiritual" and flies away from the fire just like Mercury <term>Mercury: quicksilver; in alchemy, it represents the principle of volatility, or the tendency of a substance to evaporate when heated</term>, which is a marvel. This occurs because of its internal heat; in this state, it possesses an infinite power of coloring or tincture <term>tincture: a potent alchemical substance or "spirit" capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold</term>, and this is called the sperm or the masculine seed.

If, however, silver <note>original: "argentum"</note> is dissolved into liquid water, it nonetheless remains fixed <note>fixed: in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that remains stable and does not evaporate when exposed to high heat</note> just as it was before. It possesses no prepared tincture of its own, yet it is suited to receive and fix a tincture through the tempering of heat and cold; this is called the feminine sperm. Thus, their joining is most appropriate.

There is also another reason why these two bodies are joined: because while silver is very difficult to melt, and gold is similarly difficult to liquefy when each is by itself, yet if they are joined together, they dissolve and melt very easily. Goldsmiths know this when they make solder for gold. Therefore, if only one of these were present in our stone, the medicine would never easily flow by any ingenuity, nor would it possess a tincture; and even if it did provide a tincture, it would not transform <note>original: "tingeret" — literally "to dye," referring to the alchemical transformation of a metal's color and nature</note> things to the same extent as itself, because...

<vocab>alchemy, gold, silver, masculine seed, feminine seed, tincture, Mercury, philosopher's stone</vocab>

<summary>This page explains why alchemy requires the union of gold and silver, casting gold as the volatile 'masculine' active principle and silver as the stable 'feminine' receptive base. It uses the practical example of goldsmiths' solder to prove that these metals melt more effectively when combined than when alone.</summary>
<keywords>gold, silver, masculine seed, feminine seed, tincture, fixation, volatility, Mercury, soldering, alchemical marriage</keywords>

--- Page 268 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary by Hortulanus on the Emerald Tablet. The previous page discussed the chemical union of gold (the masculine seed) and silver (the feminine seed) to create the Philosopher's Stone. This page explains the subsequent stages of the "birth" of the Stone, interpreting the allegorical roles of the wind and the earth.</meta>

GARLANDIUS

it would not be a receptacle for the tincture <term>tincture: a potent alchemical substance or "spirit" capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold</term>. And our final secret is this: to possess the medicine that flows before the life-giving flight of Mercury <term>Mercury: quicksilver; in alchemy, it represents the principle of volatility, or the tendency of a substance to evaporate when heated</term>. Therefore, their joining is necessary, because when these two receive each other in the union of the stone, they are in conflict in the "belly of the wind," and this is what he says later: *The wind carried it in its belly* <note>original: "Portauit eam ventus in ventre suo" — a famous line from the Emerald Tablet describing the gestation of the alchemical embryo in the air.</note>. It is clear that the wind is air, and air is life, and life is the soul. I have already spoken above regarding the soul, which gives life to the entire stone; thus it is necessary that the wind carries it, brings it back, and gives birth to it through the mastery of the art.

Then it follows that it should receive nourishment from its mother, namely the earth; therefore he says, *Its nurse is the earth* <note>original: "Nutrix eius est terra"</note>. Just as a fetus nourished without food never reaches maturity, so our stone would never reach its full effect without the "fermentation" of its earth. This fermentation is called nourishment. For in this way, from one father and the union with the mother, and by the nourishment of the nurse, many "sons" are generated who are like the father. If these sons lack a long cooking <term>decoction: a process of long, steady heating or "boiling" used to concentrate substances</term>, they will be like the mother in their whiteness, though they will retain the weights of the father <margin>they will by no means obtain [the final redness]</margin>.

### CHAPTER VI.
### That the Stone is perfect if the soul is fixed in the body.

<margin>Telesmi <note>original: "Telesmi" — a term from the Emerald Tablet often translated as "perfections" or "the father of all works."</note></margin>

In this way, the whole substance of the stone is fermented by the nurse, which is the earth, so that the entire stone is converted into a leaven [ferment]. Just as in the making of bread, a little leaven nourishes and ferments a very great quantity of dough, and in turn converts the whole substance of that dough into leaven, which then possesses that same power to transform another batch of dough; in this same way, the philosopher intends that our stone be so fermented that it acts as a leaven for the multiplication of other stones.

### *How the volatile stone is to be fixed again. CHAPTER IX.*

Afterward, it is necessary to wax <note>original: "incerare" — Ceration is the alchemical process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency, allowing it to melt and penetrate other materials</note> the stone itself, thus exalted, upon a marble slab with oil, or with the single element extracted from the stone itself in the first operation, which is called the "water of the stone." One must then roast it by subliming <note>Sublimation involves heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, purifying it</note> it so many times until, once again, by the power of the fermentation of the earth—exalted <margin>with spirits</margin> together with the bodies—the entire stone descends again from the heaven to the earth and remains fixed <note>original: "fixus" — A substance is 'fixed' when it can endure the heat of the fire without evaporating</note>, that is to say, flowing <note>The stone is "fixed" because it is stable, but "flowing" because it can melt like wax to transform other metals</note>. And this is what he says: *And again it shall descend to the earth, and thus it receives the force of things superior*—namely, by subliming—*and of things inferior*—namely, by descending. Thus, that which is corporeal becomes spiritual in its sublimation, and that which is spiritual becomes corporeal in its descent.

### *Concerning the fruit of the art and the efficacy of the stone. CHAPTER X.*

*And thus you shall have the glory of the brightness of the whole world.* That is to say, by this stone, thus composed, you shall possess the glory of this world. Therefore, all obscurity shall flee from you—that is, all poverty and sickness—because the stone thus composed is a cure for every illness. *And this is the strongest strength of all strength*, because there is no comparison between this stone and the other strengths of this world.

Indeed, if it possesses such power, many miracles would occur within the work of alchemy. And afterward he says that *it descends into the earth,* which means that if those four elements have ascended, they must descend again into the earth, so that they are fixed in the unity of the fifth essence. But since the perfection of any stone consists in the power of its own "earth"—which is called its nurse <note>original: "nutrix"</note> or ferment—according to the testimony of the philosopher <note>The philosopher refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the "Emerald Tablet."</note> who says: *Its nurse is the earth.* <note>A direct quote from the Hermetic "Emerald Tablet."</note> Without this ferment of the spirit, the stone cannot be perfectly contained, nor can it reach the fullness of its power. This is what the philosopher means when he says: *Its power is entire if it be converted into earth.* <note>Another foundational maxim from the "Emerald Tablet," suggesting that the spiritual energy must be grounded in physical matter to be effective.</note> When this occurs, it is called the **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note>; and if you distill it many times from its earth, it will be the rectified and perfected water of life.

**W**HAT are the species <note>original: "species" — here referring to the specific types of matter or substances.</note> that come together in the composition of the Elixir? Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum" — Mercury.</note> and volatile yellow sulfur, fixed green sulfur (which has a black core <note>original: "ventrem nigrum" — literally "black belly," likely referring to the internal state or "soul" of the substance.</note>, though it appears clear), and fixed white sulfur. These are the three sulfurs. They are fluid and meltable, just like wax; the new ones are better than the old. Good green sulfur is that which, when broken, has a clear and shining fracture, like glass, and is found in large pieces. Fixed white sulfur is better when it is thoroughly white, shining in its fracture, and clear; it is better when it consists of oblong grains, both small and large, but especially in the larger pieces. Volatile yellow sulfur is "living sulfur" <note>original: "sulphur vivum" — native or virgin sulfur found naturally in the earth.</note>; it is better when it is in large pieces and not stony. Moreover, quicksilver is combined with the yellow sulfur so that they are altered and become one in a single shining, red, heavy mass; from this composition, two species are sufficient for composing the Elixir. ...seal it with clay <term>clay: known in alchemy as 'lute,' a specialized paste (often made of clay, dung, and hair) used to make glass vessels airtight.</term> carefully, and hereafter nothing of the spirit shall escape through the clay; and this is called by the philosophers the **Work of Spring** <note>original: "opus Veris"</note>. This composition made from the three aforementioned substances is called the **Blessed Stone**, and is also called **mineral**, **animal**, and **vegetable**, because it has no proper name of its own. It is called **mineral** because the things from which the medicine is composed are minerals. It is called **vegetable** because it lives and grows. It is called **animal** because it possesses a soul, a spirit, and a body, just like living animals.

By another name it is called the **Stinking Black** <note>original: "Nigrum foetens"</note>, because it has a black interior and is composed of a stinking spirit. In another way it is called **Chaos**, or the **origin of the world**, or the **confused mass**; we, however, call it **earth**.

# ON ALCHEMY.

Fire and weight are the masters in this art. From these, extract the **blessed water** <note>original: "aquam benedictam"</note>, in the same way as from the other for the **white stage** <note>original: "ad album", referring to the Albedo or whitening phase</note>, neither more nor less. Afterward, take some **red earth** <note>original: "terra rubea", often referring to a metallic oxide or a specific state of the "Stone"</note> and shape it into thin plates, or into scraped filings, and place it in the water as has been said. It will not be dissolved in it, but instead will only be **calcined** <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</term> into a red powder. When this is done, carefully remove the water and put it in another vessel similar to the one it is in, so that the calcined powder of the red earth remains in its own vessel without water.

In the water you removed, place the **white earth** <note>original: "terram albam"</note> and it will be dissolved; thus the water will be of use to you and will not be wasted. The earth that remained calcined should be dried and kept well. The water produced by these weights is stronger than the first, because without a doubt it dissolves **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>, whereas the other does not. Even though it appears to be the same color as the first, it differs because it is golden—that is, it tints things toward **citrine** <term>Citrinitas: The "yellowing" stage of the alchemical work, which falls between the white and red stages.</term>—whereas the first tints things toward black.

This [golden water] dissolves all bodies and the white earth, except for the red earth, which it merely calcines. For this reason, the first water is called by the names of all whitenesses, greennesses, leaves, and trees. The second, however, is called by the names of whitenesses, **yellowings** <note>original: "citrinitatū"</note>, rednesses, blacknesses, and **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris"</note>. And this same water will perfectly dissolve the red earth, which before this point is always imperfect. 

White and red earth, cleansed and refined, are found for sale, so we shall say nothing further about them. This "body" of ours is dissolved more quickly if the **decoction** <term>Decoction: A method of extraction by boiling a substance in a liquid.</term> is performed in many ways— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "mo-" for "modis" (ways).</note>

<summary>This page provides technical instructions for preparing a "golden water" that is stronger than the initial "blessed water," specifically for its ability to dissolve mercury and advance the work toward the citrine (yellow) stage. It emphasizes the different effects these waters have on "white earth" and "red earth."</summary>

...dissolves, and it is called the **first decoction** <term>Decoction: The process of boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence; in alchemy, it refers to prolonged heating.</term>, which is the separation of parts through the power of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note> performed in the common way. Alchemists, however, call it **amalgamation** <term>Amalgamation: The process of blending a metal (like gold or silver) with mercury to create a soft paste or "amalgam."</term>, which is to amalgamate the body—that is, to boil the body with raw Mercury. 

In this process, Mercury assists in our operation according to its own nature; and thus, quicksilver is not our medicine itself, yet it is a help. Some people do not perform this decoction, and that is well, if the body could be dissolved without such a decoction. We shall not [directly] hand over the **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of this science, but we only wish to entice the wise to investigate it. 

Take one pound (of twelve ounces) of **green sulfur**, nine ounces of **white sulfur**, and nine ounces of heavy **red earth**—a total of thirty ounces. Extract the water from these entirely, just as before. To this, add more than double of its **phlegm** <term>Phlegm: A watery, tasteless distillate produced during the heating of substances; considered the "moist" element.</term>, because there is more material present here, until the aforementioned sign appears upon the blade of a knife. 

Afterward, place the calcined powder of the red earth into the resulting water. If it liquefies or "flows" (which are the same thing), the water is good. If it does not, then remove the earth as before, dry it, and make another water, and put in the earth as before. In making this second water, always increase the weight by three ounces of white sulfur and an equal amount of heavy red earth, but do not increase the green sulfur, whose weight always...

<header>### ON ALCHEMY.</header>

...is always equal: and by always adding more of the **phlegm** <term>Phlegm: A watery, tasteless distillate produced during heating; considered the "moist" element of a substance.</term> in double the amount of the others, until you find the water that dissolves our **red earth**. 

Some say that the water which descends before the **alembic** <term>Alembic: A vessel used for distillation, consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap with a long beak that directs steam into a receiver.</term> achieves **rubification** <note>The process of turning red; in alchemy, this is often the final stage of the Great Work.</note> dissolves the **white earth**; and that which descends after the reddening of the alembic should be received in another vessel, because it dissolves the **red earth**. Once this water is perfectly discovered, and the red earth is dissolved in it, it must be kept in a sealed vessel, just as was done before with the other water for the **white work** <note>original: "ad album"</note>. In a similar way, you must repeat the water process until you have a good quantity of it. 

Into the singular water prepared from the red earth—which has been reduced into thin plates and into powder—place two **drachms** <term>Drachm (or Dram): An ancient unit of weight; here, two drachms equal a quarter of an ounce.</term> (that is, a quarter of an **ounce** <term>Ounce: A unit of weight; traditionally one-twelfth or one-sixteenth of a pound.</term>). If it can dissolve more, add more, but do not exceed one additional drachm. Understand this to apply to both **calcined** <term>Calcined: A substance reduced to a powder or friable state by the action of heat.</term> red earth and uncalcined earth. If any of the aforementioned earth remains undissolved in the water, keep that undissolved part aside, so that it may be dissolved in another solution and with other water, because water only dissolves what it is capable of. 

The **white water** is called **Alphido** <note>Likely referring to Alphidius, a legendary figure in alchemical literature often cited in medieval texts.</note>, or the Virgin, or the Maiden with a beautiful face, whose eyes are black and whose eyebrows are joined, Pregnant, having one breast. Otherwise, it is called by **Hortolanus** <note>A 14th-century alchemist, also known as Ortholanus, famous for his commentaries on the Emerald Tablet.</note> "white and cold **female seed**" <note>original: "sperma fœmininum"</note>. The **red water** is called by **Alphidius** a handsome youth with a black head, wearing a beautiful garment because it is golden.

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>### ARNOLD <note>Referring to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist whose works were foundational to the medieval tradition.</note></header>

Alternatively, according to **Hortulanus** <note>The Gardener (Hortulanus) was a legendary alchemical author, famously known for his commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, the male seed <note>original: "sperma masculinum"</note> is red and hot. In another way, the **first water** is named—before the body is dissolved in it—the **urine of girls** <note>Alchemists often used "human" names like urine, milk, or blood as code for different chemical distillates or acids.</note>. This **second red water** is called the **urine of men**; and the mixture of both is called the **urine of infants**. Note that when the weights are increased to make the red water, the vessels must also be increased—that is, the material must be placed in a larger vessel, which should be half-full and no more. 

Take equal parts by weight of the white water and the red water, and put those two waters together in a single **cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit: A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the lower part of a still for heating materials.</term> made of glass, strong and thick, having a mouth like a **urinal** <term>Urinal: A specific shape of glass vessel, wide at the bottom with a narrow neck, resembling those used by medieval doctors for inspecting urine.</term>. Afterward, all the water will turn a lemon-yellow color, or will do so quite quickly, and thus it will be the perfected, true **Elixir** for both <note>Likely referring to the Elixir's ability to transmute metals into both silver (white) and gold (red).</note>, a perfect **impregnation**, and a true union. This water is called our gold <note>original: "aurum nostrum"</note>, our silver <note>original: "argentum nostrum"</note>, heavenly water, and glorious water, because of the **Fifth Essence** <term>Fifth Essence (Quintessence): The purest, most spiritual part of a substance, thought to be the "spirit" that remains after the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water) are refined away.</term> existing within it. 

Similarly, it is called our brass, our vinegar, and our **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In medieval alchemy, this did not refer to the element magnesium, but to a mysterious "prime matter" or a dark mineral substance essential to the Work.</term>, in which there are four bodies—that is, the elements. These four bodies are the extracted clouds and snows, the volatile part and the butter, and the foam or spirit of the **Moon** <note>Moon (Luna) is the common alchemical code for silver.</note>. Likewise, it is called the **ferment of the stone** for both works, and **black lead**, and our whole operation, and the wisdom of all philosophers, and of all **hens** <note>The "hen" is a metaphor for the heat of incubation and the "Philosophic Egg," the vessel in which the alchemical transformation takes place.</note>, and our wisdom. As soon as you have placed the waters in the cucurbits, cover the vessel so that none of the spirit of the **Fifth Essence** escapes, until they have been joined together and become one single thing.

<header>### ON ALCHEMY.</header>

...itself, a red and clear water. These two **seeds** <note>original: "spermata" — referring to the generative fluids or principles of the matter.</note> are necessary in this art: its father is the **Sun**; its mother is the **Moon**. They are necessary because the **Sun** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold or the hot, dry masculine principle.</note> and the **Moon** <note>The Moon represents Silver or the cool, moist feminine principle.</note> are difficult to melt when they are alone, but joined together they flow and liquefy easily. Goldsmiths know this well, and therefore this union was necessary because the final secret is to possess a medicine that flows before the **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium vivum" — quicksilver, known for its extreme volatility and tendency to evaporate when heated.</note> which flies away from the fire. For this reason, take care that the spirit of the **fifth essence** <term>Fifth Essence (Quintessence): The fifth element, beyond earth, air, fire, and water; it was thought to be the celestial "breath of life" within matter.</term> does not escape, as it is held back by this union; and thus the work will be completed, God permitting. 

When these two waters are joined, the **Blessed Stone** <note>original: "lapis Benedictus" — another name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is conceived in the belly of the wind; the earth is the nurse of this water. Note that the mother and father of the stone are called **Sun** and **Moon** during the composition of the **Elixir** <term>Elixir: A refined substance sought by alchemists to transform base metals and prolong life.</term>; later, during the operation of the stone, they are called the "earth" or the "nurse."

**Azuria**, that is, grace <note>While "Azuria" typically refers to the color blue (azure), the definition "gratia" (grace) suggests a symbolic or spiritual interpretation of the color's purity.</note>.

**Arabic**, that is, great saffron. <note>original: "crocum magnum" — in alchemical terms, "saffron" usually refers to a fine red or yellow powder, often an oxide of iron or mercury.</note>
**Arsubar**, that is, *bodequar*.
**Assagen**, that is, dragon’s blood. <note>A bright red resin obtained from certain plants, used as a pigment and in medicinal preparations.</note>
**Arfiora**, that is, ceruse. <term>Ceruse: White lead, a common pigment and alchemical ingredient produced by exposing lead to vinegar vapors.</term>

If, however, the spirit be joined with a white body <note>original: "corpore albo"; refers to silver or the lunar stage of the work.</note>, it will be the medicine or Elixir for the white [silver]. Sublimated mercury <note>Mercury that has been heated into a vapor and solidified again, usually as a corrosive powder.</note> will be quickened <note>original: "viuificabitur"; to be restored to its liquid, "living" metallic state from a powdered or "mortified" state.</note> only a little; however, if the mercury is quickened, it will cause all the white mercury to be quickened. The first operation, therefore, is that you should sublime mercury with Roman vitriol <note>original: "vitriolo Romano"; blue vitriol or copper sulfate.</note>, or copperas <note>original: "coporosa"; green vitriol or iron sulfate.</note>, until it is well mortified <note>original: "mortificatus"; a process where a metal loses its metallic form and luster, appearing "dead" or as a dull powder.</note>, so that there is one part mercury and another part vitriol or copperas; or, if you wish, you can use two parts of copperas or vitriol. ...with vitriol <note>original: "vitriolo"; typically copper or iron sulfate used as a reagent.</note>, as much as of the sublimated mercury. However, in each instance, new vitriol must be mixed with the aforementioned sublimated mercury; and this shall be the **first operation**, which is called the **operation of the spirit** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are substances like mercury or sulfur that can be vaporized by heat.</note>.

There follows the **second operation**, which is that you should take equal parts <note>original: "ana"; a traditional pharmaceutical and alchemical term meaning equal parts of each ingredient.</note> of the aforementioned mercury (sublimated seven times) and of the purest "sun" <note>original: "solis"; the alchemical name for gold.</note> which has been very well calcined <note>original: "calcinati"; the process of heating a metal until it is reduced to a fine, brittle powder.</note>. These two similar substances, once mixed and incorporated upon a marble slab, place in a glass round flask <note>original: "rotumba"</note> or ampoule, and close the opening or mouth of the vessel with the **lute of wisdom** <note>original: "luto sapientiæ"; a specialized airtight sealant used to prevent the escape of vapors during heating.</note>.

Then, let it be placed in a weak fire of ashes <note>original: "igne cinerum"; a method of gentle, indirect heating where the vessel sits in a bed of warm ash or sand.</note>, and let it stay there for at least nine days in the said ampoule. Let the ashes be buried over the vessel in a small quantity, for it is sufficient only that it be covered by the ashes. Leave it thus under the aforementioned ashes until you see that all the mercury has risen to the top of the sides of the said round flask. Then, release [the material] and cause the calcined body <note>The gold powder.</note> to fall, or sit upon the mercury. Then, once again leave the said round flask in the same manner under the hot ashes.

And know that all the mercury usually rises within twelve hours. When the nine days have finished, provide a stronger fire, so that whatever can be sublimated may rise and be sublimated. Once this is done, empty the vessel with caution, lest the sublimated material be mixed with the material which remained in the lower part of the aforementioned round flask.

# ON ALCHEMY.

...completed. Following this is the **third operation**, which consists of taking that which was sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process where a substance is heated until it turns into vapor and then collects again as a solid on a cooler surface; it was a primary method of purification in alchemy.</note> according to the method described before. One need not worry about what remains in the bottom of the vessel for this work; however, you could reduce that residue back into a "body" <note>The "body" refers to the solid, metallic state of a substance as opposed to its "spirit" or vaporous state.</note>, and it will be as good as, or perhaps better than, it was before.

And place that sublimated material into a round flask <note>original: "rotumba"; a spherical glass laboratory vessel.</note>. Set this over a slow fire as you did before, and rotate it just as you did above. Continue turning it until the sublimated substance within falls back down drop by drop. This process will take place over the course of one month—either thirty days, or forty at the most.

When you see that the matter has settled at the bottom of the round flask and will no longer rise through sublimation, then leave the flask and that same matter over the same weak fire for another thirty days. At that point, the **medicine** <note>The "medicine," also called the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, is the final transformed substance capable of performing transmutation.</note> will remain, fused into a single brittle mass.

One weight of the aforementioned brittle mass converts thirty weights of **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturni"; the alchemical name for lead.</note> into true **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical name for gold.</note> or into true **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for silver.</note>, depending on how the medicine was initially prepared.

Following this is the **fourth and final operation**, through which the **multiplication** <note>Multiplication is the process of increasing the quantity and the "potency" or power of the alchemical medicine so that it can transmute even larger amounts of base metal with a smaller dose.</note> of the medicine is achieved, both in terms of increasing its quantity and increasing its effectiveness in quality.

Take one part of this medicine and two parts of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"; quicksilver.</note> that has been sublimated seven times. Mix these together and place them in a round flask. Cook the mixture by rotating and turning it as before until it falls back drop by drop. This is completed in eight days. And know...

Give it a slow fire at first, then gradually strengthen it. Then, once the vessel has cooled, see what has ascended (the sublimate) and what remained in the bottom. Combine them and grind them together without adding any more of our water. Then cook it over a slow fire, strengthening the heat as before. Repeat this until the matter remains entirely **fixed** <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixa"; referring to a substance that has become stable under heat and will no longer vaporize or escape the vessel.</note> in the bottom of the cucurbit, so that nothing more can be sublimated from it.

The essence <note>original: "ratio"</note> in animals and mineral spirits, and in arsenics, is the soul <note>In an alchemical context, the "soul" refers to the vital force or internal essence that gives a substance its specific properties.</note>, and it is mineral. Whatever is desired from arsenic is that it should whiten its union <note>original: "uinitionem"; likely a variant of "unitionem" or union with other metals.</note> and that we should remove its burning quality from it. And **Geber, son of Hayyam** <note>original: "Geber filius Haiem"; the Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century figure in the history of chemistry and alchemy.</note>, said that God would help him in the stripping away <note>The text ends mid-sentence: "spoliatio-".</note>...

### Concerning Mercury, Chapter V.

The nature of quicksilver <note>original: "viuo argento"; literally "living silver," the standard Latin term for mercury</note>. Know that it is cold and moist, and God created all minerals from it: therefore, it is their origin. It is airy and flees from fire, but if it remains with the fire for even a little while, it will perform wonderful and profound works. It alone is a pure spirit <note>original: "spiritus mundus"; in alchemy, a "spirit" is a substance that can be vaporized by heat</note>, and there is nothing else in the world of such a nature that it can perform what this performs. It is that which enters any body—that is, it penetrates, lifts, and exalts <note>to "exalt" a substance meant to refine it or raise it to a higher state of "perfection"</note> bodies. 

Therefore, when it has mixed itself with any body, it will vivify and illuminate it, and it will transmute it from one state to another state, and from color to color. If it is mixed or joined with a body, it will be the ferment <note>a substance that acts like yeast, "leavening" the base metal into a noble one</note> of that body, and then the whole will become <term>Yefir</term> <note>a term likely derived from Arabic alchemical vocabulary, referring to a specific state of the elixir or the "philosopher's stone" in its powdered form</note> toward whiteness and redness. 

It is the perennial water, and it is the "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note> and "virgin’s milk" <note>original: "lac virginis"; a common alchemical metaphor for a white, corrosive, or transformative liquid</note>, and it is the cleansing and washing herb. It is the "fountain of living things" <note>original: "fons animalium"</note>, because if anyone were to drink from it, they would not die for eternity. It is a retainer of color and a medium of color, and it makes bodies receptive to color. It mortifies <note>to "kill" or strip a metal of its outward characteristics</note> and vivifies <note>to "bring to life" or restore a substance to a noble state</note>, God willing; it dries and moistens, and it cools and heats.

### ON MINERALS

...you speak of, but I gave birth to you, and you draw your origin from me, and a certain part of me gives life to many parts of you. One seasoning is the exaltation of <term>salt of atramentum</term> <note>original: "salis atramenti"; likely vitriol or ferrous sulfate used for its acidic properties</note>, and also of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used as a flux</note>, and also with bodies <term>fragmentation</term> <note>original: "bucellatio"; the process of breaking metals into "bucella" or small morsels</note>, that is, reduction <note>original: "abatio"</note>, and with the scent <note>the vapors or fumes</note> of <term>tin</term>, and with the scent of <term>sulfur</term>.

Afterwards, place it in an <term>aliphea</term> <note>a specific type of alchemical flask or crucible</note>, but see that no humidity remains in it. Let the <term>quicksilver</term> first be roasted in a <term>bread oven</term> for one night; in the morning, extract it from the oven and "drench" it <note>original: "potabis", literally "to give a drink to"; meaning to saturate the dry powder with the liquid salt solution</note> with the dissolved salt, and afterwards replace it in the oven. Do this many times until it turns black, for the more you place it in the oven, the more color it acquires for itself.

### Another method for the same matter. CHAPTER VII.

Take clear water in some vessel and put in it crushed **almartat** <note>original: "almartat"; a term likely derived from the Arabic *al-martak*, referring to litharge or lead oxide</note> and let it boil several times; afterward heat **gold leaves** <term>auri folia</term> and quench them in it many times, until the gold can be ground. Put this in your works, and you will rejoice in it. 

Another good method as well: Take gold filings and mix **arsenic** <note>original: "arsenicum"; used here as a corrosive agent to break down the noble metal</note> with them, and place this in a thick cloth. Coat the cloth with the **clay of wisdom** <term>luto sapiétiæ</term> <note>a specialized airtight sealing clay used to protect vessels from direct fire</note> and roast it with fire for one night. Then take it out and grind it, and wash it with salt water. Add an equal amount of well-ground salt and place it in a vessel in the furnace until it becomes **white lime** <term>calx alba</term> <note>a fine white powder produced by intense heating, or calcination</note>.

### Concerning the same. CHAPTER VIII.

Take the finest gold, as much as you wish, and make leaves from it. Heat these and quench them in salt water, and afterward in another water in which **lead** <term>plumbum</term> has been melted for so long that the water became black. Then grind these leaves until they are well pulverized, so much so that you cannot feel them with your fingers; and afterward work with it, God willing.

## On Iron CHAPTER XI.

The nature of iron is as follows. Iron belongs to the domain of **Mars** <note>original: "Martis"; in alchemy, each metal is governed by a celestial body; iron is linked to the god of war</note>, and its nature is hot and dry—though some have called it cold and dry—and it is both masculine and feminine in taste. It is the very source of strength, enduring fire while struggling against fire. It is dissolved by four things: namely **arsenic**, **lead**, **magnesia** <note>a term used broadly in alchemy for various mineral ores, often manganese or magnesium oxides</note>, and **marcasite** <note>iron pyrite, often called "fool's gold"</note>. It can be mixed and joined with gold, and is never separated <note>original: "examinatur"; tested or refined out</note> from it, neither by those same things nor by any other. But when you mix silver with gold, iron colors it with a beautiful **tincture** <note>a substance capable of staining or transforming the color and quality of a metal</note>; it will be improved if it is "cooked," and this is the greatest secret among the secrets of the **Indian sages**. 

Choose iron among the other [metallic] bodies because it completes its work quickly and easily, and its tincture is lasting in our Great Work, both in the white and the red <note>referring to the *albedo* (whitening) and *rubedo* (reddening) stages of the alchemical process</note>. Its **preparation** <term>condimentum</term> <note>literally "seasoning," but here refers to the chemical treatment of the metal</note> is to dissolve it through melting and **sal ammoniac** <term>sale armoniaco</term> <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note>; we shall name all these things later. This is the account of its preparation:

We have already said that iron is harder and stronger than all other bodies, and it does not dissolve in fire except through great effort. This is how you proceed: take thin sheets <note>original: "foliis"; literally "leaves" or filings</note> of it and heat them in the fire until they glow red, then quench them in oil in which lead has been melted several times. Continue until they are diminished—that is, they break into fragments which are also light. Then, cut them with shears as small as you can

## Chapter 12: On Copper

**The relation of gold to copper.** **Copper** <note>original: "cuprum"</note> shares in the nature of gold; it is hot and dry, except that its dryness is less than the dryness of **iron**. It possesses the same hardness as **silver** <note>original: "argento"</note> and the same melting point, except that it is red in color. Therefore, if anyone were to remove its redness, it would be silver, because on the surface it is copper, but inwardly it is silver. Pythagoras says that lead is a "magnitude" <note>likely meaning a fundamental bulk or prime matter</note>, and that everything is hidden within it. This is because lead is a "sulfurated water" and a "burning coldness," for it extinguishes [cold] with the heat of its "masculine" principle <note>alchemists viewed metals as having balanced gendered qualities; lead was often seen as "cold" externally but "hot" internally</note>. Indeed, lead is the "brother" of **gold** in all its properties, but **gold** is a lasting and heavy body, unified, which endures beneath the earth and withstands air and water without being changed, just as we have said.

Dissolve that in salt ammoniac <term>sale armoniaco</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux to clean metals.</note> which has been dissolved in vinegar, and "wax" <note>The process of *inceration*, or adding liquid drop by drop to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy consistency.</note> the material with it until it is all "drunk up" or absorbed.

Then it will be a very good Elixir <note>The "Elixir" or Philosopher's Stone was the sought-after substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver.</note>, and you will not need anything else, God willing. Place one part of it upon a clean substance and it will bind and harden it; it will also remove its "velocity" <note>likely referring to the metal's volatility or tendency to oxidize quickly</note> and its foul smell. Afterward, cast one part of that upon red copper, and it will whiten it with a beautiful whiteness. Therefore, join it with silver however you wish; you will have your profit in a single day. It is the best and closest [to silver] that can be, and it is sufficient for you in place of all others. Therefore, hide this secret.

### On Salts. Chapter XXIII.

**The theory of salt.** Know that there are many types of salts, and the most noble is that which is called rock salt <note>original: "sal gemma"; literally "gem salt," referring to pure mineral halite.</note>, and next is common salt <note>original: "sal panis"; literally "bread salt," the type used for food.</note>, and next is Indian salt, which is red, and then Nabataean salt <note>Salt sourced from the Nabataean regions, likely near the Dead Sea.</note>, and then salt of Lime, and finally Bitter salt. This last one is found in the "island" of Spain <note>original: "insula Hispaniæ"; medieval geographers often referred to the Iberian Peninsula—Al-Andalus—as an island.</note> which is called Al-Andalus, near the Pool of Maria and in the place called Belinchot. Its nature is hot and dry; it is essentially water that fire has dried. 

Among its properties is that it dissolves silver through the strength of fire, adding a whiteness to that silver, and changing it from a "bodily" state into a "spiritual" one <note>In the alchemical tradition, "spiritual" refers to a state where a metal has been refined or made volatile, losing its dense, "dead" physical form to become more subtle.</note>. It acts similarly with gold, increasing its redness; it washes bodies of their defilement and removes their impurities. You should calcine <term>calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures, usually to oxidize it or reduce it to a fine powder.</term> metallic bodies with this salt and no other. For this reason, the wise have called it "the silver of the people" <note>original: "argentum populi"; this may imply that salt is as ubiquitous and essential as common currency.</note>, because all nations require it and use it in all things and seasonings of the whole world. All creatures are improved by it, and God has greatly praised it in the histories...

# GARLANDIVS

...thrice and place it in a glazed pot, and for each pound of this same alum, add six pounds of pure and fresh water. Cook it over the fire until the water is reduced to a fifth part, and leave it until it clears and assumes its clarity. Throw away the dregs, and afterwards place it in a glazed [pot] or a copper pot and let it boil gently and very softly. Let it coagulate <term>coagulate: to thicken or solidify from a liquid state.</term> and be clarified in the manner of crystal; this will be **noble salt** <note>original: "sal nobile"; a highly refined salt believed to have superior transformative powers.</note>. Keep it well and rejoice with it.

### The Work of Atracar
The **Work of Atracar** <note>original: "Opus de atracar"; likely a Latinized version of an Arabic alchemical term referring to a process of preparation or joining.</note>, which is made from the salt we mentioned before: Take as much of that **noble salt** as you wish, and dissolve it in double the amount of lime water <note>original: "aqua calcis"; water treated with calcium oxide (quicklime), used as a caustic solvent.</note> after it has been cleared for several days. Then, take as much **common salt** <note>original: "sale panis"; literally "salt of bread," meaning common table salt or sea salt.</note> as you took of the aforementioned salt, and dissolve it in double the amount of cold water in which two ounces [℥] of bee's honey have been dissolved. Mix both waters together afterwards, and cook them over the fire with a light heat until the mixture coagulates in the manner of crystal. Then hide it and keep silent, because here is one of the highest utilities.

Then, when you wish to dissolve any body <note>original: "corpus"; in alchemy, this usually refers to one of the seven metals.</note>, take it—and let that body which you desire to dissolve be powdered, or calcined <term>calcined: reduced to a powder by thorough heating or roasting.</term>, or in the form of filings; or if it is a stone, let it be well ground. Place it in a glazed vessel smeared around with sealing clay <note>original: "argilla ableuersi"; likely referring to *lutum sapientiae* or "lute of wisdom," a paste used to seal alchemical vessels airtight.</note> and kindle a fire under it until it is dissolved like tallow <note>original: "sepū" (sepum); animal fat or grease, implying the metal reaches a liquid or oily consistency.</note>. Then hide this **noble salt** and praise God, who has granted this to you, because with this, **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury (Latin: vivum argentum).</term> will be coagulated, and it exalts or...

The reasoning regarding sal ammoniac. <header>GARLAND</header>

# THE LIFE OF JOHN
## *Garland, a most excellent*
### *philosopher.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' within a square border, depicting a figure in a scholarly or clerical robe standing amidst scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

**John of Garland**, Grammarian and Poet, from his tender years of childhood, consecrated himself entirely to the **liberal arts** <term>liberal arts: the traditional medieval curriculum consisting of the trivium (grammar, logic, and rhetoric) and the quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy).</term> as that age offered them. Afterwards, as the years passed, while England was being ravaged by Viking invasions <note>original: "Danorum incursionibus"; literally "incursions of the Danes."</note>, he left the schools of his homeland and betook himself to studies overseas, where he drank in the liberal arts in great abundance and with a full mouth, as if from the source itself. 

Through this persistent diligence and industry following an honorable education, which he devoted to his studies, he easily surpassed every single person who was learning alongside him. This labor was by no means useless, for he immediately earned a name for himself of exceptional glory. For certain noblemen, delighted by his skill and eloquence, retained him under honorable conditions so that he might cultivate the youth in the elements of the Latin language and poetry. 

Because of this, a great number of scholars soon flocked to him, whom he inspired toward honorable studies through his public lectures. Finally, for the benefit of posterity, he produced many short works, nearly all of whose titles **Bolton of Bury** <note>referring to John Boston of Bury, a 15th-century English monk and pioneering bibliographer.</note> records in his great **Catalog**.

<summary>This page introduces the biography of John of Garland, a noted English grammarian and poet who fled the Viking invasions to study abroad and eventually became a celebrated teacher of Latin and poetry.</summary>
<keywords>John of Garland, biography, liberal arts, Viking invasions, Latin education, poetry, John Boston of Bury, medieval scholars</keywords>

# A POEM BY LEONARD
## PROEBSTEL.

Behold, for you who strive toward the sacred citadel of Alchemy,
*A book has come forth, full of a not-unpleasant art,*
Which teaches how to form the stone through tireless effort,
*Than which this vast world possesses nothing greater.*
For it strengthens minds weighed down by care and bodies by disease,
*And this stone increases wealth immensely.*
<margin>a</margin>From this, it is said that Medea, driven by excessive grief,
*Restored life to the Thessalian Leader.* <note>original: "Thessalico uitam restituisse Duci." In mythology, the sorceress Medea used her alchemical-like potions to restore youth to Aeson, the father of Jason (the leader of the Thessalians).</note>
From this, it is well known that the Arabs, relying on these riches,
*And with a firm heart, did not fear Roman leaders.*
See how great things are taught in such a slender book:
*How a small field is cultivated with such a charming flower.*
Nor does it merely dye base metals for a double purpose, <note>original: "tingit." In alchemy, "tincturing" refers to the process of transforming the properties and color of a metal, usually into gold or silver.</note>
*As the unlearned crowd does everywhere.*
But because those [metallic] bodies swell with cruel diseases,
*It applies divine medical hands through its art.*
It removes what is excessive and provides everything that is lacking,
*It purifies all metals in wondrous ways.*
The idle crowd wastes wealth and reputation and stirs up heavy anger,
*While it constructs deceits with a blind art.*
It does not know how to weigh the secret meanings of the ancients,
*And it neglects your books, O learned Geber.* <term>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 9th-century polymath whose works were considered the foundation of European alchemy.</term>
Therefore, whoever you are who plows the treacherous sea of Alchemy with your vessel,
*So that you may safely seek the depths amidst the waves,*
I ask that you look upon this table with an open brow,
*May this learned table nourish your mind.* <note>original: "Tabella." Here referring to the book or the summarized knowledge presented within it.</note>

<summary>A prefatory poem by Leonard Proebstel praising the virtues of alchemy and the Philosopher's Stone, which is credited with healing bodies, increasing wealth, and even restoring youth. The author contrasts the true "learned" art with the deceptive practices of the ignorant and invokes the authority of the master alchemist Geber.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Leonard Proebstel, Medea, Geber, Transmutation, Medical Alchemy, Tincture</keywords>

<sig>H 5</sig>

Once, Thrice-Greatest Hermes founded with his genius <note>original: "ter maximus Hermes." This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure credited as the father of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>
   This art, so that Hermes might aid the wealth of the Assyrians: <note>The "Assyrians" here represent the ancient, wealthy empires of the East where alchemical secrets were said to have originated.</note>
Here, as it were, he established the first principles of the highest Stone, <term>lapis</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note>
   And here he teaches the true seeds of the Elixir. <term>Elyxirij</term>
He wrapped it in mists and hid it with thick darkness,
   Lest the wicked crowd grasp the sacred meanings.
The Jacobite indeed unfolded it with much labor, <note>original: "Iacobita." This likely refers to the author, John of Garland (Johannes de Garlandia), whose name was sometimes associated with Jacobite or English origins in medieval bibliographic traditions.</note>
   And he dispelled the heavy mists with his skill.
At last, Herold brings this work forth out of the shadows, <note>Johannes Herold (1514–1567) was the editor and printer responsible for publishing this collection of alchemical texts.</note>
   So that it may benefit your studies, friendly reader.
To this, add immediately the writings of the ancient sages <term>sophorum</term>
   Nor let all things be proven to you in easy ways;
Weigh the hidden courses of nature in your mind,
   For great advantages fall only to great labor.
You will receive no fruits with any somber profit,
   Unless you steer the proper ship by the art of Alchemy. <term>Chymia</term> <note>The image of "steering a ship" was a common alchemical metaphor for managing the volatile heat and materials within the laboratory vessel.</note>

<summary>A prefatory poem tracing the transmission of alchemical knowledge from Hermes Trismegistus through John of Garland to the editor Johannes Herold, warning that the art requires great effort.</summary>

**A**LCHEMY can be counted among the mechanical <term>mechanical arts: in the Middle Ages, these were practical crafts like weaving, smithing, or agriculture, distinguished from the "liberal arts" like logic or music.</term> arts, and it is of no small use to several of the others, such as to smithing and medicine. To smithing indeed, it is useful for the examination, mixing, separation, and transformation <note>original: "transmutationem," the alchemical process of changing one metal into another.</note> of metals. Likewise, it is useful to medicine for the separation of healthy substances or qualities from harmful ones, which are frequently mixed together even in simple medicines. 

<margin>From the doctrine of Alchemy.</margin> 

Alchemy is properly the art of transforming mineral bodies from their own species into others, such as metals and similar things. This descends from that part of natural philosophy <note>natural philosophy: the study of nature and the physical universe, which was the precursor to modern science.</note> which deals with minerals, just as agriculture descends from that part which deals with plants. For craftsmen adopted this from the students of nature, although the things produced [by art] are not as certain or specific as those produced by nature.

From the things stated above, it seems to be implied that

For the regions of the East, where precious stones are found, are closest to the **Sun**. So too with glass: the more it is touched by the heat of the Sun, the more it is worth. ### On the multiple kinds of fire.

Fire is of many kinds, and its quality is diverse, distinguished by certain degrees. For one type of fire is hot in the first degree and moist in the second, such as the fire of the **horse’s belly** <term>ventris equi: the gentle, moist heat produced by a heap of fermenting horse manure, used for slow digestion of materials</term>, which was mentioned in the previous chapter. Its property is that it does not destroy the oil, but increases it because of its moisture. For other fires destroy it because of their dryness. Nothing else in the world is likened to this except for the natural heat of a healthy human body. Indeed, the **fire of the Sun** is hot in the same degree, but it is dry. This [fire] is the one that masters the matter; it is remade and nourished by animate things, just like a child who is given milk in the beginning. For a child grows from heat and moisture; in the same way, the horse-fire increases the oil with its moisture, and fixes the **stone that is not a stone** <note>original: "lapidem non lapidem," a famous alchemical riddle referring to the Philosopher's Stone, which is a "stone" in name and power but not in physical substance.</note> with its heat.

# ON ALCHEMY

Besides these two <note>Referring to the "fire of the horse's belly" and the "fire of the sun" from the previous page.</note> there is also another, which is hot and dry in the second degree, such as the **fire of an oven** after the bread has been removed; this melts gently and does not burn, because there is no flame in it nor intensity of heat. For the heat recedes by gradually declining; but if it remained steady, it would fix the spirit <term>fix: the process of "fixation," making a volatile substance (like mercury or sulfur) stable and resistant to heat so it does not evaporate</term> within the body or outside the body. The **fire of the horse** <note>original: "ignis equi"; referring to the heat of fermenting manure</note>, however, does not melt nor burn, but masters the substance and increases its moisture. There is also the **furnace of fixation**; this melts and fixes, but does not burn, because there is no flame; it does not differ from the preceding except that in this one there is continuous heat, while in that one there is not.

The fifth is called **flaming** <note>original: "flammalis"</note>, and it is hot and dry in the third degree; this only calcinates <term>calcination: heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or "calx" without melting it</term> and does not melt—specifically in comparison to gold and silver, and other bodies in the same degree or beyond. This fire is also used in the **furnace of calcination**.

The sixth is hot and dry in the fourth degree, and here it melts and fixes strongly, softening the bodies gently, and does not dissipate or disperse them; this is the **fire of the furnace of fusion** <term>fusion: the alchemical process of melting a solid into a liquid</term>. In the same degree is also the **fire of the bellows** <note>original: "ignis follium"</note>, which dissipates, disperses, and melts bodies: and this is the seventh.

The eighth is that which melts and calcinates, and it is flaming, because in it only the flame operates, and it does not dissipate the matter; such is the **glassmaker’s fire** <note>original: "ignis vitrearius"</note>. This fire is like coals and flame, but in this specific one, there is only the flame of wood. This also is in the same degree as the preceding ones. In this same degree as well is that which is the master of all, such as the fire...
