### ***On mineral bodies, from the fourth book of the Meteorology.*** <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Meteorologica*, which provided the foundational theory that minerals were formed from "vapors" and "exhalations" trapped in the earth.</note>

Mineral bodies are divided into four species, namely into stones, liquefiable substances <term>liquefactiua: materials that can be melted</term>, sulfurous substances, and salts. Some of these are of a rare substance and weak composition, while others are indeed of a strong substance; some are ductile <term>ductility: the property of a metal that allows it to be hammered thin or drawn out into wire without breaking</term>, and some are not.

Among those that are of a weak substance, some are salts, which melt gently from moisture, such as burnt alum <note>original: "alumen calfiuatū"; likely calcined or roasted alum, used as a mordant in dyeing and in medicine</note> and sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to clean metals and "spiritualize" substances</term>. Some are oily <note>original: "vnctuosa"</note> and do not easily melt by moisture alone, such as sulfur and orpiment <term>orpiment: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and thought to contain the "seed" of gold</term>. 

However, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> belongs to the second group, even though it is the element of ductile things and is similar to certain ductile substances. For the most part, all things that can be liquefied are ductile, and those that cannot be liquefied are not ductile, nor can they be softened except with great force. 

Now, the material of ductile things is a watery substance mixed together with an earthy substance in a strong mixture, so that one cannot be separated from the other. Its substance is congealed with cold after the action of heat upon it, which is *optesis* <note>original: "optesis"; a Greek term used by Aristotle to describe "roasting" or "baking" by dry heat, as opposed to "hepsesis" or boiling</note>, that is, a digestion <term>digestion: a process of chemical ripening or transformation through heat</term> which comes from dry heat. ...is like the example of wine which has not yet frozen <note>original: "gelauit"</note> because of its oiliness <note>original: "unctuositatem"</note>, and for this reason, it is ductile <term>ductibile: here meaning fluid or capable of being drawn out, a property the author attributes to the "oily" nature of quicksilver</term>. On the other hand, the stony parts of mineral substances are materially composed of water, but it is not water alone that solidifies <note>original: "gelatur"</note> them; rather, it is water combined with a dryness that transforms the watery nature into an earthy nature, and there is no excessively oily moisture in them. Therefore, they are not ductile, and because their solidification <term>coagulatio: the process of thickening or becoming solid</term> arises from dryness, they do not dissolve easily except through natural arts <note>original: "ingenia naturalia," referring to clever chemical or physical processes</note>.

Alum and sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, highly valued for its ability to "spiritize" or sublimate other materials</term> belong to the category of salts, except that the fire in sal ammoniac is greater than the earth; for this reason, the whole substance is sublimated <term>sublimation: the process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid, used here to describe the "fiery" nature of the salt</term>. It is essentially water mixed with an extremely subtle hot smoke of great fieriness, and it is solidified by dryness.

The wateriness of sulfurous substances, however, is mixed with earth in a powerful combination, through the fermentation of heat, until they become oily, and afterward, they are solidified by cold.

Vitriols <term>attramenta: literally "blackening substances," these are metallic sulfates used to make ink and dyes</term> are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; there is in them some power of liquefiable bodies because they are formed from them. For instance, blue vitriol <term>chalchantum: copper sulfate</term> and *alachar* <note>original: "alachar"; likely a medieval Latin transliteration of an Arabic term for a specific mineral salt or burnt substance</note> are generated from the more substantial parts of heavy vitriol. Its saltiness <note>original: "falsedo"; likely a transcription error for "salsedo," meaning saltiness or brine</note> is not dissolved except along with the sulfurous part within it, and afterward, the remainder solidifies. This substance has now taken on a mineral power in certain bodies. That which has taken on the power of iron will be red or saffron-colored, while that which has taken on the power of copper <note>original: "vim æream"; *aes* can refer to copper or bronze</note> will be green; hence it is possible for these two to be [produced] artificially...

### Concerning metals and their creation. Avicenna in his book *On the Soul*. <note>While the famous Persian philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina) wrote on minerals, the work *De Anima in arte alchimiae* mentioned here was a later medieval Latin text attributed to him by alchemists to lend it authority.</note>

The philosophers say that there are six things which can be drawn out with a hammer at the furnace: the Sun, the Moon, bronze, iron, tin, and lead, and they are created naturally beneath the earth. <note>In alchemical shorthand, the Sun (Sol) refers to gold, and the Moon (Luna) refers to silver.</note> For gold is made in the belly of the earth with the great heat of the Sun, from living gold <term>auro viuo: traditionally "argentum vivum" (quicksilver/mercury); the author here uses "living gold" to describe the pure mercurial essence</term>, beautiful and with red sulfur, clear and without stones, cooked for a hundred years and more. Silver is made from living gold—that is, clear [quicksilver]—and clear sulfur, cooked for a hundred years. Copper <note>original: "Cuprum," often used interchangeably with bronze or brass "æs" in this period</note>, however, is made from thick living gold and thick red sulfur, cooked for hundreds of years. 

But gold indeed is excessively cooked and hardened; therefore, neither fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth destroys it. Silver, however, is raw and not [fully] cooked; therefore, the earth quickly destroys it <note>This refers to the tendency of silver to tarnish or corrode when buried, unlike gold.</note>. Copper, truly, is burnt; therefore, the earth does not destroy it except over many years, but fire consumes it quickly. 

But the philosophers say lead is made beneath the earth from thick and dense living gold, and from the worst and mixed sulfur, raw and little cooked, so that lead is indeed of such a bad nature that with its odor <note>original: "odore," likely referring to the fumes or the "spirit" of the metal during smelting</note> it breaks gold and binds living gold. ### *Concerning Gold, from the Book on Alums and Salts* <note>original: "De aluminibus & salibus"; this was a highly influential alchemical treatise, likely of 12th-century Arabic origin, often attributed to the Persian physician Al-Razi (Rhazes).</note>

Gold is hot and moist <note>In medieval science, every substance was defined by its "complexion" or balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, more noble than all other bodies, their king and lord. It is corrupted by neither earth, nor air, nor water, nor fire; nor is it destroyed or diminished in the fire. Instead, the fire refreshes and moistens it. The sulfurs that burn other bodies do not burn gold, because the composition of its nature is upright, balanced, and clear. In it, the four natures <note>the four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> are complete and equalized, such that there is nothing in it to be added or taken away. 

For this reason, the wise men praised it and based the composition of the Great Elixir <term>Elixiris magni: the "Philosopher's Stone" or ultimate medicinal catalyst capable of transforming base metals into gold</term> upon it, because its substance is outstanding, permanent, and fixed forever. It belongs to the domain of the Sun, and it exists among physical bodies just as the Sun exists among the stars. Just as the Sun is the king of the stars and their light—and through it the things of the earth are brought to completion, including plants, fruits, and minerals, and through it their essence grows and is increased—similarly, gold among bodies preserves every body, and they are preserved with it. It is the ferment <term>fermentum: much like yeast in bread, a "ferment" in alchemy was a small amount of a substance that could transform or "leaven" a larger mass into its own nature</term> of the two Elixirs, the red and the white, because they cannot be rectified or completed except through gold, just as dough cannot be completed without leaven.

In truth, there are commonly seven ways by which gold is tested and recognized through the Art: namely, by solution, by the [touch]stone, by weight, by taste, by fire, by sublimation, and by fusion.

Furthermore, the nature of natural gold is hot and dry. And just as iron possesses a nature of dryness and hardness, gold possesses a nature that is good and soft. It is formed in the belly of the earth from very high-quality "living gold" <note>original: "auro viuo"; in this context, the author likely means the pure 'sophic mercury' that acts as the seed of gold</note> and from sulfur that is not excessively red when it is cooked.

### On Tin, from the book on alums and salts.

Tin belongs to the division of Jupiter; <note>In alchemical tradition, tin is the metal of the planet Jupiter, reflecting its bright color and relative lightness.</note> its nature is hot and moist, but its heat has been diminished because its temperament <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a substance's nature</term> was corrupted by the dominance [of other qualities] within its ore. Within tin, there are four qualities: softness, a "creaking" <note>original: "stridor"; referring to the "cry of tin," a distinctive crackling sound made when a bar of pure tin is bent</note>, a high speed of melting, and acidity. Therefore, whoever removes these four infirmities from it restores it to silver. It possesses a heavy dye <note>original: "tincturæ"; the power to impart color or properties to another substance</note> and specifically whitens copper <note>original: "æs"</note>, because it has a unique affinity with it.

### On Lead, from the book on Alums and Salts.

Lead belongs to the division of Saturn <note>In alchemy, metals were linked to planets; lead’s dullness and weight associated it with the slow-moving, outermost planet Saturn</note>. In it are gold and silver potentially <note>meaning they exist as a hidden possibility within the metal's essence</note>, though not to the sight. It is a heavy body, quick to melt, slow of movement, and receptive to tincture <note>original: "tincturam"; the coloring agent or "elixir" used to transform the metal's appearance and nature</note>. From it comes silver, and from it are made litharge <note>lead oxide</note> and ceruse <note>white lead, a common pigment</note>, and the greater elixir of redness and whiteness <note>referring to the two goals of the "Great Work": the white stage to make silver and the red stage to make gold</note>, and also the waters with which quicksilver is held. Philosophers have agreed that of all bodies, lead is closest to gold, because its hidden nature is hot and moist. The hidden nature of gold, however, is cold and dry. Therefore, the manifest <note>the outward, visible qualities</note> part of this body is lead, because it is cold and dry; but its hidden part is gold, because it is hot and moist.

### *On the mineral spirits.*

There are four spirits: Sulfur, Orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</note>, Sal ammoniac <note>original: "Sal armenia"; ammonium chloride, used to clean metals and in sublimation</note>, and Mercury. These are called "spirits" because through them the body is impressed <note>meaning the "spirit" acts upon or penetrates the physical metal</note> so that it can be joined with the soul. These are indeed bodies themselves, but they differ from other bodies because these are sublimated <note>the process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then back into solid form, used for purification</note> while others are not. Therefore, they are called spirits because no thing can be sublimated without a spirit. For a stone does not ascend by itself, nor do other bodies; however, these spirits ascend by their own power—that is, they are sublimated—and they are easily dissolved, and they cause other things to be dissolved. They also burn and cool, and dry and moisten the four elements.

**Alchemist.** Those things are said to be spirits, or to have the nature of spirits, which flee from the fire. For those things which are said to have "bodies" <note>referring to stable metals like gold or lead</note> do not do this, which is why they are called "fixed" <note>original: "fixa"; substances that remain stable and do not evaporate when heated</note>. Accordingly, all things that come out of a plant or any other thing through distillation have the nature of spirits because they flee the fire. Every such thing is called "volatile" and "fugitive," which is why quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> is called the **fugitive servant** by the Sages of alchemy. 

There is a two-fold remedy for the weakness of spirits: namely, in their fixation <note>the process of making a volatile spirit stay in the fire without evaporating</note> and in their coloration. That which does not flee the fire is called "fixed," such as the bodies of stones and metals. This, however, is a matter of degree. For to speak the truth, no [kind...]

### *On Salt, Arsenic, and Sulfur, from the book*
### *on Alums and Salts.*

Salt is water that has been solidified by the dryness of fire. Its nature is both hot and dry. Its specific property, however, is that it liquefies gold and silver with the intensity of fire and increases their natural color—namely, redness in gold and whiteness in silver. It converts them from a state of "body" <term>corporality: the dense, physical form of matter</term> to a state of "spirit" <term>spirituality: a refined, more active or volatile state</term>. It washes the bodies of filth—that is, rot—and eats away at their foulness—that is, their sulfureity <note>the presence of excess sulfur, which alchemists believed caused impurities and corrosion in metals</note>. 

With salt, too, bodies are calcined <note>original: "calcinantur"; the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder through prolonged heating</note>, and by no other means. Moreover, it is found in all ashes of plants, in the lime <note>powdery residue</note> of stones and animal bones, and indeed in all things. Therefore, the wise ones called it "common silver" <note>original: "argentum communitatis"</note>. They called it "silver" because of its whiteness, and "common" because all people need it and use it in all things, and through it, the created world is set right. Even God the Most High praised this created thing in the Law <note>likely a reference to Biblical passages regarding salt as a sign of a covenant or its purifying properties</note>...

### *Concerning Quicksilver, according to Avicenna as cited above.*

Quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," known today as the element mercury</term> is born beneath the earth, due to the great humidity existing in that place; and this happens because of the sun and the air which touch it. Therefore, it is made flowing because of the humidity and coldness within it, nor is it produced except in a cold place. For this reason, it also flees from the fire, because the greater part of it consists of water, which is contrary to fire. 

When, however, it begins to heat up, it is dried out and descends like fire <note>this may refer to the density of the metal or its behavior during distillation</note>; and if they apply much fire to it while it is in a closed place, the humidity withdraws from it, and it accidentally turns itself into the color of fire; and the natural philosophers <note>original: "naturales"</note> say that it is "living gold" <note>original: "aurum vivum"</note>. 

From the *Book of Alums and Salts*: Quicksilver is a cold and moist element, from which God created all minerals, and it is "airy" <note>volatile</note>, fleeing from the fire. Therefore, when it is fixed by force <term>fixed: the alchemical process of "fixation," turning a volatile liquid or gas into a stable solid that can withstand heat</term>, any such fixation performs a sublime work; it is the one and only spirit, and there is nothing like it in the world. It penetrates into every body <note>meaning every metal</note>, raising it up and converting it from one state to another, and from one color to another, when it is joined and mixed with it. It is also that which kills and gives life, and moistens and dries, heats and cools, and performs contrary operations.

Among its properties is this: it prevents every "fugitive" <term>fugitive: "fugitivum"; a volatile substance, such as mercury or spirits, that easily evaporates or escapes when heated</term> from fleeing.

### *On Glass, from the Book of Alums and Salts*

Glass comes from a division <note>original: "sectione"; likely referring to a refined or separated part</note> of Mercury, and the quality that prevails over its nature is coldness. Because of this, it liquefies iron and all metallic bodies, making them flow in a state of fusion. Moreover, if you melt glass, it retains whatever color you cast upon it. **Mixed substances.** <note>original: "Amista"; likely a reference to complex or compounded materials</note> Glass is made from the ashes of certain plants, which are first "clavelated" <term>clavelated: "clavellatum"; referring to the process of making potash or refined wood-ash (cinis clavellatus), which acts as a flux</term>, and then placed in a strong fire until they melt; in this way, that ash is turned into glass. 

That oily humidity which remains in the ash after the "clavelating" process is non-combustible <note>original: "inadustibilis"</note>. Nor, in the combustion itself when the fire moves it, can it evaporate in any way, on account of its strong binding. It cannot be separated because of the dryness and the dominance of the dregs <note>original: "fecis"; the solid residue or sediment</note> themselves. Instead, it flows with the material, softening and liquefying it until it is turned into glass. Furthermore, glass is among stones what a madman <note>original: "amens"; an alchemical analogy suggesting that glass, like a person without a fixed mind, has no "will" or stable form and is easily influenced by external colors</note> is among men, for it receives all tinctures <note>color-giving essences</note>, is quickly dissolved in fire, and just as quickly returns to its stony state. It softens, cleanses, and liquefies all bodies, then withdraws itself from them through melting, or as salt does through washing. Therefore, salt and glass

->are the two things in which the whole<-
->secret of the art lies; nor can the Stone<-
->be made without them, especially<-

### *On the natural generation of mineral stones, from Avicenna as cited above.*

A natural stone is indeed a thing which is produced in the belly of the earth without human labor, by its own means; thus it is born and neither grows nor diminishes, such as living gold <note>original: "aurum viuum"; in this context of "spirits," the author likely refers to mercury or a refined, "living" state of metal</note>, orpiment <term>orpiment: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>, sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: "salt of Ammon," a mineral salt used as a flux</term>, and sulfur. These are natural stones and "spirits" <note>In alchemy, "spirits" were volatile substances that could be vaporized or sublimated by fire</note>. An herbal stone, however, is born and grows <note>This likely refers to organic or plant-based concretions, or perhaps coral</note>. Furthermore, vinegar, sperm <note>likely referring to generative fluids or biological seeds</note>, and urine are the natural medicines for our "stone," the water of which hardens mercury—that is, glass <note>original: "vitrum"; the text draws a parallel between the fluidity of mercury and the molten state of glass</note>—and tints all things just as *spaul* <note>original: "spaul"; an Arabic-derived term for blood or a deep red tincture</note> does, which is to say, blood. There is, moreover, a difference between the spiritual and the natural: for the natural acts immediately, while the spiritual acts only at a designated time.

From the additions to the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Meteorologica," a foundational text for medieval science</note>. There are certain stones formed from viscous mud by the heat of the sun, or from coagulated water through the power of dry earth, or through a hot drying cause. Likewise, certain vegetables and certain animals are turned into stones by a certain mineral "stone-making" power <term>stone-making: "lapidificatiua"; the power of petrification</term>. And this happens in a stony place, when they are suddenly disrupted by a certain power which comes out of the earth at the hour of an earthquake, which converts into stones whatever it encounters in that hour. And this transmutation of animal and vegetable bodies is just as nearly related [to nature] as the transmutation of waters. It is, however, impossible for any substance of a [certain] complexion...

For stones are often made from fire when it is extinguished, and it often happens that iron and stony bodies fall during lightning-flashes <note>The author is describing meteorites, which medieval scholars often called "thunderstones," believing they were forged in the atmosphere during storms</note>, since fire at its termination is made cold and dry. There also fell near Georgen <note>Likely Gorgan (Jurjan) in modern-day Iran</note> a piece of iron almost unbreakable due to its hardness, a part of which was sent to the King of Coracen <note>original: "Coraceni"; referring to the region of Khorasan</note>. When he had commanded that swords be made from it, the material was unworkable. However, the Arabs say that Leancene swords <note>original: "enses leanceni"; possibly a corruption of "Laini" or "Al-Hini" (Indian) swords, which were prized for their superior steel</note>—otherwise called Leantene, which are the best—are made of such iron. When that mass fell, it bounced several times from the earth like a ball, and it was composed of very small fragments clinging to each other, about the size of millet grains. Something similar also happened at Trepasten.

### *Concerning the Stone of the Elixir, through which art imitates nature.*

Therefore, in mineral bodies (as was also said above), in imitation of the work of nature, Alchemists have attempted to accomplish in a short time what nature does in a thousand years. For this reason, they taught how to make a certain thing which transforms the bodies upon which it is cast <note>This refers to the "projection," the final step in the alchemical process where a small amount of the Elixir is thrown onto a base metal to transmute it</note>. This is called by them the **Elixir**, and it is said to be a "stone, yet not a stone." It is a stone because it can be ground <note>into powder</note>, but not a stone because it can be melted and flows toward evaporation like gold; nor is there any other thing to which that property belongs.

Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were foundational to medieval science</note>, as cited above: The Elixir, therefore, is a thing which is cast upon a greater body, and changes that thing from its own nature into another. It is produced, moreover, when a "lesser body" is mixed with <term>spirit</term> <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that can "fly" from the fire</note>, and elements, and <term>ferment</term> <note>A substance, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical preparation to "leaven" the mass and direct the transformation</note>, and one single preparation is made from them all. And "Elixir" is a Greek word <note>The author is mistaken; "Elixir" actually derives from the Arabic *al-iksīr*, though medieval scholars often sought Greek roots for technical terms</note>, which signifies "great treasure," or "the best of treasures."

->*Concerning the double nature of the Elixir and the Alchemist.*<-

Now, the **Elixir** is made in two ways. One way is from mineral <term>spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances such as mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that "fly" from the fire</note> and prepared, pure bodies. ### *On the completion of the white and yellow Elixir, from Avicenna in his Letter to Hasen.*

The **Elixir** <note>The transformative substance, often equated with the Philosopher's Stone</note> tints with its **tincture**, is submerged in its **oil**, and is fixed by its **lime** <note>original: "calce"; 'calx' is the powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or oxidized</note>. The white elixir is indeed achieved with three parts in which there is no "fire," while the yellow <note>original: "citrinum"; the yellow or red elixir was intended for the creation of gold, whereas the white was for silver</note> is completed with four. <gloss>It is true that the **white Elixir** requires only three things: namely, oil, tincture, and lime. But the **red** requires four: oil, lime, tincture, and yet another tincture which is called **fire**.</gloss> Thus, in an Elixir made from minerals, **glass** <note>original: "vitrum"; likely referring to a fusible, glass-like chemical flux</note> is used for the tincture, **arsenic** for the oil, and **calcined silver** for the lime—this is for the white work. But in the red work, **gold** or **calcined bronze** <note>original: "æs calcinatum"</note> is used for the lime, glass for the tincture, and **sulfur** for the oil—that is, the "redness of sulfur," which reddens the spirits and the limes. Alternatively, if they were reddened by the "fire" of the **Greater Stone**, it would be of equal value. Therefore, the yellow elixir is said to be completed in four ways. The same occurs in the Stone made from **living matter** <note>original: "re animata"; continuing the "animal path" discussion from the previous page using biological materials</note>, which consists of oil, water, fire, and earth; this is for the red elixir. But for the white elixir...

### *On the Calcination of mineral bodies, from the book of Rhazes on alums.* <note>Rhazes (al-Razi) was a famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist whose works were foundational to Western alchemy</note>

The treatment of the aforementioned bodies is fourfold: namely, **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to change its physical state, often to a powder</note> with salt, **creation** <note>original: "creatio"; likely a transcription error or variation of "ceratio" (waxing), a process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, **solution** <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note>, and then **coagulation** <note>Turning a liquid back into a solid</note>. Calcination is burning with intense fire and salt, so that the corrupting **sulfurs** <note>In alchemy, sulfur represented the principle of combustion and impurity that needed to be purged from metals</note> are deleted from them, and they remain pure like a calx. Indeed, it is not necessary to calcinate gold and silver, except for the sake of a suitable balance and preparation of their parts—namely, so that once their moisture is dried out, they might be more receptive to **foreign moisture** and faster to melt. However, it is necessary to calcinate lead, and **bronze** <note>original: "æs"; can refer to copper, bronze, or brass</note>, and iron...

...for the preceding reason, namely, so that their corrupting **sulfurs** <note>original: "sulphura"; in alchemy, sulfur was the principle of combustion and impurity that caused base metals to tarnish or "rot"</note> may be destroyed, and their burning **oiliness** <note>original: "vnctuositas"; a greasy quality thought to reside within metals that made them prone to being consumed by fire</note> may be removed. **The Alchemist** [says]: From these things, it is clear that the aforementioned definition of **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine powder or oxide</note> does not apply to the **pure bodies**, which are gold and silver. For unless it were made into a dry powder, it would not receive the moisture, because the dry thirsts for the moist and is penetrated by it. 

Now, **intense fire** <note>original: "Ignis vehemens"</note> is properly described here as that which, like a **vehicle**—that is, a **four-horse chariot** <note>original: "quadrigę"; an analogy for a fire that maintains a steady, rhythmic, and continuous "pace" or temperature</note>—continues its course evenly. A flaming fire cannot do this, but such is the heat of a furnace that is heated and closed, except for when the coals are removed. For there is a continuous heat there without **violent fluctuation** <note>original: "robustione"; refers to the "unruly" or flickering bursts of an open flame</note>. Such is also the fire of a furnace in which coals are placed that do not produce smoke. Also the fire of glowing, consumed coals, or of glowing, consumed wood, or of very hot ash. This, then, is the fire that calcines bodies and does not melt them; its property is that it burns the less potent part, namely the **sulfureity**. But it leaves behind the potent part, until...

...it raises up the **body** <note>In alchemy, "bodies" (corpora) usually refers to the seven metals: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, and mercury (though mercury is often called a "spirit").</note> itself and cleanses it from blackness. **Salt** also, which is mixed with the **filings** <note>original: "limatura"; small particles of metal produced by filing, used to increase surface area for chemical reactions</note> of the body in the fire, defends it so that it is not melted or burned up. And if the body is impure, it renders it clean from **sulfureity** <note>The presence of sulfur, which alchemists believed caused metals to be "sick" or tarnished</note> and blackness, because it dries out, corrodes, and swallows up the sulfureity on account of its own purity and dryness.

If, however, the body is already clean, it renders it cleaner, and increases the **redness** in the red and the **whiteness** in the white <note>Alchemists used "red" to refer to gold and "white" to refer to silver</note>. This is because it always corrodes and cleanses the body from that particle of sulfur which remained from when it was first generated by nature. When, however, it must meanwhile be separated, the body itself is washed with water; then the salt is dissolved in the water, and the body settles to the bottom. For every salt and **alum** <note>A group of hydrated double sulfates, used here as a cleansing or astringent agent</note> is dissolved and separated from bodies and **spirits** <note>Volatile substances that "flee" from the fire, such as mercury, sulfur, or arsenic</note> by washing in hot water, which ought to be done until the saltiness departs from the water, and thus the work is completed.

### *On the Fourfold Preparation of Bodies and Spirits according to Avicenna.*

The prince **Abohali** <note>The Latinized version of Abu Ali, referring to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the most influential philosopher-physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, that is to say, **Avicenna**, says that it is necessary for bodies first to be burned until they can be reduced to powder, then to be **calcined** <note>Reduced to a dry powder through intense heat</note> in prepared salt, and afterwards washed. And to calcine them is nothing other than to extract the **corrupting moisture** <note>The internal "greasiness" thought to make base metals unstable</note> and to introduce the **rectifying fiery moisture** <note>A refined, spiritualized fluid that gives the metal "life" or stability</note>, through which is their life.

<sig>c 4</sig>

...and essence, afterwards standing in the fire of examination <note>The "fire of examination" or *ignis examinationis* refers to a controlled heat used to test the purity and stability of a substance.</note>. In a similar way, **gold** and **silver** are **calcined** <note>original: "calcinatur"; the process of heating a metal to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note>—namely, with prepared salt, added at double its own weight, and with the flame of the furnace. **Rhazes** <note>original: "Razi"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most cited authorities in Western alchemy.</note>, as cited above, says: **Ceration** <note>original: "ceratio"; a process of softening a substance by adding liquid and grinding it until it reaches a wax-like consistency (*cera*).</note> is the sublimation of the parts of the waxed material itself, so that the moisture entering the **body** <note>In alchemy, the "body" refers to the solid metal.</note> is diminished, refined, and spread through it. This is not accomplished except by grinding and soaking <note>original: "imbibitione"; the process of a solid material absorbing a liquid.</note>, until it is refined like wax, which melts over a fire with the least heat. After ceration is skillfully performed, **solution** <note>original: "solutio"; the dissolving of a solid into a liquid state.</note> follows, then **coagulation** <note>original: "coagulatio"; the turning of a liquid back into a solid form.</note>.

**The Alchemist.** Therefore, the preparation of mineral bodies is fourfold: **calcination**, **ceration**, **solution**, and **congealing**. The **Prince** <note>original: "Princeps"; a common title for Avicenna (Ibn Sina), referring here to his influential *Letter to Hasen* (Arsenium).</note> indeed says in his *Letter to Hasen*: "That it is necessary for them first to be scorched, then calcined." But "to be scorched" is said improperly, because they are scorched without the possibility of blackening or burning. **Clean bodies**—namely gold and silver—are therefore calcined so that moisture may reach their depths, and so that it might be possible to wax them and dissolve them in water. **Unclean bodies**, however, are calcined so that the burning oiliness and the blackness which resides in them from their sulfurous nature <note>original: "sulphureitate"; the presence of sulfur, which was thought to cause impurities in base metals.</note> may perish.

They are **cerated** while they are ground on **porphyry marble** <note>A hard purple stone highly prized for grinding alchemical materials without contaminating them.</note> until they become a fine powder and are fit for dissolving. Afterwards they are dissolved into clear water, and can be mixed with the **water of spirits** <note>original: "aqua spirituum"; liquid preparations of volatile substances like mercury, acids, or alcohol.</note>, so that from many things one thing may be made, born anew. And it is perhaps what is said at the end of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteororum"; referring to Book IV of Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which discusses the composition of minerals and metals.</note>: "Unless perhaps they are reduced to their primary matter..."

...Finally, they are **coagulated** <note>original: "congelantur"; the process of turning a liquid or dissolved substance back into a solid form.</note>, when that which was dissolved into water is converted into a stony substance, so that the Alchemist may achieve his intention from it. **Spirits** <note>In the alchemical tradition, "spirits" are volatile substances that can be vaporized by heat. The four primary spirits were usually considered to be mercury, sulfur, orpiment, and sal ammoniac.</note> are also prepared in four ways: which are **mortification**, **sublimation**, **solution**, and **coagulation**. They are **mortified** <note>original: "mortificatio"; literally "killing." This refers to changing a substance's physical state—specifically stopping the "flight" or volatility of a substance so it can be handled or heated without escaping.</note> in many ways and for many reasons. For **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury.</note> is mortified so that it may be fit for sublimation, because unless its "running" <note>The Latin "cursus" refers to the fluid, mobile, and highly volatile nature of liquid mercury.</note> is taken away, it cannot be sublimated. But **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "sal armonia"; ammonium chloride, often used as a cleaning agent or flux in metallurgy.</note> does not need this preparation. Afterward, the spirits are **sublimated**, so that they may be purified and do not blacken the bodies. Sublimation occurs when a spirit, through the heat of the fire, is resolved into vapor and smoke. Then that vapor is held in the top of the vessel and thickened there, so that it can be collected. Finally, the spirits are dissolved and coagulated as has been said.

### *That the liquidity of oil is the cause of mixing.*

Moreover, the substance of mixing is everything that has **oil** <note>In alchemy, "oil" does not necessarily refer to vegetable oil, but to a fundamental "moist" and "fatty" principle believed to exist within minerals and metals that allows them to fuse together.</note> within itself, such as gold and silver, and even a **spirit** <term>spirit: a volatile substance, such as mercury or sulfur, that can be vaporized or "sublimated" by heat.</term> that has been sublimated and impregnated. And only those things are mixed together which are of the same nature and weight. For the body of a metal and glass do not mix, because they are diverse. Similarly, neither stone nor metal will mix, as one of them is dry and the other is moist. Therefore, mixing occurs between bodies which are proportioned to one another in their moisture and weight.

This is always true, except when the moist is mixed with the dry, and the hot with the cold, in the composition of the Elixir. But in the composition of the Elixir and the "body" upon which it is **projected** <note>The "projection" is the climactic moment of the alchemical work where the Elixir is cast into a crucible of molten base metal to transform it.</note>, there must be a similarity, because otherwise they would not be joined. No Elixir—whether it is made from a body or from a spirit—can be formed or consolidated with the body upon which it is projected unless there is mixed with it that which consolidates bodies to one another; that is, the oil found in "burned" substances <note>original: "oleum in adustis"; this refers to a fundamental substance alchemists believed could be extracted from the ashes or residues of organic and inorganic matter.</note>, whether from a plant or an animal. A substance is indeed called **fixed** <term>fixed: a "fixed" substance is stable and will not evaporate or change its nature when exposed to the intense heat of a furnace.</term>,

They cannot be moved because of the intensity of the mixing.

The cause of **combustion**, truly, is a commonality with the fire. ### *How the transmutation of metals is brought about through the Elixir, according to some.*

Therefore, the **Elixir** is cast upon the melted mineral body, and tinges it with its **tincture**, and is submerged by its **oil**, and is fixed by its **calx** <term>calx: the powdery residue or "lime" left after a metal or mineral has been roasted or calcined; here it refers to the solidifying element.</term>; and thus it transmutes the body according to its own property, just as has been stated above. From the additions to the fourth book of **Aristotle's** *Meteorology* <note>original: "Aristo. Quarti Metheororum." These skeptical "additions" were actually written by the Persian philosopher Avicenna but were frequently appended to Aristotle's works in medieval Latin translations.</note>: Let the practitioners of alchemy know that the species of nature cannot be truly changed, but they can make things similar to these. For example, they can tinge a white substance with a citrine <note>A yellowish-orange color associated with gold.</note> color so that it appears to be **gold**, and they can also wipe away the impurities of **lead** so that it appears to be **silver**. Nevertheless, it will always be lead, but they will obtain in it qualities of this sort so that men are deceived by it. Moreover, I do not believe it is possible that the "specific difference" <note>In medieval philosophy, the 'specific difference' is the essential quality that makes a thing what it is (e.g., what makes gold 'gold' rather than just a yellow heavy metal).</note> can be removed by any human ingenuity; rather, there occurs a stripping away of the **accidents** <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities like color, taste, or smell that can change without changing the underlying substance.</term>, such as color, taste, or weight. Artificial things are not the same as natural things, nor are they as certain, although they may be close and similar, since **art** is weaker than **nature** and does not overtake it, even if it labors much. Furthermore, the proportion of the composition of these substances will not be the same for all. These things, therefore, cannot be changed into another, unless...

perhaps they may be reduced into their first matter, even if they are changed into something that did not exist before; however, this does not happen through **liquefaction** <note>original: "liquefactionem"; the process of melting or making liquid.</note>. **The Alchemist**: It seems, however, that through **solution** <note>original: "solutionem"</note> into water first, then through **distillation**, and finally through **congelation** <note>original: "congelationem"; the process of solidifying or thickening a liquid into a solid.</note>, they might be reduced into their first matter. Truly, if **silver** is diminished during melting and produces **dross** <term>scoria: the rocky or metallic slag left over after a metal has been smelted or refined.</term>, it is artificial; but if not, it is natural.

Therefore, regarding the **transmutation** <note>original: "transmutationem"; the changing of one substance into another.</note> of noble bodies <note>In alchemy, "noble bodies" refers to precious metals like gold and silver.</note>, this art seems to have something of vanity and falsehood. Nevertheless, there is in it a sublime subtlety and no small utility regarding the **disaggregations** <note>original: "disgregationes"; the process of breaking a substance down into its component parts.</note> and transmutations of those things which are constantly produced in the world for various human uses—partly by nature and partly by human industry—such as the production of **minium** <note>original: "Minij"; red lead, used as a pigment.</note>, **vermilion**, **niter** <note>original: "nitri"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate.</note>, and **brass** <note>original: "aurichalcus"; a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc.</note>. For this reason, it is also called **occult philosophy**, because the investigation of the reasons and causes by which these things are made is difficult and hidden.

It is also possible to **disaggregate** the four things from any plant through **distillation**, so that in each resulting part there remains the dominion of a particular **element**. This consists of extracting water first, then oil, thirdly fire—which is a red liquid—and in the fourth place, earth remains as the dregs. Through this, one can know which element dominates most in the plant being treated. However, water is not extracted from a dry plant, because the watery moisture has already evaporated from it; water evaporates more quickly than oily moisture. It is the oil which, remaining longer, protects plants from **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactione"; the process of decaying or rotting.</note>.

The same can also be done with certain things derived from animals, such as bone, hair, eggs, and similar items. For this reason, **Avicenna** <note>An influential Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037 AD) whose works were central to medieval science.</note> teaches in the chapter on the **complexions of the limbs** <note>original: "complexionibus membrorum"; the specific balance of qualities like heat and moisture in body parts.</note> to distill bones and hair, in order to know in which of them <meta>catchword: plus (more)</meta>

In this way, one can also extract **salt** from all the ashes of plants, bones, and animals, and from the **calxes** <note>original: "calcibus"; the powdery remains left after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burnt or "calcined."</note> of stones. However, these salts differ among themselves in this: that in the salt of calxes there is no oil, because it lacks both kinds of humidity <note>In medieval science, "humidity" often referred to both internal moisture (which allows growth) and oily moisture (which allows flexibility/combustion).</note>, and it is neither grown nor nourished like a plant or animal. For an animal is nourished according to the moist and the cold, and lives according to the hot and the moist; thus, life and nourishment proceed from moisture in both plant and animal, as **John of Damascus** <note>A 7th-century Syrian monk and scholar whose works on natural philosophy and theology were widely cited in the Middle Ages.</note> says. But in the salt [derived] from the ashes of plants, bones, and animals, which fire could not break apart, it is indeed **non-combustible** <note>original: "inadustibile"; something that cannot be consumed or destroyed by fire.</note>. For everything that comes forth through distillation flees the fire and has the nature of **spirits** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances that vaporize easily when heated.</note>, as was said above. In every mineral thing also—whether from the earth, or from a plant, or from an animal—there is an **oil**, without which it could not be melted and flow <note>The author suggests that "oil" is the principle of fusibility, allowing solids to turn into liquid when heated.</note>.

### *On the Work of Vermilion, Cinnabar, and Brass.*

When heated intensely, it undergoes a chemical change to become red lead or "minium."</note> alone, which, although it is very white, is placed in a fierce fire and becomes red, because its hidden nature is red, although...

Thus, that which is manifest in fire is placed into the hidden, and that which is hidden is placed into the manifest.

The transmutation of **cinnabar** <term>cinnabar: a bright red mineral (mercury sulfide) that is the primary ore of mercury</term> happens because of the property of its composition; for it is made from **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> and white or yellow **sulfur**. These substances acquire a redness—which they do not possess on their own—upon their joining. This occurs through the violence of the sulfur inflicted upon the quicksilver by means of fire and the skill of the craftsman. For just as a power arises in a compound from the composition of diverse things that is not present in the simple components—as in **theriac** <note>original: "tiriaca"; a famous "universal" medical compound made of dozens of ingredients, believed to have more power than its individual parts.</note>—so too is the color produced in cinnabar.

**Copper** <note>original: "Aes"; while often meaning bronze, in this context it refers to the base metal (copper) being transformed into a golden alloy.</note>, however, is transmuted into **aurichalcum** <term>aurichalcum: a golden-colored alloy, specifically brass, made by alloying copper with zinc</term>, which is done by means of **calamine** <term>thucia: also called tutia or tutty, an impure zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>. This occurs because its smoke "whitens" the metal and immediately takes on the nature of a **spirit** <note>In alchemy, a "spirit" is a volatile substance that vaporizes or "flees" when heated.</note> when its smoke is cast over the molten copper or mixed with sheets of copper.

During the melting of the copper, the calamine itself is heated and seeks flight like a spirit; therefore, it is necessary that its flight occurs through the molten body of the metal itself. In this way, it **turns the metal yellow** <note>original: "citrinat"; literally "to make lemon-colored." In alchemy, "citrination" was a stage of transformation toward a gold-like color.</note>, because its smoke is moderately white; such whiteness, when mixed with the red of the copper, suppresses the redness, a yellowing occurs, and thus brass is made. Therefore, **arsenic** and calamine have the specific property of impressing themselves upon copper. But the effect of each is not equal. For the smoke of yellow arsenic...

## On the Investigation of Metals
### Pliny, Book 33

Thus there are metals and riches, and the prices of things are purchased, while the earth is searched deep within with manifold care. In one place, the earth is dug for riches by those seeking gold, silver, bronze, and electrum <note>original: "electrum"; a natural alloy of gold and silver highly valued in antiquity</note>. In another place, for luxuries: gems and pigments for walls and fingers <note>referring to mineral-based paints for murals and stones for rings</note>, and in yet another, for audacity, iron. Indeed, iron is pursued even more greedily amidst wars and slaughter. We also see mountains excavated from above, gaping in a way that causes wonder. Sometimes the earth itself even trembles. We descend into its very bowels and seek riches in the seat of the spirits of the dead <note>original: "sede manium"; the Roman concept of the underworld or the ghosts of the departed</note>, as if the earth were not kind and fertile enough where she is trodden upon; and among these things, we search for the sake of the smallest of remedies. For who has medicine as a cause for digging? Even though she [the earth] provides medicine from her uppermost part, being not at all stingy but generous in all things that are beneficial. However, the things that weigh us down, those things also drive us toward the underworld, which she [the earth] has hidden and submerged. What end is there to all these ages, or how far will greed penetrate? How innocent, how blessed—nay, indeed, how delightful the life of man would be, if only...

...if it is cooled, it will remain as dust. For **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," known today as mercury</term>, because of the penetrability of its substantial moisture, separates the moisture of the gold and does not allow it to maintain its continuity. Thus the **Saracen** <note>original: "sarraceni"; referring to Muslim alchemists and craftsmen who were highly influential in medieval European metallurgy</note> craftsmen say they carry their gold from one earth to another; and when they wish to have pure gold, they place it in a furnace and melt it, and the quicksilver evaporates without any loss of the gold. 

It can also be hidden under the appearance of earth's dust if ash is mixed with the molten gold and it is stirred with a **small earthen vessel** <term>testula: a small piece of pottery or a cupel used in assaying</term> until it is pulverized; for the vessel, being deprived of its own moisture by the heat of the furnace, draws all the moisture of the gold to itself. The same thing will also happen if it is stirred with a fresh **hazel rod**. For the heat of the melting gold extracts and takes the moisture of the rod, which causes the rod—now emptied of its own moisture—to attract the moisture of the gold in its place. In this way, the gold is left entirely fragmented. 

All of these processes can also be done with lead. If, however, **brass** <term>Auricalchum: orichalcum, a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc</term> is mixed with gold, it becomes brittle and will be like glass.

**Gold**, therefore, is not only the most precious among metals, but also the most solid. It possesses a fiery, splendid color that soothes the sight. Likewise, gold is joined by clay to iron; in gold, those things that shine with a spark are earth, in some places reddish and in other places ashen. The better the gold is, the more beautiful it is. All things indeed float upon <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, except for gold, which is the only thing it draws to itself. And for that reason, it also purifies the gold best. By spitting out its other impurities through frequent shaking in earthen vessels, the defects are thus cast aside; but so that the mercury itself may depart from the gold, it is poured out into processed skins, through which it flows like a kind of sweat, leaving the gold pure. Thus this—that is, the parts of chickens—is the poison of gold <note>A curious folk belief recorded by Pliny; he claimed that gold could be "consumed" or dissolved by the fat or flesh of poultry</note>. The same author in Book 35: Gold is purified with <term>black alum</term> <note>A mineral salt used as a flux in traditional metallurgy</note>.

### *On the special and manifold preeminence of gold.*
#### *From the Book on the Nature of Things.*

Gold is more precious, more durable, and more workable than other things or metals; it shines at all times, and though defiled, it is not consumed by <term>rust</term> <note>original: "rubigine"; refers to any form of metallic corrosion or oxidation</note>; it soothes the sight, and the redder it is, the better it is. It is also twice as heavy as silver, copper, or tin. And although it is the most noble above all metals, it is nevertheless the most <term>ductile</term> <note>Capable of being hammered thin or drawn out without breaking</note> above all. It is more temperate than any metal, and for this reason, because its heat [is] mo- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "dici," likely leading to "moderata" (moderate)</note>

## BOOK II.

...to be called an excess, it is not placed in a degree, nor is it alone dissolved. **The Author.** Gold, therefore, is not only the most precious among metals, but also the most solid; it has a fiery, splendid color that soothes the sight. When placed in fire, it is not consumed, but is purified and tested. Therefore, it is put into fire for three reasons: for examination, for testing, and for crafting. It is also extremely suitable for the human body, wherefore when consumed in food, it is of great benefit <note>Medieval and Renaissance medicine often valued "aurum potabile" or edible gold as a restorative for the heart and vital spirits</note>.

**Pliny** in Book 33: I judge that the chief favor toward gold was [not] for its color <note>Pliny argues that silver actually has a more practical color for visibility</note>. For the color in silver is brighter and more like daylight, and therefore more familiar for military standards, because it shines from a greater distance. There is a manifest error among those who believe that the color of the stars was what made gold pleasing, since in gems and other things, that color is not the most outstanding.

Nor is gold preferred over the rest for its weight or the ease of the material, since it yields to <term>lead</term> <note>original: "plumbeo"; while gold is denser than lead, Pliny likely refers to the ease of working or perhaps specific alloys commonly used in his era</note> in both respects. But because nothing of its substance is lost, it is surely safe in fire, even in conflagrations and on funeral pyres. Indeed, the more often it has burned, the more the quality of the gold improves. The test of gold is fire: it must glow with a color similar to the flame; they call this <term>obrisum</term> <note>original: "obrisum"; a technical term for gold that has been assayed and proven pure through fire</note>.

The first proof of its quality is that it is ignited with the greatest difficulty; moreover, it is remarkable that while it remains untamed by the coals of the most violent wood fire, it catches fire very quickly with straw, and is "cooked" with lead so that it may be purified. But another greater cause for its value is that its use is least [diminished by wear]...

gold is more perfect, as if it were polished by its own movement and friction. In another way, it is dug out by the digging of pits, or in the collapse of mountains; for which reason both methods shall be described. Those who seek the gold of waters first of all remove the *segulum* <note>original: "segulum"; a layer of earth that serves as an indicator of gold-bearing sand beneath</note>, for so the *indicator* is called. The stream bed is where the sands are washed, and from that which settles at the bottom, an estimate is made so that the gold may be found. Sometimes, however, it is found immediately on the surface of the earth by a rare stroke of luck, as occurred recently in *Dalmatia* during the time of *Nero*. For the rest, the mountains of *Spain*, though dry and barren and producing nothing else, are known to be fertile with this good <note>referring to gold</note>; in other ways they are forced to be so. 

That gold which is dug from shafts is called *canalitium* <note>original: "canalitium"; gold found in veins or "channels" within the rock</note>, clinging to the gravel of marble—not in the way it sparkles in the East in sapphire and *Theban stone* <note>original: "Thebaico"; likely a red-spotted granite or porphyry from Egypt</note> and other gems, but embracing the flakes of marble. These channels of veins wander through the marble and the sides of the shafts, twisting here and there; hence the name was devised. The earth above is held up by wooden columns, and that which is dug out is crushed, washed, burned, and softened into a fine powder. For that which they beat in mortars, they call *mortar-beaten* <note>original: "pilastudem"; a technical term for ore crushed by a pestle</note>; the silver <note>The text uses "argentum," though the context suggests the metallic yield or perhaps an alloy like electrum</note> that comes out of the furnace is called the 'sweat' which is cast out from the flue. 

Indeed, the waste in every metal is called <term>scoria</term> <note>slag; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note>. In the case of gold, this is cooked again and crushed. The crucibles for cooking are made from *tasconia* <note>original: "tasconia"; a refractory white clay used for making heat-resistant smelting pots</note>, which is a white earth similar to clay. For no other substance can withstand the blast of the fire and the burning material.

### *Again, concerning another method of investigation.*

The third method of finding gold actually surpasses the legendary labors of the **Giants**. Through tunnels driven across vast distances by the light of lamps, mountains are hollowed out. Through long vigils lasting many months, the light of day is never seen. Sudden collapses occur, and the workers are crushed. Therefore, frequent arches <note>original: "fornices"; referring to pillars of rock left behind as supports</note> are left to hold up the mountains. In both types of mining, hard flint stones are encountered. These they break apart using **fire and vinegar** <note>original: "igni & aceto"; a Roman engineering technique where rock was heated with fire and then doused with cold vinegar to make it brittle and crack</note>. More often, because the vapor and smoke in the tunnels are suffocating, they must retreat; they carry out 150-pound loads of broken rock on their shoulders day and night. Recent miners move such quantities of earth that it now seems less reckless to seek pearls from the deep sea. There is a type of clay, a soil mixed with gravel <note>original: "glacie mixta"; likely a corruption of "glaria mixta" (mixed with gravel) from the source text</note>, almost impossible to break, which they call *the white* <note>original: "candidam"</note>. They attack this with iron wedges and hammers, and they consider nothing harder—except that among all things, the **hunger for gold** is the hardest of all. 

When the work is finished, they cut away the "necks" of the support arches. A collapse gives a signal from the furthest end; thus the shattered mountain falls far away from itself with a great crash and an incredible blast of air. The victors watch this ruin of nature, and yet, for such great dangers, the cause is simply that they desire what they hope for. Elsewhere, even inaccessible cliffs are cut away and forced to provide a seat for hollowed-out beams. The man who cuts the rock hangs by ropes, so that from a distance he looks like...

Likewise, on the ridges of mountains, reservoirs <note>original: "piscinae"; literally "fishponds," here referring to massive man-made tanks</note> are hollowed out, long and narrow, so that the captured water running with such force might break through and roll away boulders. There is yet another labor on the plains: trenches are dug into which the water flows, and they are paved in stages. *Gorse* <term>Ulex: a prickly, rosemary-like shrub used in mining to trap gold particles in its rough branches</term> is a shrub similar to rosemary, rough and gold-retaining. The sides of the channels are closed with planks or beaten earth and suspended over steep drops. Thus, as the channel flows from the land into the sea, the gorse is dried and burned, and its ash is washed over a bed of grassy sod so that the gold may settle. In this way, **Asturia**, **Galicia**, and **Lusitania** <note>Ancient regions in the Iberian Peninsula, modern-day Spain and Portugal</note> provide gold, with **Asturia** producing the greatest amount.

### *What was the first valuation of gold.*

Would that gold could be entirely banished from our lives—that "cursed hunger" <note>original: "sacra fames"; a famous phrase from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the transition of "sacred" to "accused" or "detestable" greed</note>! How much happier was the age when goods themselves were bartered with one another, as we are led to believe happened during the Trojan times by the testimony of **Homer**. For in this way (as I see it), trade was invented for the sake of survival; he records that some bought items with ox-hides, others with iron or captured goods. And yet, even he [Homer], having marveled at gold, set the value of things by it, saying that **Glaucus** exchanged golden armor worth a hundred oxen for the armor of **Diomedes**, which was worth only nine. From this ancient custom, many of the old laws regarding exchange were established in **Rome**. The worst...

Indeed, no stamped gold was used before King **Pyrrhus** <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus, a Greek king who fought Rome in the 3rd century BCE; his defeat marked a turning point in Roman expansion and wealth.</note> was defeated. Rather, the *as* <term>as: the standard unit of Roman currency, originally a cast bronze coin</term> was weighed out in pound-weights—from which even now the *libella* <note>A small silver coin, literally a "little pound."</note> takes its name—and the *dupondius* <term>dupondius: a coin worth two asses</term>. Furthermore, the officials who weighed the soldiers' pay (that is, the sum of money to be weighed) are called **libripendes** <term>libripendes: "scale-weighers" who presided over formal Roman transactions</term>. By this custom, even now a scale is used in those legal transfers of property known as *mancipi* <note>mancipi refers to *mancipatio*, a formal legal ritual for transferring ownership of high-value property like land or slaves.</note>. 

Furthermore, this luxury even increased during military service, such that tribunes began wearing glowing buckles made of gold. Gold has also been seen worn upon the feet of women. And lest we charge only rings with this crime, even some men now wear gold on their arms, a fashion which comes from the **Dardanians** <note>An ancient people of the Balkans; the text refers to *Dardanian* style bracelets.</note>, which is why they are called *Dardanum*. 

Women wear gold in bracelets, around their entire necks, on their fingers, and in their ears. Chains run from these around their sides, and pearls are inserted around the necks of these ladies; heavy gold weights hang there, so that even in their sleep they may remain conscious of their large pearls <term>uniones: literally "ones," referring to large, perfectly round pearls of such high quality that they were thought to be unique</term>. Finally, luxury adds many kinds of gems of exquisite brilliance and burdens the fingers with a wealthy man’s entire fortune. 

Soon, the gold even conceals various engraved figures, so that in one instance the artistry is prized, and in another, the raw material itself. It is a labor to wear more than one ring. Others insert thin gold leaves of lighter material, and because of the value of the gemstones, they find the whole thing a source of constant anxiety. Still others hide poison under their gems, as did **Demosthenes** <note>The famous Greek orator who committed suicide by taking poison hidden in his reed pen or, as suggested here, a ring.</note>, the greatest of the Greek orators; they keep such rings for the purpose of seeking death. Ultimately, as with most forms of great wealth, many crimes are committed by means of rings. By which luxuries also came I <note>The "I" is a catchword for the first word of the following page.</note>

Gold is of a "hot" nature <note>In medieval humoral theory, substances were classified by "complexion" as hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>; reduced to powder and mixed into an antidote, it cures leprosy and mange <note>original: "scabiem," a term used for various itchy skin diseases including scabies</note>. ...[in what] degree it is placed by some. **Avicenna** in the second book of the *Canon of Medicine* says: Gold is balanced and refined; placed in an eye-powder <term>alcohol: in this historical context, a "fine powder" or collyrium used for the eyes, rather than liquid spirits</term>, it strengthens the eye. A cautery <term>cauterium: a tool used to brand or burn tissue for surgical purposes</term> is better and more quickly healed when it is performed with gold. Its filings are included in medicines for melancholy, and for soothing ringworm <note>original: "serpugo," a creeping skin eruption</note> and alopecia <note>original: "allopicia," a condition of hair loss</note>. For those who drink it, it assists with pains and tremors of the heart, as well as with "pain of the soul" <note>likely referring to psychological distress, anxiety, or spiritual despair</note> and tremors, and for those who talk to themselves.

The same author in the same book says: *Clima* <term>clima: a variant of 'calimia' or 'cadmia,' referring to the dross, oxide, or metallic residue left after smelting</term> is actually the dregs and smoke raised above the place where gold is melted. And that which sinks to the bottom is flaky. The dross of gold is best when it is golden in color, ashen, fresh, and of a thicker flakiness.

It is, however, balanced, though leaning toward dryness in the third degree. This substance, and that which is washed from it, are more refined than the dross of silver. In it, there is a power of drying and cleansing. It fills "fraudulent" wounds <note>original: "vulnera fraudulentia," likely referring to chronic, deceptive, or non-healing sores</note>, cleanses the filth of wounds, and wears away their excess flesh when added to the "white" <note>original: "albugini," probably referring to egg white or the white of the eye used as a base for medicine</note>. It also benefits the eye, treats cataracts <note>original: "vitio aquae," literally the "vice of water," a common medieval term for cataracts</note>, and strengthens the eye.

**Pliny** in Book 34 [of *Natural History*] says: Gold is applied to the wounded and to infants so that the spells <note>original: "veneficia," referring to witchcraft, poisoning, or harmful magic</note> cast upon them might do less harm; it heals fistulas and hemorrhoids. If it is added to ground-up "foam" <note>original: "spumae," likely referring to litharge or metallic dross</note>, it cures rotten ulcers of foul odor.

The same author in Book 34 affirms: The "foam" produced in gold-smelting houses is claimed to be most useful for the eyes.

But the question arises: how does gold strengthen the body, since it is neither absorbed into the system <note>original: "incorporetur"</note> nor provides nourishment to the limbs? To this it must be said that some things strengthen the limbs by balancing the spirits <note>the "vital spirits" believed to animate the body</note>, such as aromatic substances; some by restoring the limbs, such as food and drink; some by tightening a loose limb, such as a plaster made from mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree used in medicine</note>. In this manner, therefore, gold provides strength: while through its sharpness <note>original: "asperitate," referring to a scouring or cleansing quality</note> it provides strength or wipes away that which is superfluous.

...is proven by placing filings [upon a shovel]; if they remain bright white, the metal is considered pure. The next best quality turns reddish; if it turns black, it has no value. However, fraud can interfere with this experiment: if wooden sticks are soaked in human urine, the filings are stained while being heated, thus faking a white appearance. There is also a test for polished silver using a person's breath: it is pure if it fogs <note>original: "sudet," literally 'sweats'</note> and then immediately clears the cloud. The best mirrors are usually made from the finest silver. Silver is tarnished by medicated waters and even by salty air, as occurs in the inland regions of Spain.

From the book *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "Ex libro de Natura rerum," likely referring to the work by Isidore of Seville</note>, silver is ductile and malleable, and its sound or tinkling is most sweet—especially if it is mixed with copper. For this reason, Moses commanded that hammered trumpets be made of silver, for terrifying the enemy and for exhortation to war, as well as for moving the camp and summoning the people to the standard <note>original: "hastam," literally 'spear,' used here as a military assembly point</note>.

Many veins of silver are found in many parts of the world, but it is not pure in itself like gold; rather, it is incorporated and mixed with earth and dross. Therefore, the greatest labor is required to purify it by fire. However, the smoke from its purification is extremely harmful, and a person is not easily cleansed if infected by such smoke, except by the smoke of frankincense or aromatic spices. Once silver is pure, it is durable. Impure silver, however, easily contracts corruption <note>original: "corruptelam," referring to tarnishing or chemical decay</note>. Silver consolidates <note>strengthens or binds</note> other metals.

# ON ALCHEMY

The next madness after gold is the metal **silver**. It is found only in shafts <note>original: "puteis," literally pits or wells</note> and is not born with any signs of its own presence, having none of those shining sparks found in gold. The earth [ore] is sometimes reddish, sometimes ash-colored. It cannot be smelted <note>original: "excoqui," literally 'cooked out'</note> except with black lead or with a vein of lead which they call <term>galena</term> <note>Lead sulfide, the primary ore of lead and often found with silver</note>, which is frequently found near silver veins. In almost all provinces, silver is found in this way, even in waters. But in **Spain**, in the barren soil and also in the mountains, the most beautiful silver is discovered. Wherever one vein is found, another is found not far off; this is generally true for every metallic material.

It is a marvel that in the Spanish lands, the shafts once begun by **Hannibal** <note>The Carthaginian general who funded his campaigns against Rome through Spanish silver mines</note> still endure, bearing the names of their original discoverers. Mountains are hollowed out over a great distance, and workers draw out the water day and night. A vein of silver found at the very surface is called <term>crudaria</term> <note>From the Latin 'crudus' meaning raw or crude; indicates surface-level ore</note>. Recently, however, a vein of white copper was discovered beneath the alum, which has made the hope of finding more endless. 

The odor from silver mines is harmful to all animals, but especially to dogs. # ON ALCHEMY

->**[multi]tude of images.**<- It matters so much whether the reflection is received or rejected. This effect happens because of the shape of the material, and it matters greatly whether the surfaces are concave, or depressed in the middle, or raised, or turned away, or slanted, tilted back, or straight, depending on the quality of the surface that receives the shadows of the approaching figure.

Among our ancestors, the best mirrors were made at **Brundisium** <note>Modern Brindisi, Italy</note> from a mixture of tin and bronze. But now silver ones are preferred. And it was recently discovered that a more reliable image is rendered when gold is applied to the back <note>An early reference to the technique of foiling or "silvering" a mirror, here using gold to enhance the reflection</note>. **Egypt** also tints silver so that in its vessels it may see its own clouds <note>original: "nubem suum spectet"; this refers to a technique of darkening or mottling silver to create a smoky, clouded effect</note>; it paints the silver rather than engraving it. From there the material passed even to triumphal statues, and it is surprising how the price increases when the brightness is dulled <note>This refers to the high value placed on darkened or "niello" silver finishes</note>.

This darkening is done in the following way: a third part of very thin **Cyprian bronze**, which they call <term>coronarium</term> <note>a high-quality bronze alloy used for making theatrical crowns and delicate ornaments</note>, is mixed with silver, along with as much <term>live sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphuris viui"; native or unrefined sulfur</note> as there is silver. They are thus melted together in an earthenware vessel smeared with clay. The method of cooking continues until the lids open of their own accord. Silver also turns black when rubbed with the yolk of a hard-boiled egg, though this can be removed with vinegar and chalk; it is remarkable, however, that no one became famous for engraving silver at that time. Silver vessels vary with the wonderful inconsistency of human ingenuity, as no single style of workshop remains in favor for long: now the <term>Furian</term> style is preferred, now the <term>Clodian</term>, now the <term>Gratian</term> <note>These names refer to famous Roman silversmiths or specific artistic schools of silver-working</note>, now...

->**On Quicksilver.**<-

Quicksilver <note>original: "hidrargirum"; the author distinguishes between naturally occurring "living silver" and the mercury manufactured from ore</note> is also found, a substitute for the "living silver" mentioned a little earlier. It is produced in two ways: either by grinding cinnabar <term>minium</term> <note>In ancient texts, "minium" refers to cinnabar (mercury sulfide), the bright red ore of mercury, whereas in modern chemistry it refers to red lead</note> with vinegar in bronze mortars and pestles, or by placing the cinnabar in earthen pans within an iron bowl, covered with a lid and sealed with clay, then heated by a constant fire from bellows beneath the pans. In this way, a "sweat" is wiped from the lid, which has a silvery color and a watery fluidity. It is easily divided into drops and flows back together with a slippery moisture. 

Since it is well known that this is a poison, I believe all the medicinal instructions involving cinnabar are reckless. Perhaps it might be used to stop bleeding from the head or belly, provided it does not enter the internal organs or touch an open wound. Otherwise, I do not believe it should be used at all. Nowadays, quicksilver is used almost exclusively for gilding silver, although it should be applied to bronze in a similar way. But the same deceit, which is so clever in every area of life, has devised a cheaper material, as we have explained. Following the discovery of gold and silver is the stone they call a <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: "coticula"; a hard, dark stone used to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves when rubbed</note>, which is found only in the river **Himocho**—which others [never...]

### On Litharge, by Isidore.

**Litharge** <note>original: "Lithargirum"; lead monoxide, a byproduct of refining silver</note> is said to be the refinement of silver, which we call "silver dross" <note>original: "argenti spumam", literally "foam of silver"</note>, for it is made from silver and lead. **Pliny** says in the place cited above: In the aforementioned metals, a substance is also produced which is called silver dross. There are three types of this: the one they call **chrysitis** <term>gold-colored litharge</term> is the best; the second is **argyritis** <term>silver-colored litharge</term>; and the third is called **molybditis** <term>lead-colored litharge</term>. Most often, all these colors are found in the same slabs or cakes. The most highly regarded is the Attic variety, and the second is the Haspamensian.

**Chrysitis** is made from the ore itself. **Argyritis** comes from silver, while **molybditis** is the smelting of the lead itself; it is produced at Puteoli <note>A major Roman port city, modern Pozzuoli</note>, and takes its name from there. All of these, however, are produced from their own cooked material, flowing down from an upper crucible into a lower one. Finally, it is lifted out from there with small iron spits and rotated within the flame itself on the spit, and it becomes light in weight.
