Some distinguish two types of foam, which they call **stelerythida** and **peumenem**. A third, **molybdaina** <note>original: "molibdenam"; likely referring to a lead-based oxide or ore</note>, is to be discussed under the subject of lead. 

In order for the foam to be useful, it is cooked again, with the slabs broken into the size of rings; thus, once heated with bellows, it is washed to separate the coals and ash. To ensure it is as white as silver-colored litharge <term>argyritis</term>, it is ordered to be broken into bean-sized pieces and cooked in an earthenware vessel with water, adding fresh wheat and barley wrapped in linen cloths until the foam is purified. 

Afterward, for six days they grind it in mortars, washing it three times a day with cold water; when they finish, they add salt to the hot mixture, one obol <note>A small Greek unit of weight</note> for every pound of foam. On the final day, they store it in a leaden vessel. Others cook it with white beans and barley-water <term>ptisana</term>, and dry it for forty days during the hottest part of summer. There are some who do not cook it at all, but instead grind it with salt and, after discarding the water, wash it.

Its property is to soften, to cool, to fill in [hollow wounds], to temper, and to soothe the swellings of ulcers. In such things also...

There is also a certain sharpness <term>ponticitas: a harsh or astringent quality</term> in it, which is why it helps grow new flesh in moist ulcers.

### *On Bronze or Copper, from the book on the nature of things.*

Bronze or copper <note>original: "Æs siue cuprum"; the Latin term 'aes' can refer to copper, bronze, or brass</note> is of the same hardness as silver, and of the same liquid nature <note>referring to its melting point or fusibility</note>, except for the fact that it is red in color. Bronze is not corrupted by any rust; it has a foul smell, and yet it sounds sweet.

From the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorology*, Book IV, was a primary source for medieval understanding of how materials are formed and changed</note>. Bronze, just like lead, ice, and whatever things are coagulated <note>hardened</note> by the deprivation of heat, is liquefied by heat. Bronze yields to a strike. To "yield to a strike" is to pass into the depth of the surface <note>original: "empipedi" (a corruption of the Greek 'epipedo'); referring to the way a metal indents when hammered</note>. Likewise, some things are ductile <term>ductile: capable of being hammered thin or drawn into wire</term>, such as bronze; and whatever things are led into breadth by the same blow are likewise shifted in depth according to that part. Bronze is also liquefiable but not flammable; and whatever things are liquefied by fire are more "watery" <note>in the Aristotelian sense, containing more of the element of Water</note>, such as silver and bronze. Furthermore, if there should be quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term> of good substance, and impure sulfur (namely, that which has a burning power within it), it converts that substance into bronze. 

Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose 'Etymologies' served as a standard medieval encyclopedia</note>. Bronze <note>original: "Æs"</note> is named from the "splendor of the air" <note>original: "aeris"; Isidore often used phonetic similarities to explain the origins of words</note>, just as gold and silver are. Among the ancients, the use of bronze was known before that of iron. Indeed, the first people used to plow the earth and wage the struggles of war with bronze, and bronze was held in higher value. Gold and silver, on the other hand, were rejected because of their uselessness. Now, however, the situation is reversed: bronze lies low, and gold has yielded to the highest honor. The use of bronze first passed into statues, later into vessels, and into the structures of buildings, for the sake of perpe- <note>the word continues on the next page as "perpetuity" or permanence</note>

...antiquity <note>original: "tuitatem"; the end of the word 'antiquitatem'</note> of monuments, public laws were inscribed in bronze. Bronze gathers rust more quickly unless it is smeared with oil. However, they say it is best preserved in liquid pitch. Among all metals, bronze is the most resonant <note>original: "vocalissimum"; literally 'most vocal'</note> and of the greatest power; from it, bronze plates are also made. **The Philosopher** <note>This refers to Aristotle, whose writings on natural science were the foundation of medieval study</note>. Bronze or copper <note>original: "Aes siue cuprum"; the Latin term 'aes' can refer to copper or its alloys, bronze and brass</note> is sonorous and resonant, naturally hot; its sound is harsh on its own, but when mixed with tin, silver, or gold, it is very strong and has a sweet ringing. It rings higher than other metals, but it bothers the hearing unless it is more suitably tempered with tin. It is indeed meltable <term>fusile: capable of being melted</term> and can be hammered into any work of art <term>ductile: capable of being shaped by hammering</term>, but only with great labor and the careful control of the person striking it. It can never be so purified that it does not easily contract corruption <note>referring to oxidation or the green patina known as verdigris</note>, yet it lasts for very many years. **Pliny, Book 34**. Bronze, if touched by menstrual blood, takes on a heavy, foul odor and verdigris, and even more so if this occurs while the moon is waning. **The same [Pliny] in Book 34**. Bronze is usually gilded legitimately with quicksilver or mercury <note>original: "argento viuo aut hidrargiro"; ancient writers sometimes distinguished between naturally occurring 'quick-silver' and mercury refined from ore</note>. But a fraud has been devised: the bronze is first "tortured" <note>subjected to intense heat and chemical treatment</note>, and when heated, it is quenched with vinegar, salt, and alum. Afterward, it is cleaned of grit, and if it has been sufficiently boiled down, it attains a brilliant shine. It is also reduced to ash by the heat of the fire, so that once subdued by a mixture of pumice, alum, and quicksilver, it can receive the application of gold leaf <term>brateas: very thin sheets of beaten gold</term>.

### *On the different types of bronze, according to Isidore.*

There are, moreover, various species of bronze, such as Cyprian bronze, Corinthian, pyropum, wrought bronze, and Campanian. Cyprian bronze <note>original: "æs cyprium"; this is the origin of the word "copper"</note> was first discovered on the island of Cyprus, from which it takes its name. It is produced from a weathered stone which they call calamine <note>original: "cadmiam"; likely a zinc-bearing ore used to produce brass</note>, and it is ductile <term>ductile: capable of being shaped or hammered thin without breaking</term>; if lead is added to this, it takes on a purple color. Corinthian bronze is a mixture of the sort that was famously made at Corinth. The "coronary" type, however, is drawn out from ductile bronze into thin sheets; when coated with the gall of bulls, it provides the appearance of gold in the crowns of actors, which is also where it gets its name <note>original: "coronarium," from "corona," meaning crown</note>. Pyropum, however, was named for its fiery color. For when six scruples of gold are added to every ounce of bronze, it glows in thin sheets and mimics flames. Wrought bronze <note>original: "regulare"</note> is the name given to what others call "ductile," because it can be drawn out by the hammer, just as its opposite is "cast" bronze <term>fusile: metal that is melted and poured into a mold</term>, which is poured; this is also called "cauldron-bronze" <note>original: "caldarium"</note>, for it breaks under hammers. All bronze, however, becomes wrought bronze once the impurities have been more carefully purged and cooked away by fire. Campanian bronze, named after the Campania region of Italy, is most highly regarded for utensils and vessels. **Pliny, Book 34**. A vein of bronze is dug up and refined by fire; it is made from a bronze-bearing stone that they call calamine, and it is also made from another stone, which they call chalcites <note>original: "calcithen"</note> in Cyprus, where bronze was first discovered.

## On the operation of copper or bronze in alchemy; see what was said about bronze in the first book.

### On its power in medicine. Platearius. <note>Johannes Platearius was a physician from the famous medical school of Salerno in the 12th century; his work was a standard pharmaceutical reference.</note>

Bronze is prepared and burned by a certain artifice so that it can be pulverized. "Red bronze"—specifically that which was crafted by smiths long ago—is placed in an earthenware pot and kept for a long time in a furnace where there is a continuous fire; afterwards, it is ground into powder. Through this excessive roasting <note>original: "excoctione"</note>, the "earthy" parts of the metal increase while the "watery" parts decrease.

Therefore, burnt bronze <note>original: "æs vstum"</note> of this kind is hot and dry in the fourth degree <term>fourth degree: the most intense classification in Galenic medicine, indicating a substance that can cause significant changes to the body’s balance</term>. It has the power to consume the melancholic humor <note>original: "melancholicum humorem"; one of the four bodily fluids, associated with black bile and the earth element</note>, as well as to purge and thin the humors; for this reason, it is suitably used in plasters applied against ailments of the spleen. It corrodes "superfluous flesh" <note>likely referring to warts, polyps, or granulated tissue in a wound</note>. Against a fistula <term>fistula: an abnormal, tunnel-like passage in the body, often discharging fluid</term>, its powder is prepared with honey, and then applied by dipping a feather into the mixture.

**Rhazes in the *Almansor*.** <note>Rhazes (Razi) was a 9th-century Persian physician; the *Liber Almansoris* was one of the most influential medical texts of the Middle Ages.</note> Burnt bronze dyes the hair, heals <note>original: "consolidat"</note> wounds, and expels excess water from the body.

**Avicenna in the second book of the *Canon of Medicine*.** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a central figure in Islamic medicine; his *Canon* remained a standard textbook in Europe until the 17th century.</note> Bronze is hot and dry in the third degree; it heals and checks malignant, spreading ulcers and corrodes overgrown flesh. It sharpens the sight and is beneficial for hardness of the eyelids. It blackens the hair, and when smeared upon the palate, it induces vomiting. In burnt bronze, there is a quality of astringency <term>stipticitas: a drying or contracting effect, often used to stop bleeding</term>, sharpness, and healing power. Pliny, as cited above <note>original: "Plin. vbi supra"; referring to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 34, which is the primary source for this metallurgical data</note>. *Cadmia* <term>cadmia: a metallic deposit, often zinc oxide, that collects on the walls of smelting furnaces</term> without doubt is formed in silver furnaces; it is whiter and less heavy, but in no way comparable to that of the copper works. Thus, again, another type arises in the furnaces, which receives the origin of its name <note>referring to the processed byproduct rather than the raw ore</note>. It is formed from the thinnest part of the material, driven out by the flames and the blast, in the chambers or sides of the furnaces, at the mouth where the flames break out; it is called *capnitis* <term>capnitis: from the Greek word for "smoke" (kapnos), referring to a light, soot-like zinc oxide deposit found at the furnace opening</term>. It is thoroughly burnt and, due to its extreme lightness, is similar to ash. 

The best type, however, is that found inside, hanging from the chambers, and for this reason is nicknamed *botryitis* <note>original: "botrifentos"; a corruption of the Greek *botryitis*, meaning "grape-like," describing the clustered, bulbous shape of the mineral deposits</note>. This is heavier than the former but lighter than those that follow. It has two colors: the gray is inferior, while the reddish-purple is better; it is brittle and most useful for eye medicines. 

The third type is found on the sides of the furnaces; because of its weight, it could not reach the upper chambers, and this is called *placitis* <term>placitis: a crust-like deposit of zinc oxide, named after the Greek word for a "plate" or "tablet" because of its flat shape</term>. This is more like a crust than pumice on the inside; it is quite useful for various types of *psora* <term>psora: a historical term for itchy or scaly skin diseases, including scabies and psoriasis</term> and for removing scars. 

From this, two other types flow: *onychitis* <term>onychitis: a variety of furnace residue resembling the markings of an onyx stone</term>, which is almost blue on the outside and similar to onyx spots on the inside; and *ostracitis* <term>ostracitis: a dark, shell-like deposit</term>, which is entirely black and the dirtiest of them all, yet extremely useful for wounds. ...loosens the stiffness of the eyelids. **Zemarum** <term>Zemarum: likely a Latinization of a Persian or Arabic term for verdigris (copper acetate), a green pigment used for its caustic and healing properties</term>, that is, hot "copper green," eats away excess flesh; it is "incisive" <note>meaning it has a sharp, penetrating or caustic quality</note> if it is mixed with wax and olive oil. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), the Roman author of the *Natural History*</note>, as cited above: The **flower of copper** <term>flos aeris: the fine metallic dust or oxide that forms on the surface of molten copper as it is poured</term> is also a useful medicine. It is made when copper is melted and moved to another furnace. There, by frequent blowing of air, flakes like millet seeds are shaken off, which they call **lepidas** <note>original: "lepidas," from the Greek word for scales</note>. The "flower" is sometimes adulterated so that the "scale" is sold in its place. There is also a **copper scale** <note>original: "squama aeris"</note> struck off by the force of hammers when copper cakes are forged together. All this happens mostly in the workshops of Cyprus <note>Cyprus was the most famous source of copper in antiquity; the word "copper" (cuprum) is derived from the island's name</note>. The difference is this: the scale is shaken off by those same hammer strikes, but the "flower" falls off the copper cakes spontaneously. There is another, finer type of scale struck from the very surface "down" <note>referring to the fine, fuzzy oxidation on the surface of the metal</note>, which they call **stomoma** <term>stomoma: the finest, purest particles of metallic scale, often used in ancient eye salves</term>.

Both the scale and the flower are burnt in clay or copper pans, then (as described above) they are washed for the same medical uses. Furthermore, it removes fleshy defects of the nostrils and "heaviness" of the seat <note>likely referring to rectal pressure or hemorrhoids</note> and the ears when blown into them through tubes. When applied as a powder, it removes swellings of the uvula <note>original: "vuas," literally "grapes," describing the shape of a swollen uvula</note> and other mouth ulcers, and it treats the tonsils when mixed with honey. However, the scale made from "white Cyprian copper" is far less effective.

Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), whose encyclopedic *Etymologies* was a standard reference in the Middle Ages</note>, as cited above: The flower of copper is produced during smelting when the copper is melted and liquefied; when cold water is poured over it, the "flower" is separated from the liquid by a sudden thickening.

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037 AD), the Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the primary medical text in Europe for centuries</note>, as cited above: The flower of copper is styptic <term>styptic: an astringent substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</term>, corrosive, and stinging.

...they sprinkle it with vinegar and turn it with spatulas several times a day until the copper is consumed <note>original: "absumatur"; meaning the metal has fully reacted to become verdigris</note>. Others, however, prefer to grind these same filings with vinegar in bronze mortars. **Crown-copper** <note>original: "coronarium"; a high-quality copper alloy used for making crowns or jewelry</note> produces verdigris most rapidly when its clippings are added to vinegar. 

Rhodian verdigris is frequently adulterated with crushed marble. Others use pumice or gum, but the most deceptive adulteration is with **shoemaker's black** <term>shoemaker's black: "atramentum sutorium," typically ferrous sulfate or green vitriol, used for dyeing leather</term>. A test for purity is performed with an iron rod: pure verdigris retains its own color, while that mixed with shoemaker's black turns red. It is also detected using papyrus previously soaked in **gall-nut** <term>gall-nut: "galla," an oak growth rich in tannin used to make ink; it turns black when reacting with iron salts</term>; it turns black immediately when smeared with adulterated verdigris. It can also be identified by sight by a sickly green color. 

But whether it is pure or adulterated, once dried, it is best to burn and stir it in a new pan until it becomes ash; afterward, it is ground and stored away. Some also mix in **male frankincense** <note>original: "thus masculum"; high-quality, tear-shaped frankincense resins</note>. Verdigris is washed in the same manner as **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: a zinc-rich mineral or furnace deposit used in ancient medicine</term>. 

Its power is highly suitable for **eye-salves** <term>eye-salves: "collirijs," medicated preparations for the eyes</term>, and it is beneficial for watery eyes by its biting action. However, it must be washed away with warm sponges until it stops stinging. Raw verdigris is mixed into wound plasters; it also wonderfully heals ulcerations of the mouth and gums, and ulcers of the lips <note>original: "laborum"; likely a scribal error for "labiorum" (of the lips)</note> when mixed with oil. If wax is also added, it cleanses the wound and leads to the formation of a scar. Verdigris also eats away the callosity of fistulas and ailments around the seat <note>original: "sedem"; the anus or rectal area</note>, whether applied by itself or with **ammoniacum** <term>ammoniacum: either a medicinal gum resin or a salt (sal ammoniac) depending on the preparation</term>, smeared on, or in the manner of an eye-salve...

...[it is] pushed into medicinal tubes <note>original: "fistulas"; small tubes used to store or apply ointments</note>. There is also another kind of rust <term>rust: "rubigo," referring here to copper corrosion products like verdigris</term> found in Cyprian copper, which they call **scolecia** <note>original: "scolecia"; from the Greek word for "worm"</note>. This is prepared by grinding it with alum, salt, or nitre <term>nitre: "nitrum," likely sodium carbonate or natron, used as a cleaning agent and flux</term> in equal weight, together with the sharpest possible white vinegar. This cannot be made except during the most sweltering days around the rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, the Dog Star, rises in late July, marking the hottest part of the summer</note>. It is ground until it becomes rotten or green, and it takes on the appearance of little worms, from which it gets its name. To correct any defect in it, two parts of a young boy’s urine are mixed in for every part of vinegar used. 

It produces the same effect in medicines as *santerna* <term>santerna: a gold-solder or fluxing agent used in metalworking</term>, which we previously mentioned is used to solder gold; both are used in the same way as verdigris <note>original: "erugo"</note>. **Scolecia** is also produced naturally by scraping it from the copper-bearing stone called **chalcites** <term>chalcites: a copper-bearing mineral, likely copper pyrites or a sulfate-rich ore</term>, about which it now remains to write.

### On Chalcites.

Indeed, the stone is called **chalcites**, from which copper itself is smelted. It differs from **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: a zinc-rich mineral or furnace deposit used in ancient medicine and brass-making</term> because the latter is harvested from surface rocks in subsidial pits <note>original: "subsidialibus petris"; referring to open-cast or shallow mining</note>, whereas this [chalcites] is taken from deep underground. 

Furthermore, chalcites crumbles immediately when rubbed because of its soft nature, so that it looks like congealed down <note>original: "lanugo concreta"; describing a soft, fibrous, or fuzzy texture</note>. There is also another distinction, namely that chalcites contains three kinds of copper: [the stone itself], *misy*, and *sory* <note>original: "miseos & soreos"; these are related sulfate minerals (yellow and green/black vitriol) described in later sections</note>, about which we will speak below. It has oblong veins of copper; the best quality is proven by a honey color with a fine distribution of veins, and it is crumbly rather than stony. They also think...

Egyptian **sory** is most highly praised, greatly surpassing that from Cyprus, Spain, and Africa, although some think Cyprian sory more useful for treating the eyes. But in any nation, the best is that which has the strongest scent, and which turns fatty black when ground, and is spongy. It is so offensive to the stomach that for some, the mere smell provokes vomiting. Egyptian sory is of this kind. The sory of other nations shines when ground.

It is burned on coals just like **chalcitis**. 

However, some have handed down to me that it is made from stone burnt in pits, its yellow flower mixing with the ash of pine wood. Furthermore, misy is truly made from the aforementioned stone, naturally congealed and separate...

Its properties are styptic <note>original: "stiptica"; causing the contraction of body tissues to stop bleeding</note>, thermantic <note>original: "termantica"; warming or heat-producing</note>, and escharotic <note>original: "scarotica"; caustic or capable of producing a scab/eschar</note>, cleansing the eyelids and eyes. -># BOOK II.<-

**Chalcantum** <term>chalcantum: blue vitriol or copper sulfate, characterized by its vibrant blue crystals</term> is so named because it is the "flower" of chalcitis <note>original: "calcithis est tynnu i. flos"; the scribe uses a corrupted Greek-derived term "tynnu" to mean "flower" or "bloom"</note>, which is why it is called the "flower of copper" among the Latins. Formerly, in the wells or ponds of Spain that contained this type of water, they would boil it down and pour it into wooden basins. They hung ropes over these, weighted with small stones, to which the sediment would adhere in the likeness of glassy grapes; once removed, it was dried for thirty days. 

It is also produced now in other places, such as in caves, where it is collected in liquid form and then spread out to solidify into certain clusters <note>original: "botros"; referring to a botryoidal or grape-like crystal formation</note>. It is also formed in hollowed-out pits, where the drops falling from the sides coalesce. It is even made in the manner of salt by the heat of a blazing sun. 

It possesses such a powerful constricting quality that if it is sprinkled into the mouths of lions and bears, it has so much astringent force that they are unable to bite. 

**Dioscorides** <note>a Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work "De Materia Medica" was the primary source for pharmacology for 1,500 years</note> [says]: There are three species of **chalcantum**. One is that which drips from metal-working shops or certain drains and is thickened and thus collected. Another is found in caves; once collected, it is poured into vessels and there it coagulates. The third type, made in Spain, is weak and discolored. 

It is prepared by being mixed with water and boiled. The finest quality is of a deep blue <term>cyanei: a rich, dark blue color, similar to lapis lazuli</term> color, heavy, dense, shining, pure, and clear. When cooked <note>roasted or calcined</note>, it is useful for blackening and for the dyeing of materials.

In these same workshops, what the Greeks call **diphryges** <term>diphryges: literally "twice-roasted," a residue or slag from the smelting process</term> is distinguished, so named because it is twice-scorched. Its origin is found to be threefold. It is also produced in Cyprus from the mud of a certain cave, which is first dried and then gradually surrounded by burning brushwood. Thirdly, it is produced in copper furnaces from the dregs that settle at the bottom. The difference is that the copper itself flows into the crucible, the slag <term>scoria: the refuse or dross left after smelting metal</term> remains outside the furnaces, the "flower" floats on top, and the **diphryges** remains behind. Some report that balls of stone are cooked in the furnaces to be fused together, and the copper boils around them. This material is not fully cooked until it is moved to other furnaces. It is a certain "knot" of matter; that which remains after the cooking process is called **diphryges**. Its function in medicine is similar to the substances mentioned above: to dry, to consume growths, and to cleanse. It is tested by the tongue; it should dry the tongue immediately upon contact and return a taste of copper. 

They call **antispodium** <term>antispodium: a medicinal substitute for metallic ash, typically made from the ashes of specific plants</term> the ash of the fig tree, or the wild fig, or of myrtle leaves together with the most tender parts of the branches, or of the wild olive, or the quince, or the mastic tree. ### On Orichalcum, according to Isidore.

For "The Philosopher" <note>Aristotle; though the work cited here is likely an alchemical text falsely attributed to him</note> says in the book *On Light*: "The light that is produced from a boy’s urine and orichalcum becomes the finest gold." ### On Iron, from Isidore, Book Sixteen.

Iron <note>original: "Ferrum"</note> is so named because it stores grain <note>original: "farra," meaning seeds or crops; Isidore suggests a folk etymology that iron is named for the tools used to harvest grain</note>. ...though the prize goes to Parthian iron <note>original: "palma Parthico"; the Parthians were renowned for their high-quality steel used in heavy cavalry armor and weaponry</note>. Nor are other kinds of iron tempered from a pure cutting edge. For in others, a softer mixture is blended in. There are many differences in types of iron according to the nature of the earth. For one type is soft and close to lead, suitable for use in wheels and nails. Another is brittle and pitted, convenient for tilling the soil. Another is favored for its small size alone, and for boot-nails <note>original: "clauis caligarijs"; the iron hobnails used in Roman military footwear, the caligae</note>. Another suffers from rust more quickly. 

There is a very great difference in the waters in which white-hot iron is plunged. This water, being more effective in some places than others, has brought fame to certain locations for the excellence of the iron produced there—as at Bilbilis <note>a city in Roman Spain, modern-day Calatayud, famous for its cold-water tempering</note> and Turiaso in Spain, and Como in Italy. In sharpening iron, the edge becomes finer when using oil; for this reason, it is the custom to quench <note>original: "restingui"; the process of rapidly cooling metal to harden it</note> thinner items in oil, so they are not hardened into brittleness by water. 

Human blood takes its revenge upon iron, for once touched by it, the metal draws rust more quickly <note>a folkloric explanation for the oxidation of weapons used in combat</note>. The lodestone <note>original: "magnes lapis"</note> has a natural harmony with iron; for this material alone receives force from this stone and retains it for a long time. Using this same stone, a certain architect in Alexandria vaulted a temple so that an iron statue within it would appear to hang in the air <note>this legend refers to the architect Dinochares and his plan to suspend a statue of Queen Arsinoe using magnetic attraction</note>. Unless heated iron is hardened, it is ruined by hammer blows. It is not suitable for turning on a lathe when it is red-hot, nor until it begins to turn white. Iron smeared with vinegar or alum becomes similar to bronze.

The same author <note>likely referring to Aristotle in *Meteorology*, Book 4</note> says in his fourth book: Certain things can be softened by fire, such as iron and horn. Thus, iron becomes soft and malleable. They say that when it is liquefied by heat, it is solidified again when cooled. That iron is considered better which requires less purging.

### Again on the Nature of Iron, Pliny, Book Thirty-Four.

Next, the ores of iron must be described—the best and the worst instrument of life. For with this we cleave the earth, plant orchards, and lay out fruit gardens; by pruning away withered growth, we force the vines to grow young again each year. With this we build houses, cut stones, and employ iron for all manner of uses. But we also use the same material for war, slaughter, and robbery, not only in close combat but also as a flying missile—sometimes launched from siege engines <term>tormentis; mechanical devices like catapults or ballistae used for hurling projectiles</term>, sometimes by the strength of the arms, and sometimes even winged. I consider this the most wicked deception of the human mind. For so that death might reach man more swiftly, we have made it fly and have added feathers to iron <note>a reference to the fletching of arrows, which Pliny views as a perversion of nature's tools</note>. Finally, in the treaty which the Roman people [made] after the expulsion of the kings...

...gave Porsenna <note>Referring to Lars Porsenna, the Etruscan king. And iron ores are found almost everywhere. Indeed, the Italian island of Elba <note>original: Ilua</note> produces it, and it is recognized without difficulty by the manifest color of the earth, though the method for smelting the veins remains the same. In Cappadocia, there is a question whether the metal is a gift of the water or the earth, because when a certain earth is drenched by a flooding river, it yields iron from the furnaces in no other way.

The varieties of iron are numerous; the first distinction depends on the type of earth or the climate. In some places, the vein itself provides the quality, as among the Noricans <note>The Norici inhabited a Celtic kingdom in modern-day Austria; "Noric steel" was world-renowned in antiquity.</note>. In other places, it is the workmanship, as at Sulmo <note>A town in Italy famous in Pliny's time for its ironworks.</note>. In others, it is the water. For indeed, just as oil-stones and water-stones differ when used for sharpening, a finer edge is produced with oil. It is a marvel that when the vein is smelted, the iron is liquefied like water, and afterwards it is broken into sponges <term>spongias; porous, bloom-like masses of iron that have been smelted but not yet forged</term>. Of all metals, the vein of iron is the most abundant. In the coastal part of Cantabria <note>northern Spain</note>, where the ocean flows, there is a steeply high mountain—incredible to say—that consists entirely of this material.

From the book *On the Natures of Things* <note>Likely referring to the 13th-century encyclopedia by Thomas of Cantimpré, a standard reference in the Middle Ages.</note>. Iron is of a cold nature, hard, solid, and sharp; it masters all things by its strength, and is consumed only by itself <note>A reference to iron's tendency to be destroyed by its own rust.</note>. Above all metals, it contracts corruption <note>rust</note> more easily, and even infects things connected to it with that corruption. It has a hoarse sound, grows soft in fire, and becomes ductile.

### ON ALCHEMY

Steel <note>original: "Calybs"; this term for steel is derived from the Chalybes, an ancient people of Asia Minor famed for metallurgical skill.</note> is a type of very hard iron, which is commonly called *aciarium* <note>A medieval Latin term for steel, ancestor to the French "acier" and Italian "acciaio."</note>. Iron is indeed more earthy than steel, and therefore drier. Steel, compared to iron, abounds in a congealed aqueous substance. However, steel is more brittle than iron, just as ice is more brittle than horn <note>The transcription reads "cor-," likely "cornu" (horn).</note>.

Iron has a double moisture: one that is earthy and coarse, causing scaly impurities <note>original: "scabiositates"; referring to the dross, scale, or rust that forms on the metal's surface.</note>, and this evaporates through the action of fire. The other is a subtler aqueous moisture, and this remains, becoming more purified and condensed by the heat. The opposite happens in the double moisture of wine and many other things. 

Furthermore, because iron is dry, it is also porous. While it is in such a state, it is not suitable for making a sharp-pointed cutting instrument. Therefore, it is thoroughly "cooked" <term>excoquitur; the process of smelting or refining through intense heat</term> in the fire so that, once its earthy roughness is wiped away, the aqueous substance is left behind. This substance is extremely dense and, since it is ductile like water, it is suited for cutting and for every shape. Iron is hardened <note>original: "Desatur"; likely a contraction of "densatur" (is thickened/hardened).</note> and its porosity is filled up through the admixture of steel, and thus it becomes more suitable for cutting instruments. 

If steel is hollowed out, and lead is placed in its cavity, and the whole thing is placed in the fire, the lead will evaporate, but not without leaving the steel somewhat softened. From this, if the process were repeated enough times by adding more lead, the steel would eventually lose its great hardness and thus be loosened...

### On the difference between Iron and steel, from the book
### *On Vapors*.

Iron lacks "vapors." For in iron, there is no evaporation caused by the action of fire; rather, when heat acts upon the iron, its earthy scaly quality <note>original: "squamositas terrestris"; the dross or impurities found in raw iron.</note> prevents the moisture from evaporating, and the steel remains behind as something more aqueous <note>In medieval science, "aqueous" or "watery" referred to the elemental quality that gave metals their shine and flexibility, while "earthy" made them dull and brittle.</note>. And because this earthiness, through its dryness, creates porosity, iron will be more porous than steel. Therefore, the smith, in the edge of a knife, mixes steel with the iron so that through the steel in the edge, the pores of the iron are blocked <note>original: "opilatio"; a sealing or closing of the microscopic gaps.</note>, and it becomes good for cutting. For the heaviness and coarse earthiness of iron prevent a knife from being drawn out to the thinness suitable for cutting. And since that which is aqueous is ductile into every shape, steel—because it is more aqueous—is used for the edge of the knife. If, however, it is asked why...

...steel <note>original: "calybs"</note> might be more breakable than iron, even though the opposite would seem to follow if it were more "watery" than iron. I say that just as ice is more breakable than horn—due to the earthiness <term>terrestritas; in medieval science, the element of "Earth" provided solidity and binding, while "Water" provided fluidity or brittle coldness</term> of the horn, which tends toward a viscosity that resists breaking—so too the earthiness in iron is more viscous, making the iron less breakable. Furthermore, just as an earthy moisture remains when the liquid evaporates from wine, so when the moisture is consumed by heat (which binds the earthy and scaly parts of the iron with the watery and coagulated parts), the steel remains in a watery and "frozen" substance. It possesses tighter pores than iron, and because of this, it lacks flexibility when dry, whereas iron and copper possess a greater width of pores.

And then, because steel is more "watery," it happens that one watery substance can be worn away or altered by another. It happens that when steel is treated with lead through the action of heat (as was said above), the lead evaporates; yet, during that evaporation, the steel remains somewhat softened. This can be done so many times that the steel loses all its hardness and may receive impressions in the manner of wax, because of the moisture it has received from the lead, which acts to re-soften hardness. This can be seen similarly in those with paralysis, where the hardness of a nerve is relaxed without any "filling" <term>repletio; a medical term referring to an excess of bodily fluids or humors</term> by the moisture

### On the operation of iron in Alchemy. *The Philosopher.* <note>original: "Philosophus"; in medieval texts, this usually refers to Aristotle, though in alchemy it may refer to a specific authority like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</note>

Iron is mixed with gold. It is never removed from it, neither by boiling <note>likely referring to smelting or decoction</note> nor by any other means. And when it is joined to silver while standing with gold, it tints it with a beautiful color, and it appears just like gold. The nature of iron is hot and dry. Certain people, however, have said that it is cold and dry, and both masculine and feminine. Of this metal, the manifest <term>manifestum; the outward, observable physical properties of a substance</term> is hot, dry, and hard. Its hidden <term>occultum; the internal, potential qualities that can be revealed through alchemical transformation</term> nature, however, is the opposite of these. Nor is there anything in any of the "bodies" <note>original: "corporum"; referring to the seven metallic bodies of alchemy: gold, silver, iron, mercury, tin, copper, and lead</note> harder than its manifest part. Similarly, its softness is revealed when it is converted into its hidden state. 

An example of this is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver" or mercury</note>, whose hidden part is iron, and whose manifest part is quicksilver. Therefore, when its manifest part is hidden, and its hidden part is revealed, it is converted into iron. Or if you wish, diminish its heat, and its coldness will appear, and it becomes silver. Or diminish its dryness, and its moisture will appear, and it becomes gold. One should see the other operations concerning it, which we spoke of in the first book regarding iron.

# BOOK II. 109

...of the spleen and liver, it is given over a long period of time. 

The very fine powder of iron rust <term>ferrugo; the reddish-brown oxide formed on iron by moisture</term> taken with warm wine provokes vomiting in great quantities. Indeed, it does so to such an extent that it may lead to death; for this reason, after the onset—or during the onset—water should be given in which a loadstone <term>lapis magnes; a naturally magnetized mineral, believed in antiquity to have powers over iron-based substances</term> has soaked for an entire night. Also, the powder of the loadstone itself may be given in water, for it restrains the violence of the rust and stops the vomiting. This is according to the testimony of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note>. Nevertheless, vomiting in that situation is dangerous. 

Against hemorrhoids, a powder of this rust—namely of iron rust or fine iron scale—is prepared with the juice of great mullein <term>tapsi barbati; the plant *Verbascum thapsus*, used for its soothing properties</term> and applied using a soaked piece of cotton <note>original: "bombice"</note>. 

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 970–1037), the influential Persian physician and author of *The Canon of Medicine*</note> says in his second canon: Iron dross <term>scoria ferri; the stony waste matter separated from metals during the smelting or refining of ore</term> has a stronger drying effect than all other substances. In itself, it has the power to dissolve water. It is, moreover, dry in the third degree <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a substance's primary qualities; the third degree indicates a very potent effect</note>. The dross of copper is similar to it, while other types of dross are less so; yet all of them dry out excess humors. 

Iron dross dissolves abscesses <term>apostemata; inflammatory swellings or cysts</term>, helps with the roughness of the eyelids, and strengthens the stomach when given mixed with aged wine; it removes the stomach's moisture and sluggishness. It prevents pregnancy, stops the flow of hemorrhoids and menstrual blood, and, when smeared on the anus, it constricts it. 

The same author says in Book 4: From iron filings and iron dross, there sometimes occurs a vehement pain in the belly, as well as dryness in the mouth, bloating, and a severe headache. The cure for this is to give milk to drink with oil of roses and violets, and to apply the juice of crushed willow leaves <note>original: "salicibus"</note> with vinegar upon the head.

### On Tin. Isidore.

The etymology of tin <note>original: "stanni ethimologia"</note> is "separating" and "dividing" <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD) incorrectly linked the Latin word *stannum* (tin) to the idea of separating metals</note>. For through fire it dissociates mixed and adulterated metals from one another; it separates lead from gold, silver, and bronze. It also protects other metals from the fire. And although the nature of bronze and iron is very hard, if they are without tin, they are scorched and consumed by fire. Tin coated onto bronze vessels makes the flavor more pleasant and restrains the poison of verdigris <term>eruginis; the green film or "rust" that forms on copper or bronze, often considered toxic</term>. Mirrors are also tempered from it. Ceruse <term>cerussa; white lead, a pigment and medicinal substance</term> is also made from it, just as it is from lead.

Pliny says in book 34 <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), whose *Naturalis Historia* was the primary Roman encyclopedia of science</note>: Tin is used to solder bronze items together, and silver is soldered with tin. In former times, the best Brundisian mirrors <note>Brundisium (modern Brindisi, Italy) was a famous center for the manufacture of bronze mirrors</note> were made from a mixture of tin and bronze, though silver mirrors are now preferred over them. The same author says as above: Black lead <term>plumbum nigrum; the standard Roman term for lead</term> is sometimes found with silver and produced from mixed veins. The first liquid that flows in the furnaces is called tin <note>original: "stannum"</note>, and the second is silver. Now, however, tin is adulterated by adding a third portion of "white bronze" to white lead <term>plumbum album; Pliny's term for tin, distinguishing it from 'black lead'</term>. It is also made in another way, by mixing pounds of white lead and black lead. And some now call this "silver-mixture" <note>original: "argentarium"</note>. These same people also call it "tertiary" <note>original: "tertiarium"</note>, in which...

...two portions are of black <note>original: "nigri"; referring to *plumbum nigrum* or lead</note>, and the third is of white <note>original: "albi"; referring to *plumbum album* or tin</note>; its price is estimated at 30 pounds, and with this, pipes are soldered. More dishonest makers, by adding equal parts of white to the third part, call it "silvery" <note>original: "argentarium"; an alloy used for plating</note>, and with it they coat whatever they want at their own price. Of this, they make 130 pounds weight. For pure white [tin] by itself, the price is 30. For black [lead], it is 17. Aristotle, in the 4th book of *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica* was a foundational text for medieval science</note>, proves that tin is "watery" as previously stated, since it is melted by heat. And it appears that tin contains good quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, but poor sulfur. These are not well mixed, but rather joined together as if by small particles. And that is why it becomes such a metal. From the book *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "Ex libro de natura rerum"; likely referring to the 13th-century encyclopedia by Thomas of Cantimpré</note>: Tin is of a very tempered nature. In former times, they were only accustomed to find it in Britain, but now in parts of Germany, a very abundant vein has been discovered. It is very ductile and manageable, and melts more easily than all other metals. By itself it is also "mute" <note>it does not ring when struck</note>, but mixed with bronze, silver, or gold, it is resonant and harmonious. It shines on the inside, but on the outside it easily contracts corruption; this is a matter of tarnish <term>squaloris; a dulling or fouling of the surface</term> and not rust, for it never rusts. When lying in water for a long time, it easily decays. For this reason, human skill has devised that water supply pipes, which used to be made of lead and soldered with tin under the ground, should in modern times be joined with hot and molten lead; this is because pipes joined with tin could not last for a long time, whereas lead always lasts when buried underground.

### *Regarding the operation of tin in Alchemy, from Averroes on vapors.*

Lead is the binding agent <term>consolidativum; a substance used to solder or join metals together</term> of tin, and tin that of lead. The fact that lead is solidified by tin is not due to the nature of lead itself, but rather the nature of molten tin, which penetrates the "moist" molten lead. Through this penetration, a viscous moisture is generated between the two, which binds the parts of the tin. However, regarding tin binding with tin—since both resist the viscosity that must arise from a specific balance of moisture and dryness—there is no such binding of tin with itself. Borax, however, when it solidifies silver with silver, or tin with tin, makes this possible only because it shares a common "root" or elemental essence with them, as will be discussed below. From the books *On the Nature of Things* <note>likely referring to the 13th-century encyclopedia *De natura rerum* by Thomas of Cantimpré</note>: From tin is made an excellent salt with which they make "sharp water" <term>aquam acutam; a corrosive acid or solvent used in alchemical processes</term>, and with it they dye <note>original: "tingut" (tingunt); to color or chemically transform the surface</note> quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>. Once tin has been melted and then infused with vinegar in which quicksilver is present—since it is highly penetrative, and with the vinegar aiding even further—it enters all parts of the tin and softens the dryness of the tin with moisture, as was stated above regarding this matter.

Lead <term>Plumbum; in ancient texts, this term covered both lead and tin</term> is so named because it was from this material that [sounding] lines <note>original: "lis," likely a contraction of "lineis"</note> were first made, by which the depth of the sea was tested. There are two kinds of this metal: black and white <note>original: "nigrum & candidum"; white lead usually refers to tin in this context</note>. But the white kind is better, which was first found in the islands of the Atlantic Ocean. It is produced similarly in **Lusitania** <note>the Roman province covering most of modern Portugal</note> and in **Gaul**, extracted from a sandy earth of black color and heavy weight. Small pebbles are also found, mostly from dried-up torrents. The miners wash these sands, and that which settles, they cook in furnaces. Black and heavy pebbles are also found in gold mines when water is let in. And while the gold is being collected, these remain with it. Afterward, they are separated and smelted, and are resolved from a powder into a white metal. From this, lead has the same density <note>original: "grauitas"; weight or heaviness</note> as gold. Black lead abounds around **Cantabria** <note>a region in northern Spain</note>. Its origin is twofold: for it either emerges alone from its own vein, or it is born with silver and smelted from a mixed vein. Of this mixture, the first liquid to melt in the furnaces is tin <term>stannum</term>, the second is silver, and that which remains in the furnace <insert>after the silver is separated</insert> and smelted again becomes black lead. **India** has neither bronze nor lead; it trades only in gems and pearls. We use black lead for pipes and for sheets <note>original: "fistulas lamique"</note>. Lead is extracted with great labor in **Spain** and **Gaul**; however, in **Britain**, it is found in the very surface of the earth <note>original: "sum terrae corio"; literally "the skin of the earth"</note>. From the fourth book of the *Meteorologica* <note>referring to the work by Aristotle</note>: Lead is likewise melted so that it flows, and when flowing, it is frozen again by cold; it is black in color and similar to...

# ON ALCHEMY

A white kind of lead exists, which is most precious and called *cassiterion* <note>original: *cassiterium*; the Greek term for tin</note> by the Greeks. It has been falsely told that it is sought from the Atlantic islands and carried in cheap ships made of stitched hides. But now it is certain that it is produced in Lusitania <note>ancient Portugal</note> and Galicia <note>northwest Spain</note> in the upper layer of the earth; it is found in sandy soil and as black stones, which are detected only by their weight. It is also found in gold mines in what is called *alutia* <term>alutia: a term for alluvial gold deposits or the soil washed to find them</term>. Indeed, when water is poured in to wash away the black pebbles, they show a slight variation in whiteness and possess the same weight as gold. And therefore, they remain in the basins <note>original: *lathis*; likely referring to sluices or troughs</note> in which the gold is collected; they are later separated in the furnaces and, once melted, they are resolved into white lead <note>tin</note>. Black lead is not produced in Galicia, even though it is so abundant in the neighboring region of Cantabria. Silver is not produced from the white kind, whereas it is produced from the black.

The origin of black lead is twofold, as stated above. The nature of the white has more of the "dry" quality, while the nature of the black is entirely "moist" <note>referring to the four qualities of Aristotelian elements: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. Therefore, white lead is of no use on its own without a mixture. Nor can silver be refined from it, because the silver melts sooner. They confirm that if even a small amount of black lead is mixed with the white, the silver is eroded by it. White lead is fused onto copper-works by a Gallic invention, so that it can hardly be distinguished from silver. The test of good lead is on paper, so that when melted it is seen to break the paper by its weight rather than by burning it with heat. Black lead cannot be joined to itself, nor to the white kind, without oil. But neither can the white...

### *On the operation of lead in Alchemy, from*
### *Book 4 of the Meteorology.* <note>Meteorologica: A work by Aristotle (though Book 4 is often considered to be by a later follower) that discusses the formation of minerals and metals from "exhalations" within the earth.</note>

The mercury <term>mercury: referred to here as "argentum vivum" (living silver), believed by alchemists to be a primary constituent of all metals</term> of thick lead is bad, heavy, and yellowish. Its sulfur is also [impure] and of a foul, stinking taste and weak, so that it does not freeze <note>In this context, "freeze" refers to solidification from a molten state or the stabilizing of the metal's internal spirit.</note>. And craftsmen perform an artificial solidification that is almost perceptible. But let the craftsmen know that the species of nature cannot be changed; they can only make things similar to them, and wipe away the impurities of lead. Nevertheless, it is always lead, even if it appears to be silver; for in that state, foreign qualities prevail, leading men into error. Concerning the rest, see above in Book 1.

### *On the various ways of pulverizing lead.*

Just as it is possible to extract moisture or watery humor <note>original: "humorositatem." In the Aristotelian tradition, "humors" or "moistures" were the fluid elements within a substance that gave it flexibility or liquidity.</note> from wine, or even to extract the moisture that binds the parts of a stone together, it is likewise possible to extract the moisture from lead, and then a powder of lead will remain. This is how the makers of jars <note>original: "ollarum artifices," referring to potters or ceramicists who used lead in their glazes.</note> do it: placing melted lead in a pot, they stir it with ash and a small piece of tile <note>original: "testula," a fragment of earthenware.</note> until it is pulverized. For the dryness of the ash and the moisture of the tile, as they depart through the heat, cause the dryness and moisture of the lead to contract; then the lead remains pulverized and spread out.

Others also say that lead is pulverized, when it has been melted in furnaces, by means of a fresh hazel branch <note>original: "virgam coryli." The hazel tree was often associated with specific physical and even magical properties in medieval metallurgy and dowsing.</note> placed into the lead. For while the branch stirs the lead, the moisture of the branch is drawn out by the heat of the furnace, and the branch itself attracts the moisture of the lead to itself in place of its own extracted moisture; and then the lead remains dry, disconnected, and separated. There is also another way of reducing it to powder...

Saracen <note>A medieval term used broadly for Arab or Muslim peoples, who were highly regarded for their advanced metallurgical and alchemical skills.</note> craftsmen use this clever trick to transport their gold from land to land under the guise of leaden earth. Similarly, there is an evaporation of lead, as we see in the refining <term>depuratione: the process of purifying a metal by removing dross or impurities.</term> of silver. The sign of health is if the matter is dissolved and urine is provoked; ultimately, the patient requires laxatives.

BOOK II.

## On White Lead, Pliny in the thirty-fourth book.

White lead <term>cerussa: basic lead carbonate, historically used as a white pigment and cosmetic</term> is produced in lead workshops. The most highly praised variety is from Rhodes <note>original: "Rhodus," an island in the Aegean Sea famous for its metallurgical traditions</note>. It is made by placing very thin shavings of lead over a vessel of the sharpest vinegar, so that they drip. Whatever falls from the shavings into the vinegar is dried, then softened and sifted. After being mixed with vinegar again, it is divided into small tablets and dried in the summer sun.

It is also made in another way: by putting lead into jars of vinegar and keeping them sealed for ten days. Then, the corrosion <note>original: "situ," literally "neglect" or "mold," referring to the lead carbonate crust</note> is scraped off and the lead is put back until the material is exhausted. What was scraped off is ground, sifted, and cooked in shallow pans; it is stirred with small sticks <note>original: "rudiculis"</note> until it turns reddish and looks like sandarac <term>sandaraca: a reddish-orange mineral, either red lead (minium) or arsenic sulfide</term>. Then it is washed with fresh water until all the "clouds" <note>referring to floating impurities or milky suspensions</note> are washed away; it is subsequently dried in the same way and divided into tablets.

Its power <note>referring to its medicinal or chemical potency</note> is the same as the substances mentioned above, yet it is the lightest of all of them, except when it is used for the whitening of women's complexions <note>white lead was a popular but highly toxic face powder in the ancient and early modern worlds</note>. However, it is a lethal drink, just like silver foam <term>spuma argenti: also known as litharge, a lead oxide formed during the refining of silver</term>. If white lead itself is cooked, it turns reddish.

Isidore in book 19. White lead is made from lead in this way: In a vessel filled with the sharpest vinegar, Aminean twigs <note>original: "sarmenta aminea," referring to a specific high-quality variety of grapevine used as a scaffold</note> are placed in the same small vessel, and very thin lead sheets are placed over the twigs. Then the vessel is most carefully closed and sealed with clay so that no vapor <note>original: "spiraminis," literally "breath" or "breathing hole"</note> can escape. After thirty days, the vessel is opened, and from the dripping...

white lead is found having formed on the plates. When this is removed and dried, it is ground up, mixed again with vinegar, divided into small cakes, and dried in the sun. By this same method, if you place copper plates over vine-cuttings, it creates the green rust known as *chalcantum* <term>chalcantum: literally "copper-flower," used here to refer to verdigris or copper acetate</term>.

Platearius <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno, author of the influential herbal "Circa Instans"</note>, as cited above: White lead is the "flower of lead," and it is cold and dry in the second degree <note>Referring to the Galenic system of medicine where substances were classified by their "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>. Those who manufacture it often suffer from apoplexy, epilepsy, paralysis, and arthritis, because of the dissolving and deadening coldness of the vinegar <note>This is an early observation of lead poisoning (plumbism), though here attributed to the "coldness" of the vinegar rather than the toxicity of the lead itself</note>.

However, white lead has the power of cleansing and wiping away "superfluities" <note>In medieval medicine, this referred to excess humors or skin blemishes</note>. Hence some women, after washing their faces, apply the finest powder of white lead over them. Others, however, because white lead is somewhat dry, prepare it in rose water and expose it to the sun, especially in summer; when the water is evaporated, they add more, and they do this until it is extremely white and somewhat aromatic. Afterward, they form it into small pills and apply it to the face.

**Note** that those who use applications of white lead for a long time suffer from toothache, decay, and foulness of the breath <note>Further symptoms of chronic lead exposure</note>.

Haly <note>Likely Haly Abbas, a Persian physician known for the "Complete Art of Medicine"</note>, as cited above: The *hespidagi* <note>original: "Hespidagi," a Latinized version of the Persian word for white lead, "ispedag"</note> of lead, which is white lead, is better when heavy, very white, smooth, and soft. It is cold and dry; when applied as a poultice, it dries out ulcers. BOOK II.

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in the West as Avicenna, whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries</note> states in the second book of the *Canon*: White lead <term>cerussa: basic lead carbonate, used historically as a pigment and skin treatment despite its toxicity</term> is the "ash of lead." It is used in plasters; it fills up ulcers, helps new flesh grow within them, and eats away "bad" flesh <note>Referring to "proud flesh" or granulating tissue that prevents healing</note>. It is beneficial for *bothor* <term>bothor: a term derived from Arabic meaning pustules, pimples, or small skin eruptions</term> of the eye, and it softens "cold" and hard abscesses <note>In Galenic medicine, a "cold" abscess was one thought to be caused by phlegm or black bile rather than "hot" blood or yellow bile</note>. White lead is produced sometimes with vinegar and sometimes with salts. That which is made with vinegar has a more powerful refining quality. It is also among the medicines suitable for treating fissures of the anus. Finally, it is also categorized as a poison.

### *On Antimony, according to Avicenna, as cited above.*

Antimony <note>Usually referring to stibnite (antimony sulfide), used since antiquity as a medicine and as *kohl* for eye makeup</note> is the "afterbirth" of dead lead <note>original: "secundina plumbi mortui" — a metaphorical alchemical term suggesting antimony is a byproduct or a related mineral "membrane" of lead</note>, and its potency is similar to that of burnt lead. The best variety is flaky, and its broken pieces have a bright shine. It should have no foreign material mixed in, it should not be dirty, and it breaks very easily. It is cold in the first degree and dry in the second <note>Referring to the substance's qualities in the humoral system</note>. Antimony has a more powerful drying effect than red vitriol <term>atramentum rubeum: literally "red ink," usually referring to calcined copperas or iron sulfate used as a drying agent</term>. 

It constricts and dries without stinging, and it stops the flow of blood. It is also suitable for ulcers; it destroys extra growth of flesh and consolidates the wound. It is also applied with fat over burns so that the area does not ulcerate. Furthermore, it prevents nosebleeds that originate from the membranes of the brain <note>The meninges; medieval doctors believed certain fluids or "vapors" could flow from the brain to the nose</note>. It preserves the health of the eye and removes filth from eye sores. It also helps with the flow of blood...

### On certain mixed metals, electrum and Corinthian bronze, according to Isidore.

Electrum is so called because, in the rays of the sun, it reflects more brightly than gold or silver. For the sun is called *Electrum* <note>original: "Electrum," derived from the Greek *elektor*, meaning the beaming sun</note>, and this metal is more refined <term>defecatius: purified or cleared of dross</term> than all other metals. There are three kinds of this substance: one which flows from the pine tree and is called *succinum* <term>succinum: amber, the fossilized resin</term>. Another is a metal that is found naturally and is held in high value. The third is that which is made from three parts gold and one part silver. Even if you break down the natural variety into its parts, you will find these same proportions; thus, it makes no difference whether it is born naturally or made by hand, for both are of the same nature. Natural electrum is of such a character that at a banquet and by the light of lamps, it shines more brilliantly than all other metals, and it reveals poison. For if you pour poison into it, it emits a hissing sound and gives off various colors like a rainbow in the sky.

From the book *On the Nature of Things* <note>Likely referring to the medieval encyclopedia *De natura rerum* by Thomas of Cantimpré or a similar compilation</note>: Electrum is twofold: artificial, which is composed of a mixture of gold and silver; and natural, which is similar in color but superior in its power. However, it is found very rarely, and it is distinguished from "sophisticated" <note>original: "sophisticatum," meaning imitation or adulterated gold</note> gold with great difficulty. But a vessel made of true and natural electrum reveals poison. If poison is poured into it—

[Ar]tificers <note>The original text "tifices" is a clipped form of *artifices*.</note> of alchemy use borax <note>A mineral salt used as a flux to help metals melt and join.</note> in the multiplication <term>multiplicatio: an alchemical process intended to increase the quantity or the "perfection" of a metal</term> of their metal. For there is one thing hidden and another thing manifest in bronze <term>æs: a general term for copper or its alloys, like bronze or brass</term>. When they wish to transubstantiate bronze into silver, they do not labor toward the goal of changing the actual substance of the bronze, but only toward removing from it the color which was concealing the substance of silver. 

Since the "moist" quality is ductile in every direction—according to Aristotle <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher's *On Generation and Corruption*, which argues that fluids (the moist) take the shape of their container.</note>—the moist will be poorly defined by its own boundary, but easily defined by the boundary of another. Therefore, a sinew is stretchable lengthwise, like a leather strap, and this is due to the moisture within it which is ductile in every direction. I mean moisture mixed with a fine earthiness, which creates a viscosity <note>In medieval physics, "viscosity" refers to the quality of being "sticky" or cohesive enough to be stretched without breaking.</note> capable of being spread out, just as we see in soft things. 

This is why makers of silver, wishing to work it into long shapes, add copper to it. By mixing dry copper with moist silver, a viscous state is generated, which is the starting point for spreading the silver in length or width. Silver is indeed a substance that is very moist and congealed; therefore, if it were worked by itself during fabrication, it would develop cracks, just as we see in ice. For when ice is struck, it breaks, and is spread neither in length nor in width. Indeed, in every congealed thing, cracking occurs upon striking. And when silver is extracted, a certain redness appears, which comes from a small amount of copper. But if there were a great amount of cop-

[co]pper <note>The text begins with the end of the word 'cuprum' (copper) from the previous page.</note>, there appeared a blackness of color, hiding the substance of silver. And take note that just as moisture softens, so also dryness causes wrinkling. Thus, since copper is both hot and dry more than it is watery, metal-workers judge that when silver has been refined <term>decoctio: literally "boiling down," used here for smelting or refining through heat</term>, it possesses wrinkling, and so it is not left pure by the refining process. 

And this is evident. For when the surface of silver is flat, yet there is a crack in the middle, I say that this crack existing at the bottom is due only to the dryness of the copper, along with the roughness of that same copper from which the silver has not been purified; hence, it is then a sign that the silver is not pure. 

Sometimes, however, quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> removes the brittleness arising from dryness, as is evident in tin, just as was said above. We see, moreover, in the purification of silver, that the mixed lead exhales <note>original: "exhalare"; refers to the lead vaporizing or being oxidized and drawn away during the process of cupellation</note> through the motion of the heat; lead is added for this purification. Not because the lead itself purifies the silver, but because the heat attaches itself to the lead as if by consuming it—heat which would otherwise consume the substance of the silver itself. And meanwhile, the silver is purified by the heat, which causes the copper to pass to one side and the silver to the other by its own warmth. Whence Aristotle says that "the hot is that which separates heterogeneous things" <note>A foundational principle in Aristotelian physics: heat separates unlike substances (heterogeneous) and joins like substances (homogeneous).</note>.

# ON ALCHEMY.

Some believe that salt <term>sal: the Latin word for salt, here linked by the author to the verb "salire," meaning to leap or jump</term> is named for the way it "leaps" in the fire; for it flees from the flame, even though it possesses a fiery nature. It follows this behavior because fire and water are always enemies to one another. Others believe salt is named for the sea <note>original: "salo," referring to the salt sea or brine</note> or for the sun <note>original: "sole"</note>. For it is produced spontaneously from sea waters, from the foam left behind on distant shores or rocks, which is then "cooked" by the sun. 

There are also lakes, rivers, and wells from which it is drawn; from there, it is cast into salt-pans and dried by the sun. Indeed, even the surfaces of certain rivers thicken into salt, while the rest of the stream continues to flow beneath the ice. In other places, it is gathered by clearing away sand, and it grows in accordance with the phases of the Moon. For example, ammoniac salt <term>hammoniacus: originally referring to salt found near the Oracle of Amun in Libya, though later used for ammonium chloride</term> is found beneath the sands in Cyrenaica <note>A region in modern-day Libya</note>. 

British salts are also transformed from water into the solidity of flint, so that they must be cut with iron tools; they are as white as snow, healthy for the body, and pleasant in food and drink. There are also mountains of "native" salt <note>rock salt found in its natural state</note> where it is quarried with iron like stone; it grows back even larger after being harvested. In some places, it is of such great hardness that people build walls and houses from blocks of salt, as they do in Arabia. 

In the nature of salt, there are also many differences: in one place it is mild, in another extremely salty, though most commonly it crackles in the fire. Salt from Tragasae <note>An ancient salt-producing site in the Troad, modern Turkey</note> neither crackles nor leaps in the fire. The salt from Agrigento <note>original: "Agrigentinum," a city in Sicily</note> flows in the fire like a liquid, which is contrary to its usual nature. 

There are also differences in color: salt from Memphis <note>In Egypt</note> is reddish, and in a certain part of Sicily where Mount Etna stands, it is purple. Likewise, at Cape Pachino <note>The southeastern tip of Sicily</note> in that same Sicily, the salt is so splendid and clear that it reflects images like a mirror. In Cappadocia <note>A region in modern Turkey</note>, it is saffron-colored. <meta>The catchword "nus ef." is a partial transcription of the final word "crocinus est" (is saffron-colored), which concludes the page.</meta>

Indeed, the nature of salt is necessary for all food; for it gives flavor to things, excites a zest <note>original: "auditatem," likely a misspelling of "aviditatem" (greed/hunger) or "aciditatem" (sharpness)</note> for them, and creates an appetite for meals. Salt exists in four modes. That which is made in a salt-pan is the common kind. There is also gem salt <term>sal gemma: rock salt, so named for its crystalline clarity, resembling a gemstone</term>. There is also Indian salt, the color of which tends toward blackness, though it is clear and hard. There is yet another called Naphthic salt, which is water coagulated from the flow of petroleum <note>original: "petreolo"</note>. However, every kind of salt is hot and dry, though not in equal measure. Ammoniac salt <term>sal Hammoniacum: used in alchemy and medicine, often referring to ammonium chloride</term> is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>A reference to Galenic medicine, where the "fourth degree" is the most intense level of a quality</note>, and it acts upon other salts; nitre <term>nitrum: can refer to saltpeter or natron</term> acts similarly. Gem salt gently purges phlegm and is even more useful than common salt. Similarly, Indian salt purges phlegm and black bile <note>original: "cholera nigra," one of the four humors associated with melancholy</note>.

...and [cleanses] various putrid humors. Naphthic salt <note>original: "Napticum"</note> is hotter and drier than the others; it cleanses and scatters them. Sal Ammoniac <term>sal hammoniacum: ammonia salt, historically named after the Oracle of Ammon in Libya where it was found in the sand</term> strains and cleanses, and acts more upon internal parts than external ones. Pliny, Book 31 <note>This refers to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 31, Chapter 39, a primary source for ancient mineralogy</note>: Salt was found between Egypt and Arabia, even in squalid places after the sands were cleared away, and through the thirsty regions of Africa as far as the Oracle of Ammon. Indeed, among these, the salt grows during moonlit nights. For the tracts of Cyrenaica are also made famous by ammoniac salt, so called because it is found beneath the sands. It is similar in color to alum, which they call *schiston* <note>original: "schiston," meaning "split" or "cleft" stone</note>, appearing in long clods that are not transparent. It has an unpleasant taste, but is useful for medicine. It is judged best when it is very clear and marked by straight fissures. It is said of this salt that it is lightest while inside its caves, but when brought out into the full light, it grows heavy with a weight that is scarcely believable; the cause is that the moist spirit <note>original: "spiritu madido," referring to the ancient belief that subterranean vapors influenced the weight and growth of minerals</note> of the tunnels assists it, just as waters assist those laboring to extract it. It is, however, adulterated <note>meaning faked or diluted</note> with Sicilian salt, and also with Cypriot salt, which is remarkably similar. In Hither Spain <note>Citerior Hispania, the northeastern part of the Roman province</note> also, it is cut from a "frozen" state <note>original: "è gelaste," referring to a specific translucent formation mentioned by Pliny</note> in clods that are nearly translucent. To this salt, the prize among all kinds of salt has for a long time been given by many physicians. Isaac <note>Isaac Israelietus, also known as Isaac Judaeus, a prominent 10th-century physician whose works were translated into Latin and became standard medical texts</note>. Salt exists in two modes: namely, metallic <note>original: "metallicum," referring to rock salt or mined salt</note> and marine. Marine salt is made in pools, which they call salt-pans, or from seawater cooked by summer heat. Metallic salt is most praiseworthy when it is free from stones and is clear, dull, and uniform.

### *On Ink and its origin, according to Pliny as cited above.* <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose "Natural History" was the primary source for Roman scientific knowledge.</note>

## Ink among the artificial colors

Although it may also be of a twofold origin from the earth. For it is either made by human art, or from sulfurous earth itself. Painters have even been found who would dig up stained coals <note>original: "carbones"; likely charcoal or charred remains.</note> from tombs. It is made in many ways, by burning resin or pitch; because of this, they even built workshops that do not let their smoke escape. The most praised kind is made in the same way from the soot of torches; it is [sometimes] adulterated with the soot of furnaces, which they use for writing books. There are some who also boil dried wine dregs. And if the dregs were from good wine, they claim it provides the appearance of Indian ink <note>original: "Indici"; referring to "India ink," which was highly valued for its deep black color.</note>. Among dyers <term>Infectores</term> <note>Artisans who dyed cloth or leather.</note>, it is also made from the black "flower" <note>A term for the fine powdery residue or oxidation.</note> that sticks to bronze cauldrons; it is also made from burnt torch-wood and coals ground in a mortar. Truly, the nature of cuttlefish <note>original: "sepiarum"; cuttlefish or squid ink was known in antiquity, though Pliny notes here it wasn't used for traditional painting.</note> is also wonderful in this regard, but painters' ink is not made from them. All ink, however, is perfected by the sun; ink for books and for plastering is mixed with glue, but that which has been liquefied with vinegar is washed away with difficulty.

### *On its application in Alchemy, from Book 4 of the Meteorology.* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s "Meteorologica," a foundational text on the formation of minerals and weather phenomena.</note>

Vitriols <note>original: "Atramenta"; while the word commonly means "inks," in alchemical and medieval scientific contexts it refers to metallic sulfates (vitriols) used to make ink and dyes.</note> are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones. There is also in them the power of certain liquifiable bodies, for they are formed from them; for example, copper-green <note>original: "calchantum"</note> and *abachar* <note>An alchemical term, likely referring to a mineral residue or a specific processed lead/tin salt.</note> are generated from larger grains of vitriol. Its instability <note>original: "falsedo," literally "falseness," referring to the presence of impurities or its chemically reactive state.</note> is not resolved except by the sulfur that is within it, after which the remainder solidifies. That remainder has already taken on mineral power in certain bodies. That which has taken on the power of iron will be red or saffron-colored, or *calathar* <note>A variant of "colcothar," which is the red oxide of iron left after the distillation of vitriol.</note>. That which has the power of copper will be green like blue vitriol <note>original: "chalcantum," specifically copper sulfate.</note>; therefore, it is possible for those two to be created artificially. See something more on this also above in the first book.

### *On its power in medicine, according to Avicenna in the Canon.* <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.</note>

Vitriol is of various colors. There is a difference between white, red, yellow, and green vitriols. *Colchatar* <note>Yellow vitriol or iron sulfate.</note> is yellow, *chalcadis* <note>White vitriol or zinc sulfate.</note> is white, *chalcantum* <note>Green or blue vitriol.</note> is green, and *assuriae* <note>A term for red vitriol, possibly related to "Syrian" vitriol.</note> is red. All of these are dissolved in water and by boiling, except for the red variety <note>original: "assure"</note>, which is of extreme solidity and density; the green is also more strongly solidified than the yellow, and has more substantial layers <note>original: "tunicas," literally "tunics" or "coverings," referring to the crystalline structure.</note>.
