Unburnt vitriol <note>original: "Atramentum"; here referring to the raw mineral metallic sulfates.</note> is stronger, while burnt <note>original: "adustum"; referring to the process of calcination or heating the mineral to change its properties.</note> vitriol is more subtle. And the more subtle among these are chalcitis <note>original: "chalchadis"; a copper-bearing mineral related to blue vitriol.</note> and green vitriol. Colcothar <note>original: "colchatar"; the red iron oxide residue left after heating vitriol.</note>, however, is moderate in its effect. "Sory" vitriol <note>original: "assuriæ"; a mineral substance often described as a variety of vitriol from Syria or Egypt.</note> is coarser; for this reason, it does not dissolve in water. The power of the vitriol in which there are golden glimmers is close to the power of colcothar; that which breaks easily is better, being of a pure copper-like nature and not old. The vitriol which is put into ink is that which is called *sahira* <note>An Arabic-derived term used in medieval translations of Avicenna to denote a specific mineral ink or vitriol.</note>. And the hard kind, possessing a sort of golden luster, is as potent as colcothar. The best of the Sory vitriol, however, is that which is brought from Egypt; it breaks away from blackness and possesses many veins of an acidic taste. It is styptic <note>original: "stipticum"; a substance that shrinks or constricts body tissue to stop bleeding.</note> and its odor is similar to its taste.

Vitriol is hot and dry in the third degree. All types are caustic and styptic; they are beneficial for moist scabs <note>original: "scabiei"; a general term for itchy or crusty skin diseases.</note>, as well as for the hardness of the eyelids and their roughness, or for abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"; inflammatory swellings or collections of pus.</note> of the groin. Yet there is in vitriol a poisonous quality that dries the lungs, so much so that it might perhaps kill. It is blown into the nostrils to stop the flow of blood, especially colcothar, from which medicinal wicks <note>original: "licinia"; small pieces of lint or fabric used to keep a wound open or to apply medicine.</note> are also made and placed in fistulas <note>Abnormal passages or tunnels in the body caused by injury or infection.</note> to root out "windiness" <note>original: "ventositatem"; in medieval medicine, this refers to trapped gases or "vapors" within the tissues.</note>. The wick also helps ulcers of the ear and its discharge, and it prevents the decay of the teeth.

Glass is cooked with light and dry wood, with the addition of copper <note>original: "cypro"; likely copper minerals used for coloring or as an alloy</note> and nitre <note>original: "nitro"; in this period, this refers to natron or soda ash used as a flux to lower the melting point of silica</note>, and in continuous furnaces it is liquefied like bronze and formed into masses. Afterwards, it is melted again from these masses in workshops; some of it is shaped by blowing <note>original: "flatu"; the technique of glassblowing</note>, some is smoothed on a lathe, and some is engraved in the manner of silver. It is also tinted in many ways, so that it surpasses the colors of hyacinths <note>original: "iacynthos"; a blue or violet gemstone</note>, green sapphires, and onyxes, or the colors of other gems. Nor is there any other material more suitable for mirrors or better adapted for painting. Glass is made from earth, herbs, stone, and plants; it is also made from the ashes of hay and fern, and likewise from boiled egg whites. From the *Book of Vapors* <note>A reference to a specific medieval or ancient scientific text on the properties of matter</note>: Glass is also sometimes made from lead and fine earth, without the ash of fern or hay. For lead is sometimes evaporating and sometimes "conviscating" <term>conviscans: a medieval term meaning to become sticky or to bind substances together</term>. Thus, when mixed with fine earth, it binds those parts of the earth and partially dissolves them through the action of heat; and when the powder is mixed with fine earth, it receives dryness from the earth. And also from the color that makes the liquefaction unifiable <note>original: "unibilem"; meaning the components merge into a single substance</note> in both, or a universal admixture. Because of this, those who wish to cook meat quickly place a piece of glass in the water with the meat; for since glass is dry, it extracts so much moisture from the meat through its boiling that the meat is immediately left fully cooked. <note>This reflects a historical belief that the "dryness" of glass could draw out excess moisture or intensify heat to tenderize meat.</note> Such meat is cooked even faster if glass is added that is made from the ash of hay and fern, because such glass is less abundant in moisture... <meta>Catchword: "in hu." (likely "in humiditate" / in moisture)</meta>

...in moisture. For the first kind of glass has a certain amount of moisture, which it received from the lead that was primary in its composition. ### On its Operation in Alchemy, from the *Book on the Natures of Things*.

Glass is said to be from the "division of Mercury" <note>original: "ex sectione Mercurij"; an alchemical concept suggesting glass shares the transformative or liquid-to-solid properties of quicksilver</note>, though I know not for what reason, unless it is because it receives tinting and color; it even dissolves iron itself, and it dissolves all bodies and causes them to flow away. Just as water, which is cold by nature, is heated by fire, and after it is cooled, becomes extremely cold; so too the ash from which glass is made, though it is dry, if it is moistened through liquefaction and then dried, it will be extremely dry. For the rest concerning this operation, see what has been said above.

...indeed, [certain things] are crafted either by art or by mixing. The florid colors are those provided by the art of crafting, such as <term>minium</term> <note>red lead or cinnabar</note>, <term>armenum</term> <note>Armenian blue, likely azurite</note>, cinnabar, <term>chrysocolla</term> <note>literally "gold-glue," a green copper mineral like malachite</note>, and <term>Indian purpurissum</term> <note>a high-quality purple-red pigment</note>. The naturally occurring colors are <term>sinopis</term> <note>red earth from Sinope</note>, <term>rubrica</term> <note>red ochre</note>, <term>parethonium</term> <note>a white volcanic clay</note>, <term>melinum</term> <note>white earth from the island of Melos</note>, <term>eretria</term> <note>Eretrian earth</note>, and <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum," a bright yellow arsenic sulfide</note>. There are also two new and very cheap colors: the green which is also called <term>apianum</term> <note>meaning "celery green," derived from "apium" (celery)</note>, and another which imitates washed chrysocolla. It is made from green chalk valued at [a few] <term>sesterces</term> <note>Roman coins</note> per pound. <term>Annulare</term> <note>Ring-white</note>, which is called a white pigment, is that with which women's portraits are highlighted. It is itself made from chalk mixed with glass gems and the rings of the common people, which is why it is called "annulare." 

Of all these colors, there are some that dislike chalk and refuse to be applied to wet plaster <note>referring to the fresco technique, where pigments must be alkaline-resistant</note>: Indian purpurissum, cerulean, Melian white, orpiment, and celery green. White lead is tinted with these same colors using wax for those paintings which use a medium foreign to walls but familiar to fleets and merchant ships <note>This refers to encaustic painting, where pigments are mixed with hot wax, often used to waterproof and decorate ships</note>. With such a great variety of colors, one must marvel at antiquity. For the ancients painted even dangers and funeral pyres. And it pleased those about to fight unto death or slaughter to be carried in such splendor.

### On Sinopis and Red Ochre, according to Isidore

<term>Sinopis</term> <note>a red earth pigment, original: "Sinopis"</note> was first discovered in Pontus, and from there it took its name from the city of Sinope. There are three kinds of it: namely, the red, the less red, and a middle variety between these. Pliny, as cited above: Sinopis is named after the city of Sinope. It is found in Egypt, the Balearic Islands, and Africa. However, the best is dug up in Lemnos and Cappadocia; that which is found in caves, having adhered to the rocks, is of excellent quality. On the outside of the lumps, the color appears spotted; the ancients used this pigment to achieve a high luster. Aside from its use in painting, it is also used in medicine for soothing plasters and <term>emollients</term> <note>original: "malagmatis," substances used to soften or soothe the skin</note>, whether in its dry or liquid composition. It is effective against ulcers located in moist areas, such as those in the mouth or the seat <note>referring to the rectum or anus</note>; it stops female discharges when the weight of a <term>denarius</term> <note>a Roman silver coin, used here as a unit of weight equal to about 3.4 grams</note> is drunk. It stops the bowels when administered as an injection. This same substance, when burnt, dries up the roughness of the eyes, especially when mixed with wine.

Isidore: <term>Red ochre</term> <note>original: "Rubrica"</note> is so called because its color is very close to red and to blood. This is produced in many places, but the best is found in Pontus, which is why it is also called "Pontic" earth. Pliny, as cited above: Some wished to rank red ochre second in authority, for they gave the palm <note>the prize of first place</note> to the earth from Lemnos. This is very close to <term>minium</term> <note>red lead or cinnabar</note> and was much celebrated in antiquity; on the island where it is found, it was never sold unless it was <gloss>sealed</gloss> <note>original: "fignata," a transcription error for "signata," referring to "Terra Sigillata" or sealed earth</note>. Therefore, they use this to underpaint or even to adulterate minium. It is used in medicine and is considered a remarkable substance. Indeed, it mitigates <term>eye inflammations</term> <note>original: "Epiphoras," watery or inflamed eyes</note> and

That which settles is washed a second time. There is a difference in the technique, however, because some produce <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "minium"</note> from the first washing, and that is more transparent; the best quality is what comes from the subsequent washing.

There is another kind found in almost all silver and lead mines, which is made by roasting stone mixed with the veins of ore, and not from that stone whose "abscess" <note>original: "vomica," a term for the pockets of liquid metal found within the ore</note> is called <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum," or mercury</note>. For that [first kind] is itself smelted into silver. But among other stones found at the same time, many "sterile" ones are also discovered, which turn red in the furnaces by color alone; once roasted, they are pounded into powder. 

A method of economy <note>referring to a way to save money on expensive pigments</note> shows that <term>cinnabar</term> [can be mixed] with <term>Siricum</term> <note>original: "Sirico," a cheaper red pigment made of red lead and ochre</note> for use on high ceilings. Another method [of saving] is used for painting in a way that is convenient for theft, by those who frequently wash out full brushes [into water]. For the pigment settles in the water and remains there for the thieves. The brightness of the pure [pigment] ought to be that of scarlet grain. The brilliance of the secondary kind on walls feels like a reflection <note>original: "imaginem fentit," perhaps referring to its metallic sheen</note>, although this is actually a certain rust of the metal. If the sand of its own vein is smelted in the cinnabar mines of the Saponenses <note>a people of the Roman province of Baetica in Spain</note> without silver, it is tested in the manner of gold: when the gold is glowing hot, the adulterated pigment turns black, but the pure pigment retains its color. I find it is also adulterated with lime, and in a similar...

Sandarac is also produced on the island of Topazos in the Red Sea; it has the color of <term>vermilion</term> <note>original: "cinabrij"</note> and the smell of sulfur. However, even <term>white lead</term> <note>original: "cerusa"</note>, if toasted in a furnace, makes sandarac, from which a flame-like color arises. But if it is toasted with an equal part of ruddle added, it produces <term>sandix</term> <note>A cheaper orange-red pigment made by mixing red lead and red earth.</note>. Avicenna, in the second book of the *Canon* <note>Referring to the "Canon of Medicine" by the Persian physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina), a foundational medical encyclopedia.</note>: Sandarac is hot and dry in the second degree. It is styptic and holds back the blood. Wrestlers use it so they may become nimble and strong, and not encounter difficulty in breathing. Likewise, it produces thinness, and its fumigation stops and dries out <term>fistulas</term> <note>Abnormal passages or sores in the body.</note>; the smoke prevents <term>catarrh</term> <note>original: "catarrhos"; excessive mucus or the common cold.</note>, best soothes the pain of teeth, restores the gums, prevents trembling of the heart and the flow of blood, and even cures "wet asthma" by its drying property. It is also beneficial when drunk by those with spleen issues, and is good for chronic diarrhea; its smoke is helpful for hemorrhoids.

Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary pharmacological text for centuries.</note>: Sandarac is born in the same places as <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic mineral often found in the same deposits as sandarac.</note>. One should choose that which is very red, easily ground, clean, having the color of <term>vermilion</term> <note>original: "cinabrij".</note> and the scent of sulfur; its power is similar to <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenico".</note>, which is of a caustic, <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>original: "diaphoreticæ"; sweat-inducing.</note>, and styptic power. ->*On Prasis and Chrysocolla, according to Isidore*<- <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD) was an influential archbishop and encyclopedist.</note>

**Prasis**—that is, green chalk—although it is found scattered in various lands, the best nonetheless comes from Cyrenaic Libya. **Chrysocolla** <note>From the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *kolla* (glue); ancient chrysocolla usually refers to malachite or other green copper minerals used as a solder for gold.</note> is so named for its leek-green color, because its vein is said to contain gold. This is also found in Armenia, but the most esteemed comes from Macedonia. For it is dug out of copper mines, the discovery of which also yields silver and indigo <note>original: "Indicum"; likely referring to a blue pigment found in association with these ores.</note>. For its vein has a natural fellowship with these, according to **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary source for medicinal substances for 1,500 years.</note>. Chrysocolla has a "prasinus" color, that is, a very deep green. The Armenian variety, however, is better. The second best is the Macedonian and the Cypriot. One should choose that which is pure, without stone or earth; its power is cutting and constricting. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> in his thirty-third book: Chrysocolla is a liquid that flows through a vein of gold, the liquid thickening during the winter frosts until it reaches the hardness of pumice. It has been found that the same substance is more highly praised when found in gold mines, and the next best in silver mines. It is also found in lead mines, though it is cheaper than that from the gold mines. However, in all these mines, an artificial version is produced which is much inferior to the natural kind, made by lightly channeling water into the vein throughout the whole winter until the month of June, and drying it in June and July. Its nature is such that it allows linen and wool to "drink" or absorb dyes. It is crushed in a mortar, then separated by a fine sieve—

...is prepared, then ground, and then more finely sifted. Whatever does not pass through is found remaining in the mortar, then it is ground again; the powder is always distributed into basins and soaked in vinegar so that all hardness is dissolved; it is pounded once more, then washed in shells and dried. Then it is dyed and colored with alum and the unique herb they call weld <note>original: "luteam"; the plant *Reseda luteola*, used for yellow dye</note> before it is purified. It matters how absorbent and receptive it is. For if it does not take the color, both *scytanum* and *turbistum* <note>These terms likely refer to specific organic mordants or chemical fixatives used by ancient dyers to help the mineral absorb the plant dye.</note> are added; thus they call the medicines that compel absorption. The most praised variety is found in Armenia. The second best is in Macedonia, and it is most abundant in Spain. There are also two types of it in Cyprus. It is of the highest recommendation that it renders a color as similar as possible to the hue of a joyfully greening cornfield. They think "lutea" <note>a yellowish-green pigment</note> is named after the "lutea" herb, which, when ground with blue <note>Latin: *caeruleum*; likely a copper-based blue pigment</note>, they apply as a substitute for chrysocolla—a very cheap and deceptive kind. They distinguish it into three types: the rough, the medium, and the fine-ground, which they call "herbaceous." For they underlay the sandy variety with black pigment <note>original: "atramento"</note> and Paraetonium white <note>original: "parethonio"; a white chalk-like pigment from the coast of Egypt</note> before they apply it, because it is by nature very greasy and very tenacious on account of its dark color. It is indeed sprinkled with black pigment lest the paleness of the chrysocolla should take on the brightness of the Paraetonium white.

# ON ALCHEMY

Goldworkers claim **chrysocolla** <note>original: "Chrisocollam"; literally "gold-glue," a term used for green copper minerals like malachite used in soldering</note> for themselves for the purpose of soldering gold; they say that all substances similarly named are used in a like manner. It is tempered with Cyprian **verdigris** <note>original: "ęrugine"; copper acetate or carbonate</note> and the urine of a pre-pubescent boy, with **nitre** <note>original: "nitro"; likely natron or soda, a mineral salt</note> added. It is ground using Cyprian copper in Cyprian mortars. They call this silver-colored variety **santerna** <note>a technical term for a specific gold-solder mixture</note>. It is a sign of quality if it becomes bright when the *santerna* is added. Conversely, if it is "eroded," it contracts and becomes dull, and the gold is soldered with difficulty. That glue is made by adding gold and **litharge** <note>original: "spuma argenti"; literally "silver froth," the lead oxide produced during silver refining</note> to the substances mentioned above, and grinding them together.

Its use is in medicine, combined with oil and wax for cleansing wounds. On its own and dry, it both dries and contracts; it is also given for **quinsy** <note>original: "angina"; an inflammation of the throat</note> or **shortness of breath** <note>original: "orthopnœaue"</note> to be mixed with honey, and it induces vomiting. It is also mixed into **eye-salves** <note>original: "colyrijs"</note> for scars on the eyes, and into green plasters for soothing pain and drawing out scars.

**Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary manual for medicine for 1,500 years</note> says: **Chrysocolla** should be chosen for medicinal use that is clean, without stones or earth. Its virtue is cleansing and astringent; it checks the flow of fluids in the gums, cleanses wounds, and does not allow **excessive tissue** <note>original: "carnes superfluas"; often called "proud flesh," which can hinder proper healing</note> to grow in wounds. It thins scars, provokes vomiting, and if taken alone it can be **fatal** <note>original: "homicidium facit"; literally "commits homicide," referring to its toxicity if ingested without a buffer</note>; it is mixed into eye-salves that produce tears.

## BOOK II.

**Blue** <note>original: "Cœruleum"; in this context, it refers to Egyptian Blue or azurite, a granular mineral pigment</note> is a sand, of which there are three varieties. In ancient times, the **Egyptian** was most highly approved. There is also the **Syrian**, which is very easily diluted, and when it is ground, it changes into four colors: whiter, darker, thicker, or thinner. Even now, the **Cyprian** variety is preferred over these. To these have been added the **Puteolan** <note>from Puteoli, modern Pozzuoli in Italy</note> and the **Spanish**, as sand has begun to be prepared in those places as well. However, all of it is dyed and cooked in its own herb <note>likely referring to a plant-based dye bath used to enhance the mineral’s color</note>, and it "drinks" the juice. The rest of the theory is the same as that for **chrysocolla** <note>the "gold-glue" discussed on the previous page</note>. 

From this blue is made what is called **loment** <note>original: "lomentum"; a lighter, more refined blue pigment</note>, which is perfected by washing and grinding; this is whiter and more precious than the standard blue. A test for pure blue is to place it on a coal to see if it burns; a common fraud is to use dried violets boiled in water, with the juice expressed through a linen cloth onto **Eretrian chalk** <note>a fine white earth from Eretria</note>, otherwise known as **Pherestrian**.

Its power in medicine is to cleanse ulcers. They add it to plasters and also to caustics. However, it is very difficult to grind. In healing, it bites gently, acts as an astringent, and expels ulcers; it is burned in earthenware vessels to make it useful.

The same author <note>Pliny the Elder</note> in his **thirty-fifth book** says: **Purpurissum** <note>original: "Purpuriſſum"; a high-quality purple lake pigment</note> is foremost among the remaining colors which we said are produced by man, because of its great price. It is dyed from **silver-chalk** <note>original: "creta argentaria"; a fine white clay used for polishing silver</note> together with purple dyes, and it absorbs that color faster than wool does. The **Puteolan** variety is more praised than the **Tyrian**, the **Gaetulian**, or the **Laconic**, from which the most precious purples come. The reason is that this particular type is most easily dyed.

### *On Cinnabar and Armenian Stone, according to Isidore*

**Cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note> is a powder of a red color. They say this is the **dragon’s blood** <note>a resin from certain trees, often confused in antiquity with the mineral cinnabar</note> created when a dragon entangles an elephant and is crushed under its weight. **Dioscorides** [says]: Many people think cinnabar is red lead, and others think it is dragon's blood, but they are mistaken. This is because **red lead** <note>original: "minium"</note> is prepared in **Spain** from a stone that is mixed with **silver-bearing sand** <note>original: "arenae argiritidi"; likely referring to litharge or silver-rich lead ores</note>. If it is roasted, it changes color. However, its odor in the mine suffocates humans. Therefore, those who work in the mines place bladders over their faces to protect their eyes <note>an early form of protective respirator to prevent lead/mercury poisoning</note>. 

**Cinnabar**, however, is produced in **Libya**; its color is blood-red, and for that reason, it is thought by many to be dragon’s blood. Its power is similar to that of **hematite stone** <note>original: "emathiti lapidi"; literally "blood-stone"</note>. Thus, it is a powerful astringent and therefore stops the flow of blood. It also helps with burns and pustules. It is added to wax salves and is usefully mixed into the preparations of **eye-salves** <note>original: "colyriorum"</note>. 

**Pliny**, as cited above: **Armenian stone** <note>often identified as azurite or a similar copper carbonate</note> is so called because **Armenia** sends it, and it is named after that place. This is prepared in the same manner as **chrysocolla** <note>the "gold-glue" or malachite-like mineral mentioned on previous pages</note>; the best variety is that which is most green,
